senses.d: A dagger; a poniard.
A large pistol formerly used.
q: The Spaniards discharged their dags, and hurt some.
A sort of pistol, called dag, was used about the same time as hand guns and harquebuts.

senses.d: The unbranched antler of a young deer.

Dag.etym: [Cf. F. dague, LL. daga, D. dagge (fr. French); all prob. fr. Celtic; Cf. Gael. dag a pistol, Armor. dag dagger, W. dager, dagr, Ir. daigear. Cf. Dagger.]

senses.d: A misty shower; dew.

Dag.etym: [Of Scand. origin; cf. Sw. dagg, Icel. dögg. √71. See Dew.]

senses.d: A loose end; a dangling shred.
q: Daglocks, clotted locks hanging in dags or jags at a sheep's tail.

Dag.etym: [OE. dagge (cf. Dagger); or cf. AS. dāg what is dangling.]

senses.d: To daggle or bemire.
To cut into jags or points; to slash; as, to dag a garment.

Dag.etym: [1, from Dag dew. 2, from Dag a loose end.]

senses.d: To be misty; to drizzle.
A short weapon used for stabbing. This is the general term: cf. Poniard, Stiletto, Bowie knife, Dirk, Misericorde, Anlace.
A mark of reference in the form of a dagger . It is the second in order when more than one reference occurs on a page; — called also obelisk.

Dagger.etym: [Cf. OE. daggen to pierce, F. daguer. See Dag a dagger.]

senses.d: To pierce with a dagger; to stab.
A timber placed diagonally in a ship's frame.
The national god of the Philistines, represented with the face and hands and upper part of a man, and the tail of a fish.
q: This day a solemn feast the people hold To Dagon, their sea idol.
They brought it into the house of Dagon.

Dagon.etym: [Heb. Dāgon, fr. dag a fish: cf. Gr. Δαγών.]

senses.d: A slip or piece.
Happening, or belonging to, each successive day; diurnal; as, daily labor; a daily bulletin.
q: Give us this day our daily bread.
Bunyan has told us . . . that in New England his dream was the daily subject of the conversation of thousands.
Man hath his daily work of body or mind Appointed, which declares his dignity, And the regard of Heaven on all his ways.
Half yet remains unsung, but narrower bound Within the visible diurnal sphere.

Daily.etym: [AS. dæglīc; dæg day + -līc like. See Day.]

senses.d: A publication which appears regularly every day; as, the morning dailies.
Every day; day by day; as, a thing happens daily.
Value; estimation; the gratification or pleasure taken in anything.
q: I ne told no deyntee of her love.

senses.d: That which is delicious or delicate; a delicacy.
q: That precious nectar may the taste renew Of Eden's dainties, by our parents lost.

senses.d: A term of fondness.
q: These delicacies I mean of taste, sight, smell, herbs, fruits, and flowers, Walks and the melody of birds.
furnished plenteously with bread, And dainties, remnants of the last regale.

Dainty.etym: [OE. deinie, dainte, deintie, deyntee, OF. deintié delicacy, orig., dignity, honor, fr. L. dignitas, fr. dignus worthy. See Deign, and cf. Dignity.]

senses.d: Rare; valuable; costly.
q: Full many a deynté horse had he in stable.

senses.d: Delicious to the palate; toothsome.
q: Dainty bits Make rich the ribs.

senses.d: Nice; delicate; elegant, in form, manner, or breeding; well-formed; neat; tender.
q: Those dainty limbs which nature lent For gentle usage and soft delicacy.
I would be the girdle. About her dainty, dainty waist.

senses.d: Requiring dainties. Hence: Overnice; hard to please; fastidious; squeamish; scrupulous; ceremonious.
q: Thew were a fine and dainty people.
And let us not be dainty of leave-taking, But shift away.
Ah ha, my mistresses! which of you all Will now deny to dance? She that makes dainty, She, I'll swear, hath corns.

senses.d: A low place between hills; a vale or valley.
q: Where mountaines rise, umbrageous dales descend.

senses.d: A trough or spout to carry off water, as from a pump.

Dale.etym: [AS. dæl; akin to LG., D., Sw., Dan., OS., & Goth. dal, Icel. dalr, OHG. tal, G. thal, and perh. to Gr. θόλοσ a rotunda, Skr. dhāra depth. Cf. Dell.]

senses.d: A female parent; — used of beasts, especially of quadrupeds; sometimes applied in contempt to a human mother.
q: Our sire and dam, now confined to horses, are a relic of this age (13th century) . . . .Dame is used of a hen; we now make a great difference between dame and dam.
The dam runs lowing up and down, Looking the way her harmless young one went.

senses.d: A king or crowned piece in the game of draughts.

Dam.etym: [OE. dame mistress, lady; also, mother, dam. See Dame.]

senses.d: A barrier to prevent the flow of a liquid; esp., a bank of earth, or wall of any kind, as of masonry or wood, built across a water course, to confine and keep back flowing water.
A firebrick wall, or a stone, which forms the front of the hearth of a blast furnace.

Dam.etym: [Akin to OLG., D., & Dan. dam, G. & Sw. damm, Icel. dammr, and AS. fordemman to stop up, Goth. Faúrdammjan.]

senses.d: To obstruct or restrain the flow of, by a dam; to confine by constructing a dam, as a stream of water; — generally used with in or up.
q: I'll have the current in this place dammed up.
A weight of earth that dams in the water.

senses.d: To shut up; to stop up; to close; to restrain.
q: The strait pass was dammed With dead men hurt behind, and cowards.

senses.d: Injury or harm to person, property, or reputation; an inflicted loss of value; detriment; hurt; mischief.
q: He that sendeth a message by the hand of a fool cutteth off the feet and drinketh damage.
Great errors and absurdities many commit for want of a friend to tell them of them, to the great damage both of their fame and fortune.

senses.d: The estimated reparation in money for detriment or injury sustained; a compensation, recompense, or satisfaction to one party, for a wrong or injury actually done to him by another.

Damage.syn: Mischief; injury; harm; hurt; detriment; evil; ill. See Mischief.
Damage.etym: [OF. damage, domage, F. dommage, fr. assumed LL. damnaticum, from L. damnum damage. See Damn.]

senses.d: To occasion damage to the soundness, goodness, or value of; to hurt; to injure; to impair.
q: He . . . came up to the English admiral and gave him a broadside, with which he killed many of his men and damaged the ship.

Damage.etym: [Cf. OF. damagier, domagier. See Damage, n.]

senses.d: To receive damage or harm; to be injured or impaired in soundness or value; as, some colors in cloth damage in sunlight.
Of or relating to Damascus.

Damascene.etym: [L. Damascenus of Damascus, fr. Damascus the city, Gr. Δαμασκόσ. See Damask, and cf. Damaskeen, Damaskin, Damson.]

senses.d: A kind of plum, now called damson. See Damson.
Same as Damask, or Damaskeen, v. t.
A city of Syria.
To condemn; to declare guilty; to doom; to adjudge to punishment; to sentence; to censure.
q: He shall not live; look, with a spot I damn him.

senses.d: To doom to punishment in the future world; to consign to perdition; to curse.
To condemn as bad or displeasing, by open expression, as by denuciation, hissing, hooting, etc.
q: You are not so arrant a critic as to damn them . . . without hearing.
Damn with faint praise, assent with civil leer, And without sneering teach the rest to sneer.

Damn.etym: [OE. damnen dampnen (with excrescent p), OF. damner, dampner, F. damner, fr. L. damnare, damnatum, to condemn, fr. damnum damage, a fine, penalty. Cf. Condemn, Damage.]

senses.d: To invoke damnation; to curse.
Liable to damnation; deserving, or for which one deserves, to be damned; of a damning nature.
q: A creature unprepared unmeet for death, And to transport him in the mind he is, Were damnable.

senses.d: Odious; pernicious; detestable.
q: Begin, murderer; . . . leave thy damnable faces.

Damnable.etym: [L. damnabilis, fr. damnare: cf. F. damnable. See Damn.]

senses.d: The state of being damned; condemnation; openly expressed disapprobation.
Condemnation to everlasting punishment in the future state, or the punishment itself.
q: How can ye escape the damnation of hell?
Wickedness is sin, and sin is damnation.

senses.d: A sin deserving of everlasting punishment.
q: The deep damnation of his taking-off.

Damnation.etym: [F. damnation, L. damnatio, fr. damnare. See Damn.]

senses.d: Sentenced to punishment in a future state; condemned; consigned to perdition.
Hateful; detestable; abominable.
q: But, O, what damned minutes tells he o'er Who doats, yet doubts, suspects, yet strongly loves.

senses.d: A young person, either male or female, of noble or gentle extraction; as, Damsel Pepin; Damsel Richard, Prince of Wales.
A young unmarried woman; a girl; a maiden.
q: With her train of damsels she was gone, In shady walks the scorching heat to shun.
Sometimes a troop of damsels glad, . . . Goes by to towered Camelot.

senses.d: An attachment to a millstone spindle for shaking the hopper.

Damsel.etym: [OE. damosel, damesel, damisel, damsel, fr. OF. damoisele, damisele, gentlewoman, F. demoiselle young lady; cf. OF. damoisel young nobleman, F. damoiseau; fr. LL. domicella, dominicella, fem., domicellus, dominicellus, masc., dim. fr. L. domina, dominus. See Dame, and cf. Demoiselle, Doncella.]

senses.d: A title of honor equivalent to master, or sir.
q: Old Dan Geoffry, in gently spright The pure wellhead of poetry did dwell.
What time Dan Abraham left the Chaldee land.

Dan.etym: [OE. dan, danz, OF. danz (prop. only nom.), dan, master, fr. L. dominus. See Dame.]

senses.d: A small truck or sledge used in coal mines.

To move with measured steps, or to a musical accompaniment; to go through, either alone or in company with others, with a regulated succession of movements, (commonly) to the sound of music; to trip or leap rhythmically.
q: Jack shall pipe and Gill shall dance.
Good shepherd, what fair swain is this Which dances with your daughter?

senses.d: To move nimbly or merrily; to express pleasure by motion; to caper; to frisk; to skip about.
q: Then, 'tis time to dance off.
More dances my rapt heart Than when I first my wedded mistress saw.
Shadows in the glassy waters dance.
Where rivulets dance their wayward round.

Dance.etym: [F. danser, fr. OHG. dansōn to draw; akin to dinsan to draw, Goth. apinsan, and prob. from the same root (meaning to stretch) as E. thin. See Thin.]

senses.d: To cause to dance, or move nimbly or merrily about, or up and down; to dandle.
q: To dance our ringlets to the whistling wind.
Thy grandsire loved thee well; Many a time he danced thee on his knee.
A man of his place, and so near our favor, To dance attendance on their lordships' pleasure.

senses.d: The leaping, tripping, or measured stepping of one who dances; an amusement, in which the movements of the persons are regulated by art, in figures and in accord with music.
A tune by which dancing is regulated, as the minuet, the waltz, the cotillon, etc.
q: Of remedies of love she knew parchance For of that art she couth the olde dance.

Dance.etym: [F. danse, of German origin. See Dance, v. i.]

senses.d: from Dance.
To move up and down on one's knee or in one's arms, in affectionate play, as an infant.
q: Ye shall be dandled . . . upon her knees.

senses.d: To treat with fondness, as if a child; to fondle; to toy with; to pet.
q: They have put me in a silk gown and gaudy fool's cap; I as ashamed to be dandled thus.
The book, thus dandled into popularity by bishops and good ladies, contained many pieces of nursery eloquence.

senses.d: To play with; to put off or delay by trifles; to wheedle.
q: Captains do so dandle their doings, and dally in the service, as it they would not have the enemy subdued.

Dandle.etym: [Cf. G. dändeln to trifly, dandle, OD. & Prov. G. danten, G. tand trifly, prattle; Scot. dandill, dander, to go about idly, to trifly.]

senses.d: To dash.
q: Till she, o'ercome with anguish, shame, and rage, Danged down to hell her loathsome carriage.

senses.d: Authority; jurisdiction; control.
q: In dangerhad he . . . the young girls.

senses.d: Power to harm; subjection or liability to penalty.
q: You stand within his danger, do you not?
Covetousness of gains hath brought in dangerof this statute.

senses.d: Exposure to injury, loss, pain, or other evil; peril; risk; insecurity.
Difficulty; sparingness.
Coyness; disdainful behavior.

Danger.etym: [OE. danger, daunger, power, arrogance, refusal, difficulty, fr. OF. dagier, dongier (with same meaning), F. danger danger, fr. an assumed LL. dominiarium power, authority, from L. dominium power, property. See Dungeon, Domain, Dame.]

senses.d: To endanger.
Attended or beset with danger; full of risk; perilous; hazardous; unsafe.
q: Our troops set forth to-morrow; stay with us; The ways are dangerous.
It is dangerous to assert a negative.

senses.d: Causing danger; ready to do harm or injury.
q: If they incline to think you dangerous To less than gods.

senses.d: In a condition of danger, as from illness; threatened with death.
Hard to suit; difficult to please.
q: My wages ben full strait, and eke full small; My lord to me is hard and dangerous.

senses.d: Reserved; not affable.

Dangerous.etym: [OE., haughty, difficult, dangerous, fr. OF. dangereus, F. dangereux. See Danger.]

senses.d: A Hebrew prophet distinguished for sagacity and ripeness of judgment in youth; hence, a sagacious and upright judge.
q: A Daniel come to judgment.

senses.d: A descendant of Dan; an Israelite of the tribe of Dan.
One of a secret association of Mormons, bound by an oath to obey the heads of the church in all things.
To have adequate or sufficient courage for any purpose; to be bold or venturesome; not to be afraid; to venture.
q: I dare do all that may become a man; Who dares do more is none.
Why then did not the ministers use their new law? Bacause they durst not, because they could not.
Who dared to sully her sweet love with suspicion.
The tie of party was stronger than the tie of blood, because a partisan was more ready to dare without asking why.
The pore dar plede (the poor man dare plead).
You know one dare not discover you.
The fellow dares not deceive me.
Here boldly spread thy hands, no venom'd weed Dares blister them, no slimy snail dare creep.

Dare.etym: [OE. I dar, dear, I dare, imp. dorste, durste, AS. ic dear I dare, imp. dorste. inf. durran; akin to OS. gidar, gidorsta, gidurran, OHG. tar, torsta, turran, Goth. gadar, gadaúrsta, Gr. θαρσει̑ν, θαρρει̑ν, to be bold, θαρσύσ bold, Skr. Dhrsh to be bold. √70.]

senses.d: To have courage for; to attempt courageously; to venture to do or to undertake.
q: What high concentration of steady feeling makes men dare every thing and do anything?
To wrest it from barbarism, to dare its solitudes.

senses.d: To challenge; to provoke; to defy.
q: Time, I dare thee to discover Such a youth and such a lover.

senses.d: The quality of daring; venturesomeness; boldness; dash.
q: It lends a luster . . . A large dare to our great enterprise.

senses.d: Defiance; challenge.
q: Childish, unworthy dares Are not enought to part our powers.
Sextus Pompeius Hath given the dare to Cæsar.

senses.d: To lurk; to lie hid.

Dare.etym: [OE. darien, to lie hidden, be timid.]

senses.d: To terrify; to daunt.
q: For I have done those follies, those mad mischiefs, Would dare a woman.

senses.d: A small fish; the dace.

Destitute, or partially destitute, of light; not receiving, reflecting, or radiating light; wholly or partially black, or of some deep shade of color; not light-colored; as, a dark room; a dark day; dark cloth; dark paint; a dark complexion.
q: O dark, dark, dark, amid the blaze of noon, Irrecoverably dark, total eclipse Without all hope of day!
In the dark and silent grave.

senses.d: Not clear to the understanding; not easily seen through; obscure; mysterious; hidden.
q: The dark problems of existence.
What may seem dark at the first, will afterward be found more plain.
What's your dark meaning, mouse, of this light word?

senses.d: Destitute of knowledge and culture; in moral or intellectual darkness; unrefined; ignorant.
q: The age wherein he lived was dark, but he Could not want light who taught the world to see.
The tenth century used to be reckoned by mediæval historians as the darkest part of this intellectual night.

senses.d: Evincing black or foul traits of character; vile; wicked; atrocious; as, a dark villain; a dark deed.
q: Left him at large to his own dark designs.

senses.d: Foreboding evil; gloomy; jealous; suspicious.
q: More dark and dark our woes.
A deep melancholy took possesion of him, and gave a dark tinge to all his views of human nature.
There is, in every true woman-s heart, a spark of heavenly fire, which beams and blazes in the dark hour of adversity.

senses.d: Deprived of sight; blind.
q: He was, I think, at this time quite dark, and so had been for some years.

Dark.etym: [OE. dark, derk, deork, AS. dearc, deorc; cf. Gael. & Ir. dorch, dorcha, dark, black, dusky.]

senses.d: Absence of light; darkness; obscurity; a place where there is little or no light.
q: Here stood he in the dark, his sharp sword out.

senses.d: The condition of ignorance; gloom; secrecy.
q: Look, what you do, you do it still i' th' dark.
Till we perceive by our own understandings, we are as much in the dark, and as void of knowledge, as before.

senses.d: A dark shade or dark passage in a painting, engraving, or the like; as, the light and darks are well contrasted.
q: The lights may serve for a repose to the darks, and the darks to the lights.

senses.d: To darken; to obscure.
To make dark or black; to deprive of light; to obscure; as, a darkened room.
q: They covered the face of the whole earth, so that the land was darkened.
So spake the Sovran Voice; and clouds began To darken all the hill.

senses.d: To render dim; to deprive of vision.
q: Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see.

senses.d: To cloud, obscure, or perplex; to render less clear or intelligible.
q: Such was his wisdom that his confidence did seldom darkenhis foresight.
Who is this that darkeneth counsel by words without knowledge?

senses.d: To cast a gloom upon.
q: With these forced thoughts, I prithee, darken not The mirth of the feast.

senses.d: To make foul; to sully; to tarnish.
q: I must not think there are Evils enough to darken all his goodness.

senses.d: To grow or darker.
Somewhat dark; dusky.
With imperfect light, clearness, or knowledge; obscurely; dimly; blindly; uncertainly.
q: What fame to future times conveys but darkly down.
so softly dark and darkly pure.

senses.d: With a dark, gloomy, cruel, or menacing look.
q: Looking darkly at the clerguman.

senses.d: The absence of light; blackness; obscurity; gloom.
q: And darkness was upon the face of the deep.

senses.d: A state of privacy; secrecy.
q: What I tell you in darkness, that speak ye in light.

senses.d: A state of ignorance or error, especially on moral or religious subjects; hence, wickedness; impurity.
q: Men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil.
Pursue these sons of darkness: drive them out From all heaven's bounds.

senses.d: Want of clearness or perspicuity; obscurity; as, the darkness of a subject, or of a discussion.
A state of distress or trouble.
q: A day of clouds and of thick darkness.

senses.d: One dearly beloved; a favorite.
q: And can do naught but wail her darling's loss.

Darling.etym: [OE. derling, deorling, AS. deórling; deóre dear + -ling. See Dear, and -ling.]

senses.d: Dearly beloved; regarded with especial kindness and tenderness; favorite.
A pointed missile weapon, intended to be thrown by the hand; a short lance; a javelin; hence, any sharp-pointed missile weapon, as an arrow.
q: And he took three darts in his hand, and thrust them through the heart of Absalom.

senses.d: Anything resembling a dart; anything that pierces or wounds like a dart.
q: The artful inquiry, whose venomed dart Scarce wounds the hearing while it stabs the heart.

senses.d: A spear set as a prize in running.
A fish; the dace. See Dace.

Dart.etym: [OF. dart, of German origin; cf. OHG. tart javelin, dart, AS. dara�, daro�, Sw. dart dagger, Icel. darra�r dart.]

senses.d: To throw with a sudden effort or thrust, as a dart or other missile weapon; to hurl or launch.
To throw suddenly or rapidly; to send forth; to emit; to shoot; as, the sun darts forth his beams.
q: Or what ill eyes malignant glances dart?

senses.d: To fly or pass swiftly, as a dart.
To start and run with velocity; to shoot rapidly along; as, the deer darted from the thicket.
To throw with violence or haste; to cause to strike violently or hastily; — often used with against.
q: If you dash a stone against a stone in the botton of the water, it maketh a sound.

senses.d: To break, as by throwing or by collision; to shatter; to crust; to frustrate; to ruin.
q: Thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel.
A brave vessel, . . . Dashed all to pieces.
To perplex and dash Maturest counsels.

senses.d: To put to shame; to confound; to confuse; to abash; to depress.
q: Dash the proud gamester in his gilded car.

senses.d: To throw in or on in a rapid, careless manner; to mix, reduce, or adulterate, by throwing in something of an inferior quality; to overspread partially; to bespatter; to touch here and there; as, to dash wine with water; to dash paint upon a picture.
q: I take care to dash the character with such particular circumstance as may prevent ill-natured applications.
The very source and fount of day Is dashed with wandering isles of night.

senses.d: To form or sketch rapidly or carelessly; to execute rapidly, or with careless haste; — with off; as, to dash off a review or sermon.
To erase by a stroke; to strike out; knock out; — with out; as, to dash out a word.

Dash.etym: [Of. Scand. origin; cf. Dan daske to beat, strike, Sw. & Icel. daska, Dan. & Sw. dask blow.]

senses.d: To rush with violence; to move impetuously; to strike violently; as, the waves dash upon rocks.
q: dashed through thick and thin.
On each hand the gushing waters play, And down the rough cascade all dashing fall.

senses.d: Violent striking together of two bodies; collision; crash.
A sudden check; abashment; frustration; ruin; as, his hopes received a dash.
A slight admixture, infusion, or adulteration; a partial overspreading; as, wine with a dash of water; red with a dash of purple.
q: Innocence when it has in it a dash of folly.

senses.d: A rapid movement, esp. one of short duration; a quick stroke or blow; a sudden onset or rush; as, a bold dash at the enemy; a dash of rain.
q: She takes upon her bravely at first dash.

senses.d: Energy in style or action; animation; spirit.
A vain show; a blustering parade; a flourish; as, to make or cut a great dash.

A mark or line , in writing or printing, denoting a sudden break, stop, or transition in a sentence, or an abrupt change in its construction, a long or significant pause, or an unexpected or epigrammatic turn of sentiment. Dashes are also sometimes used instead of marks or parenthesis.
The sign of staccato, a small mark denoting that the note over which it is placed is to be performed in a short, distinct manner.
A short, spirited effort or trial of speed upon a race course; — used in horse racing, when a single trial constitutes the race.
To smear with soft, adhesive matter, as pitch, slime, mud, etc.; to plaster; to bedaub; to besmear.
q: She took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch.

senses.d: To paint in a coarse or unskillful manner.
q: If a picture is daubed with many bright and glaring colors, the vulgar admire it is an excellent piece.
A lame, imperfect piece, rudely daubed over.

senses.d: To cover with a specious or deceitful exterior; to disguise; to conceal.
q: So smooth he daubed his vice with show of virtue.

senses.d: To flatter excessively or glossy.
q: I can safely say, however, that, without any daubing at all, I am very sincerely your very affectionate, humble servant.

senses.d: To put on without taste; to deck gaudily.
q: Let him be daubed with lace.

Daub.etym: [OE. dauben to smear, OF. dauber to plaster, fr. L. dealbare to whitewash, plaster; de- + albare to whiten, fr. albus white, perh. also confused with W. dwb plaster, dwbio to plaster, Ir. & OGael. dob plaster. See Alb, and cf. Dealbate.]

senses.d: To smear; to play the flatterer.
q: His conscience . . . will not daub nor flatter.

senses.d: A viscous, sticky application; a spot smeared or daubed; a smear.
A picture coarsely executed.
q: Did you . . . take a look at the grand picture? . . . 'T is a melancholy daub, my lord.

senses.d: The act of one who daubs; that which is daubed.
A rough coat of mortar put upon a wall to give it the appearance of stone; rough-cast.
In currying, a mixture of fish oil and tallow worked into leather; — called also dubbing.
The female offspring of the human species; a female child of any age; — applied also to the lower animals.
A female descendant; a woman.
q: This woman, being a daughter of Abraham.
Dinah, the daughter of Leah, which she bare unto Jacob, went out to see the daughter of the land.

senses.d: A son's wife; a daughter-in-law.
q: And Naomi said, Turn again, my daughters.

senses.d: A term of address indicating parental interest.
q: Daughter, be of good comfort.

Daughter.etym: [OE. doughter, doghter, dohter, AS. dohtor, dohter; akin to OS. dohtar, D. dochter, G. tochter, Icel. dōttir, Sw. dotter, Dan. dotter, datter, Goth. daúhtar,, OSlav. dŭshti, Russ. doche, Lith. duktē, Gr. θυγάτηρ, Zend. dughdhar, Skr. duhitṛ; possibly originally, the milker, cf. Skr. duh to milk. √68

senses.d: To begin to grow light in the morning; to grow light; to break, or begin to appear; as, the day dawns; the morning dawns.
q: In the end of the Sabbath, as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week, came Mary Magdalene . . . to see the sepulcher.

senses.d: To began to give promise; to begin to appear or to expand.
q: When life awakes, and dawns at every line.
Dawn on our darkness and lend us thine aid.

Dawn.etym: [OE. dawnen, dawen, dagen, daien, AS. dagian to become day, to dawn, fr. dæg day; akin to D. dagen, G. tagen, Icel. daga, Dan. dages, Sw. dagas. See Day. √71.]

senses.d: The break of day; the first appearance of light in the morning; show of approaching sunrise.
q: And oft at dawn, deep noon, or falling eve.
No sun, no moon, no morn, no noon, No dawn, no dusk, no proper time of day.

senses.d: First opening or expansion; first appearance; beginning; rise.
q: These tender circumstances diffuse a dawn of serenity over the soul.

senses.d: The time of light, or interval between one night and the next; the time between sunrise and sunset, or from dawn to darkness; hence, the light; sunshine.

The period of the earth's revolution on its axis. — ordinarily divided into twenty-four hours. It is measured by the interval between two successive transits of a celestial body over the same meridian, and takes a specific name from that of the body. Thus, if this is the sun, the day (the interval between two successive transits of the sun's center over the same meridian) is called a solar day; if it is a star, a sidereal day; if it is the moon, a lunar day. See Civil day, Sidereal day, below.
Those hours, or the daily recurring period, allotted by usage or law for work.
A specified time or period; time, considered with reference to the existence or prominence of a person or thing; age; time.
q: A man who was great among the Hellenes of his day.
If my debtors do not keep their day, . . . I must with patience all the terms attend.

senses.d: (Preceded by the) Some day in particular, as some day of contest, some anniversary, etc.
q: The field of Agincourt, Fought on the day of Crispin Crispianus.
His name struck fear, his conduct won the day.

Day.etym: [OE. day, dai,, dei, AS. dæg; akin to OS., D., Dan., & Sw. dag, G, tag, Icel. dagr, Goth. dags; cf. Skr. dah (for dhagh ?) to burn. √69. Cf. Dawn.]

senses.d: An umpire or arbiter; a mediator.
q: Neither is there any daysman betwixt us.

Daysman.etym: [From day in the sense of day fixed for trial.]

senses.d: The beginning of the day, or first appearance of light; the dawn; hence, the beginning.
q: The tender mercy of our God; whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us.

senses.d: The time during which there is daylight, as distinguished from the night.

An officer in Christian churches appointed to perform certain subordinate duties varying in different communions. In the Roman Catholic and Episcopal churches, a person admitted to the lowest order in the ministry, subordinate to the bishops and priests. In Presbyterian churches, he is subordinate to the minister and elders, and has charge of certain duties connected with the communion service and the care of the poor. In Congregational churches, he is subordinate to the pastor, and has duties as in the Presbyterian church.
The chairman of an incorporated company.

Deacon.etym: [OE. diakne, deakne, deken, AS. diacon, deacon, L. diaconus, fr. Gr. � a servant or minister, a minister of the church; of uncertain origin. In sense 2 prob. confused with dean.]

senses.d: To read aloud each line of (a psalm or hymn) before singing it, — usually with off.

With humorous reference to hypocritical posing: To pack (fruit or vegetables) with the finest specimens on top; to alter slyly the boundaries of (land); to adulterate or doctor (an article to be sold), etc.

Deprived of life; — opposed to alive and living; reduced to that state of a being in which the organs of motion and life have irrevocably ceased to perform their functions; as, a dead tree; a dead man.
q: The crew, all except himself, were dead of hunger.
Seek him with candle, bring him dead or living.

senses.d: Destitute of life; inanimate; as, dead matter.
Resembling death in appearance or quality; without show of life; deathlike; as, a dead sleep.
Still as death; motionless; inactive; useless; as, dead calm; a dead load or weight.
So constructed as not to transmit sound; soundless; as, a dead floor.
Unproductive; bringing no gain; unprofitable; as, dead capital; dead stock in trade.
Lacking spirit; dull; lusterless; cheerless; as, dead eye; dead fire; dead color, etc.
Monotonous or unvaried; as, a dead level or pain; a dead wall.
Sure as death; unerring; fixed; complete; as, a dead shot; a dead certainty.
q: I had them a dead bargain.

senses.d: Bringing death; deadly.
Wanting in religious spirit and vitality; as, dead faith; dead works.
Flat; without gloss; — said of painting which has been applied purposely to have this effect.

Dead.etym: [OE. ded, dead, deed, AS. deád; akin to OS. dōd, D. dood, G. todt, tot, Icel. dauðr, Sw. & Dan. död, Goth. daubs; prop. p. p. of an old verb meaning to die. See Die, and cf. Death.]

senses.d: To a degree resembling death; to the last degree; completely; wholly.
q: I was tired of reading, and dead sleepy.

senses.d: The most quiet or deathlike time; the period of profoundest repose, inertness, or gloom; as, the dead of winter.
q: When the drum beat at dead of night.

senses.d: One who is dead; — commonly used collectively.
q: And Abraham stood up from before his dead.

senses.d: To make dead; to deaden; to deprive of life, force, or vigor.
q: Heaven's stern decree, With many an ill, hath numbed and deaded me.

senses.d: To die; to lose life or force.
q: So iron, as soon as it is out of the fire, deadeth straightway.

senses.d: Carrying no current, or producing no useful effect; — said of a conductor in a dynamo or motor, also of a telegraph wire which has no instrument attached and, therefore, is not in use.
Out of play; regarded as out of the game; — said of a ball, a piece, or a player under certain conditions in cricket, baseball, checkers, and some other games.
q: , a ball is said to lie dead when it lies so near the hole that the player is certain to hole it in the next stroke.

senses.d: Capable of causing death; mortal; fatal; destructive; certain or likely to cause death; as, a deadly blow or wound.
Aiming or willing to destroy; implacable; desperately hostile; flagitious; as, deadly enemies.
q: Thy assailant is quick, skillful, and deadly.

senses.d: Subject to death; mortal.
q: The image of a deadly man.

senses.d: In a manner resembling, or as if produced by, death.
In a manner to occasion death; mortally.
q: The groanings of a deadly wounded man.

senses.d: In an implacable manner; destructively.
Extremely.

The state of being destitute of life, vigor, spirit, activity, etc.; dullness; inertness; languor; coldness; vapidness; indifference; as, the deadness of a limb, a body, or a tree; the deadness of an eye; deadness of the affections; the deadness of beer or cider; deadness to the world, and the like.
Wanting the sense of hearing, either wholly or in part; unable to perceive sounds; hard of hearing; as, a deaf man.
q: Come on my right hand, for this ear is deaf.

senses.d: Unwilling to hear or listen; determinedly inattentive; regardless; not to be persuaded as to facts, argument, or exhortation; — with to; as, deaf to reason.
q: O, that men's ears should be To counsel deaf, but not to flattery!

senses.d: Deprived of the power of hearing; deafened.
q: Deaf with the noise, I took my hasty flight.

senses.d: Obscurely heard; stifled; deadened.
q: A deaf murmur through the squadron went.

senses.d: Decayed; tasteless; dead; as, a deaf nut; deaf corn.
q: If the season be unkindly and intemperate, they will catch a blast; and then the seeds will be deaf, void, light, and naught.

Deaf.etym: [OE. def, deaf, deef, AS. deáf; akin to D. doof, G. taub, Icel. daufr, Dan. döv, Sw. döf, Goth. daubs, and prob. to E. dumb (the original sense being, dull as applied to one of the senses), and perh. to Gr. � (for �) blind, � smoke, vapor, folly, and to G. toben to rage. Cf. Dumb.]

senses.d: To deafen.
A part or portion; a share; hence, an indefinite quantity, degree, or extent, degree, or extent; as, a deal of time and trouble; a deal of cold.
q: Three tenth deals of flour.
As an object of science it may count for a good deal . . . as a spiritual power.
She was resolved to be a good deal more circumspect.

senses.d: The process of dealing cards to the players; also, the portion disturbed.
q: The deal, the shuffle, and the cut.

senses.d: Distribution; apportionment.
An arrangement to attain a desired result by a combination of interested parties; — applied to stock speculations and political bargains.

The division of a piece of timber made by sawing; a board or plank; particularly, a board or plank of fir or pine above seven inches in width, and exceeding six feet in length. If narrower than this, it is called a batten; if shorter, a deal end.
Wood of the pine or fir; as, a floor of deal.

Deal.etym: [OE. del, deel, part, AS. dǣl; akin to OS. dēl, D. & Dan. deel, G. theil, teil, Icel. deild, Sw. del, Goth. dails. √65. Cf. 3d Dole.]

senses.d: To divide; to separate in portions; hence, to give in portions; to distribute; to bestow successively; — sometimes with out.
q: Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry?
And Rome deals out her blessings and her gold.
The nightly mallet deals resounding blows.
Hissing through the skies, the feathery deaths were dealt.

senses.d: Specifically: To distribute, as cards, to the players at the commencement of a game; as, to deal the cards; to deal one a jack.

Deal.etym: [OE. delen, AS. dǣlan, fr. dǣl share; akin to OS. dēlian, D. deelen, G. theilen, teilen, Icel. deila, Sw. dela, Dan. dele, Goth. dailjan. See Deal, n.]

senses.d: To make distribution; to share out in portions, as cards to the players.
To do a distributing or retailing business, as distinguished from that of a manufacturer or producer; to traffic; to trade; to do business; as, he deals in flour.
q: They buy and sell, they deal and traffic.
This is to drive to wholesale trade, when all other petty merchants deal but for parcels.

senses.d: To act as an intermediary in business or any affairs; to manage; to make arrangements; — followed by between or with.
q: Sometimes he that deals between man and man, raiseth his own credit with both, by pretending greater interest than he hath in either.

senses.d: To conduct one's self; to behave or act in any affair or towards any one; to treat.
q: If he will deal clearly and impartially, . . . he will acknowledge all this to be true.

senses.d: To contend (with); to treat (with), by way of opposition, check, or correction; as, he has turbulent passions to deal with.
q: The deacons of his church, who, to use their own phrase, “dealt with him” on the sin of rejecting the aid which Providence so manifestly held out.
Return . . . and I will deal well with thee.

senses.d: One who deals; one who has to do, or has concern, with others; esp., a trader, a trafficker, a shopkeeper, a broker, or a merchant; as, a dealer in dry goods; a dealer in stocks; a retail dealer.
One who distributes cards to the players.
The act of one who deals; distribution of anything, as of cards to the players; method of business; traffic; intercourse; transaction; as, to have dealings with a person.
Bearing a high price; high-priced; costly; expensive.
q: The cheapest of us is ten groats too dear.

senses.d: Marked by scarcity or dearth, and exorbitance of price; as, a dear year.
Highly valued; greatly beloved; cherished; precious.
q: Neither count I my life dear unto myself.
And the last joy was dearer than the rest.
Dear as remember'd kisses after death.

senses.d: Hence, close to the heart; heartfelt; present in mind; engaging the attention.
q: leave you to attend him: some dear cause Will in concealment wrap me up awhile.
His dearest wish was to escape from the bustle and glitter of Whitehall.

senses.d: Of disagreeable things and antipathies.
q: In our dear peril.
Would I had met my dearest foe in heaven Or ever I had seen that day.

Dear.etym: [OE. dere, deore, AS. deóre; akin to OS. diuri, D. duur, OHG. tiuri, G. theuer, teuer, Icel. dȳrr, Dan. & Sw. dyr. Cf. Darling, Dearth.]

senses.d: A dear one; lover; sweetheart.
q: That kiss I carried from thee, dear.

senses.d: Dearly; at a high price.
q: If thou attempt it, it will cost thee dear.

senses.d: To endear.
In a dear manner; with affection; heartily; earnestly; as, to love one dearly.
At a high rate or price; grievously.
q: He buys his mistress dearly with his throne.

senses.d: Exquisitely.
Scarcity which renders dear; want; lack; specifically, lack of food on account of failure of crops; famine.
q: There came a dearth over all the land of Egypt.
He with her press'd, she faint with dearth.
Dearth of plot, and narrowness of imagination.

senses.d: The cessation of all vital phenomena without capability of resuscitation, either in animals or plants.
Total privation or loss; extinction; cessation; as, the death of memory.
q: The death of a language can not be exactly compared with the death of a plant.

senses.d: Manner of dying; act or state of passing from life.
q: A death that I abhor.
Let me die the death of the righteous.

senses.d: Cause of loss of life.
q: Swiftly flies the feathered death.
He caught his death the last county sessions.

senses.d: Personified: The destroyer of life, — conventionally represented as a skeleton with a scythe.
q: Death! great proprietor of all.
And I looked, and behold a pale horse; and his name that sat on him was Death.

senses.d: Danger of death.
Murder; murderous character.
q: Not to suffer a man of death to live.

senses.d: Loss of spiritual life.
q: To be carnally minded is death.

senses.d: Anything so dreadful as to be like death.
q: It was death to them to think of entertaining such doctrines.
And urged him, so that his soul was vexed unto death.

Death.etym: [OE. deth, deað, AS. deáð; akin to OS. dōð, D. dood, G. tod, Icel. dauði, Sw. & Dan. död, Goth. dauþus; from a verb meaning to die. See Die, v. i., and cf. Dead.]

senses.d: To cut off from entrance, as if by a bar or barrier; to preclude; to hinder from approach, entry, or enjoyment; to shut out or exclude; to deny or refuse; — with from, and sometimes with of.
q: Yet not so strictly hath our Lord imposed Labor, as to debar us when we need Refreshment.
Their wages were so low as to debar them, not only from the comforts but from the common decencies of civilized life.

senses.d: To reduce from a higher to a lower state or grade of worth, dignity, purity, station, etc.; to degrade; to lower; to deteriorate; to abase; as, to debase the character by crime; to debase the mind by frivolity; to debase style by vulgar words.
q: The coin which was adulterated and debased.
It is a kind of taking God's name in vain to debase religion with such frivolous disputes.
And to debase the sons, exalts the sires.

Debase.etym: [Pref. de- + base. See Base, a., and cf. Abase.]

senses.d: To engage in combat for; to strive for.
q: Volunteers . . . thronged to serve under his banner, and the cause of religion was debated with the same ardor in Spain as on the plains of Palestine.

senses.d: To contend for in words or arguments; to strive to maintain by reasoning; to dispute; to contest; to discuss; to argue for and against.
q: A wise council . . . that did debate this business.
Debate thy cause with thy neighbor himself.

Debate.syn: To argue; discuss; dispute; controvert. See Argue, and Discuss.
Debate.etym: [OF. debatre, F. débattre; L. de + batuere to beat. See Batter, v. t., and cf. Abate.]

senses.d: To engage in strife or combat; to fight.
q: Well could he tourney and in lists debate.

senses.d: To contend in words; to dispute; hence, to deliberate; to consider; to discuss or examine different arguments in the mind; — often followed by on or upon.
q: He presents that great soul debating upon the subject of life and death with his intimate friends.

senses.d: A fight or fighting; contest; strife.
q: On the day of the Trinity next ensuing was a great debate . . . and in that murder there were slain . . . fourscore.
But question fierce and proud reply Gave signal soon of dire debate.

senses.d: Contention in words or arguments; discussion for the purpose of elucidating truth or influencing action; strife in argument; controversy; as, the debates in Parliament or in Congress.
q: Heard, noted, answer'd, as in full debate.

senses.d: Subject of discussion.
q: Statutes and edicts concerning this debate.

Debate.etym: [F. débat, fr. débattre. See Debate, v. t.]

senses.d: That which is due from one person to another, whether money, goods, or services; that which one person is bound to pay to another, or to perform for his benefit; thing owed; obligation; liability.
q: Your son, my lord, has paid a soldier's debt.
When you run in debt, you give to another power over your liberty.

senses.d: A duty neglected or violated; a fault; a sin; a trespass.
An action at law to recover a certain specified sum of money alleged to be due.

Debt.etym: [OE. dette, F. dette, LL. debita, fr. L. debitus owed, p. p. of debere to owe, prop., to have on loan; de- + habere to have. See Habit, and cf. Debit, Due.]

senses.d: One who owes a debt; one who is indebted; — correlative to creditor.
q: bring your latter hazard back again, And thankfully rest debtor for the first.
In Athens an insolvent debtor became slave to his creditor.
Debtors for our lives to you.

Debtor.etym: [OE. dettur, dettour, OF. detor, detur, detour, F. débiteur, fr. L. debitor, fr. debere to owe. See Debt.]

senses.d: To pass gradually from a sound, prosperous, or perfect state, to one of imperfection, adversity, or dissolution; to waste away; to decline; to fail; to become weak, corrupt, or disintegrated; to rot; to perish; as, a tree decays; fortunes decay; hopes decay.
q: Ill fares the land, to hastening ills a prey, Where wealth accumulates and men decay.

Decay.etym: [OF. decaeir, dechaer, decheoir, F. déchoir, to decline, fall, become less; L. de- + cadere to fall. See Chance.]

senses.d: To cause to decay; to impair.
q: Infirmity, that decays the wise.

senses.d: To destroy.

Gradual failure of health, strength, soundness, prosperity, or of any species of excellence or perfection; tendency toward dissolution or extinction; corruption; rottenness; decline; deterioration; as, the decay of the body; the decay of virtue; the decay of the Roman empire; a castle in decay.
q: Perhaps my God, though he be far before, May turn, and take me by the hand, and more - May strengthen my decays.
His failure was not to be ascribed to intellectual decay.
Which has caused the decay of the consonants to follow somewhat different laws.

senses.d: Destruction; death.
Cause of decay.
q: He that plots to be the only figure among ciphers, is the decay of the whole age.

senses.d: Fallen, as to physical or social condition; affected with decay; rotten; as, decayed vegetation or vegetables; a decayed fortune or gentleman.
Departure, especially departure from this life; death.
q: His decease, which he should accomplish at Jerusalem.
And I, the whilst you mourn for his decease, Will with my mourning plaints your plaint increase.

Decease.syn: Death; departure; dissolution; demise; release. See Death.
Decease.etym: [OE. deses, deces, F. décès, fr. L. decessus departure, death, fr. decedere to depart, die; de- + cedere to withdraw. See Cease, Cede.]

senses.d: To depart from this life; to die; to pass away.
q: She's dead, deceased, she's dead.
When our summers have deceased.
Inasmuch as he carries the malignity and the lie with him, he so far deceases from nature.

senses.d: Passed away; dead; gone.

An attempt or disposition to deceive or lead into error; any declaration, artifice, or practice, which misleads another, or causes him to believe what is false; a contrivance to entrap; deception; a wily device; fraud.
q: Making the ephah small and the shekel great, and falsifying the balances by deceit.
Friendly to man, far from deceit or guile.
Yet still we hug the dear deceit.

senses.d: Any trick, collusion, contrivance, false representation, or underhand practice, used to defraud another. When injury is thereby effected, an action of deceit, as it called, lies for compensation.

Deceit.syn: Deception; fraud; imposition; duplicity; trickery; guile; falsifying; double-dealing; stratagem. See Deception.
Deceit.etym: [OF. deceit, desçait, decept (cf. deceite, deçoite), fr. L. deceptus deception, fr. decipere. See Deceive.]

senses.d: Full of, or characterized by, deceit; serving to mislead or insnare; trickish; fraudulent; cheating; insincere.
q: Harboring foul deceitful thoughts.

senses.d: With intent to deceive.
The disposition to deceive; as, a man's deceitfulness may be habitual.
The quality of being deceitful; as, the deceitfulness of a man's practices.
Tendency to mislead or deceive.
Fitted to deceive; deceitful.
q: The fraud of deceivable traditions.

senses.d: Subject to deceit; capable of being misled.
q: Blind, and thereby deceivable.

senses.d: Capability of deceiving.
q: With all deceivableness of unrighteousness.

senses.d: Liability to be deceived or misled; as, the deceivableness of a child.
To lead into error; to cause to believe what is false, or disbelieve what is true; to impose upon; to mislead; to cheat; to disappoint; to delude; to insnare.
q: Evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse, deceiving, and being deceived.
Nimble jugglers that deceive the eye.
What can 'scape the eye Of God all-seeing, or deceive his heart?

senses.d: To beguile; to amuse, so as to divert the attention; to while away; to take away as if by deception.
q: These occupations oftentimes deceived The listless hour.

senses.d: To deprive by fraud or stealth; to defraud.
q: Plant fruit trees in large borders, and set therein fine flowers, but thin and sparingly, lest they deceive the trees.

Deceive.etym: [OE. deceveir, F. décevoir, fr. L. decipere to catch, insnare, deceive; de- + capere to take, catch. See Capable, and cf. Deceit, Deception.]

senses.d: One who deceives; one who leads into error; a cheat; an impostor.
q: The deceived and the deceiver are his.

senses.d: Suitable in words, behavior, dress, or ceremony; becoming; fit; decorous; proper; seemly; as, decent conduct; decent language.
q: Before his decent steps.

senses.d: Free from immodesty or obscenity; modest.
Comely; shapely; well-formed.
q: A sable stole of cyprus lawn Over thy decent shoulders drawn.
By foreign hands thy decent limbs composed.

senses.d: Moderate, but competent; sufficient; hence, respectable; fairly good; reasonably comfortable or satisfying; as, a decent fortune; a decent person.
q: A decent retreat in the mutability of human affairs.

Decent.etym: [L. decens, decentis, p. pr. of decere to be fitting or becoming; akin to decus glory, honor, ornament, Gr. δοκει̑ν to seem good, to seem, think; cf. Skr. dāç to grant, to give; and perh. akin to E. attire, tire: cf. F. décent. Cf. Decorate, Decorum, Deign.]

senses.d: To cut off; to separate.
q: Our seat denies us traffic here; The sea, too near, decides us from the rest.

senses.d: To bring to a termination, as a question, controversy, struggle, by giving the victory to one side or party; to render judgment concerning; to determine; to settle.
q: So shall thy judgment be; thyself hast decided it.
The quarrel toucheth none but us alone; Betwixt ourselves let us decide it then.

Decide.etym: [L. decīdere; de- + caedere to cut, cut off; prob. akin to E. shed, v.: cf. F. décider. Cf. Decision.]

senses.d: To determine; to form a definite opinion; to come to a conclusion; to give decision; as, the court decided in favor of the defendant.
q: Who shall decide, when doctors disagree?

senses.d: Free from ambiguity; unequivocal; unmistakable; unquestionable; clear; evident; as, a decided advantage.
Free from doubt or wavering; determined; of fixed purpose; fully settled; positive; resolute; as, a decided opinion or purpose.
Cutting off; division; detachment of a part.
The act of deciding; act of settling or terminating, as a controversy, by giving judgment on the matter at issue; determination, as of a question or doubt; settlement; conclusion.
q: The decision of some dispute.

senses.d: An account or report of a conclusion, especially of a legal adjudication or judicial determination of a question or cause; as, a decision of arbitrators; a decision of the Supreme Court.
The quality of being decided; prompt and fixed determination; unwavering firmness; as, to manifest great decision.

Decision.etym: [L. decisio, fr. decīdere, decisum: cf. F. décision. See Decide.]

senses.d: To cover; to overspread.
q: To deck with clouds the uncolored sky.

senses.d: To dress, as the person; to clothe; especially, to clothe with more than ordinary elegance; to array; to adorn; to embellish.
q: Deck thyself now with majesty and excellency.
And deck my body in gay ornaments.
The dew with spangles decked the ground.

senses.d: To furnish with a deck, as a vessel.

Deck.etym: [D. dekken to cover; akin to E. thatch. See Thatch.]

senses.d: The floorlike covering of the horizontal sections, or compartments, of a ship. Small vessels have only one deck; larger ships have two or three decks.
The upper part or top of a mansard roof or curb roof when made nearly flat.
The roof of a passenger car.
A pack or set of playing cards.
q: The king was slyly fingered from the deck.

senses.d: A heap or store.
q: Who . . . hath such trinkets Ready in the deck.

senses.d: A main aëroplane surface, esp. of a biplane or multiplane.

The act of declaring, or publicly announcing; explicit asserting; undisguised token of a ground or side taken on any subject; proclamation; exposition; as, the declaration of an opinion; a declaration of war, etc.
That which is declared or proclaimed; announcement; distinct statement; formal expression; avowal.
q: Declarations of mercy and love . . . in the Gospel.

senses.d: The document or instrument containing such statement or proclamation; as, the Declaration of Independence (now preserved in Washington).
q: In 1776 the Americans laid before Europe that noble Declaration, which ought to be hung up in the nursery of every king, and blazoned on the porch of every royal palace.

senses.d: That part of the process or pleadings in which the plaintiff sets forth in order and at large his cause of complaint; the narration of the plaintiff's case containing the count, or counts. See Count, n., 3.

Declaration.etym: [F. déclaration, fr. L. declaratio, fr. declarare. See Declare.]

senses.d: To make clear; to free from obscurity.
To make known by language; to communicate or manifest explicitly and plainly in any way; to exhibit; to publish; to proclaim; to announce.
q: This day I have begot whom I declare My only Son.
The heavens declare the glory of God.

senses.d: To make declaration of; to assert; to affirm; to set forth; to avow; as, he declares the story to be false.
q: I the Lord . . . declare things that are right.

senses.d: To make full statement of, as goods, etc., for the purpose of paying taxes, duties, etc.

Declare.etym: [F. déclarer, from L. declarare; de + clarare to make clear, clarus, clear, bright. See Clear.]

senses.d: To make a declaration, or an open and explicit avowal; to proclaim one's self; — often with for or against; as, victory declares against the allies.
q: Like fawning courtiers, for success they wait, And then come smiling, and declare for fate.

senses.d: To state the plaintiff's cause of action at law in a legal form; as, the plaintiff declares in trespass.
To bend, or lean downward; to take a downward direction; to bend over or hang down, as from weakness, weariness, despondency, etc.; to condescend.
q: He . . . would decline even to the lowest of his family.
Disdaining to decline, Slowly he falls, amidst triumphant cries.
The ground at length became broken and declined rapidly.

senses.d: To tend or draw towards a close, decay, or extinction; to tend to a less perfect state; to become diminished or impaired; to fail; to sink; to diminish; to lessen; as, the day declines; virtue declines; religion declines; business declines.
q: That empire must decline Whose chief support and sinews are of coin.
And presume to know . . . Who thrives, and who declines.

senses.d: To turn or bend aside; to deviate; to stray; to withdraw; as, a line that declines from straightness; conduct that declines from sound morals.
q: Yet do I not decline from thy testimonies.

senses.d: To turn away; to shun; to refuse; — the opposite of accept or consent; as, he declined, upon principle.

Decline.etym: [OE. declinen to bend down, lower, sink, decline (a noun), F. décliner to decline, refuse, fr. L. declinare to turn aside, inflect (a part of speech), avoid; de- + clinare to incline; akin to E. lean. See Lean, v. i.]

senses.d: To bend downward; to bring down; to depress; to cause to bend, or fall.
q: In melancholy deep, with head declined.
And now fair Phoebus gan decline in haste His weary wagon to the western vale.

senses.d: To cause to decrease or diminish.
q: He knoweth his error, but will not seek to decline it.

senses.d: To put or turn aside; to turn off or away from; to refuse to undertake or comply with; reject; to shun; to avoid; as, to decline an offer; to decline a contest; he declined any participation with them.
q: Could I Decline this dreadful hour?

senses.d: To inflect, or rehearse in order the changes of grammatical form of; as, to decline a noun or an adjective.
q: After the first declining of a noun and a verb.

senses.d: To run through from first to last; to repeat like a schoolboy declining a noun.

A falling off; a tendency to a worse state; diminution or decay; deterioration; also, the period when a thing is tending toward extinction or a less perfect state; as, the decline of life; the decline of strength; the decline of virtue and religion.
q: Their fathers lived in the decline of literature.

senses.d: That period of a disorder or paroxysm when the symptoms begin to abate in violence; as, the decline of a fever.
A gradual sinking and wasting away of the physical faculties; any wasting disease, esp. pulmonary consumption; as, to die of a decline.
Declinate.

To grow less, — opposed to increase; to be diminished gradually, in size, degree, number, duration, etc., or in strength, quality, or excellence; as, they days decrease in length from June to December.
q: He must increase, but I must decrease.
The olive leaf, which certainly them told The flood decreased.
Crete's ample fields diminish to our eye; Before the Boreal blasts the vessels fly.

Decrease.etym: [OE. decrecen, fr. OF. decreistre, F. décroître, or from the OF. noun (see Decrease, n.), fr. L. decrescere to grow less; de + crescere to grow. See Crescent, and cf. Increase.]

senses.d: To cause to grow less; to diminish gradually; as, extravagance decreases one's means.
q: That might decrease their present store.

senses.d: A becoming less; gradual diminution; decay; as, a decrease of revenue or of strength.
The wane of the moon.

Decrease.etym: [OE. decrees, OF. decreis, fr. decreistre. See Decrease, v.]

senses.d: An order from one having authority, deciding what is to be done by a subordinate; also, a determination by one having power, deciding what is to be done or to take place; edict, law; authoritative ru�� decision.
q: There went out a decree from Cæsar Augustus that all the world should be taxed.
Poor hand, why quiverest thou at this decree?

senses.d: A decision, order, or sentence, given in a cause by a court of equity or admiralty.
An edict or law made by a council for regulating any business within their jurisdiction; as, the decrees of ecclesiastical councils.

Decree.syn: Law; regulation; edict; ordinance. See Law.
Decree.etym: [OE. decre, F. décret, fr. L. decretum, neut. decretus, p. p. of decernere to decide; de- + cernere to decide. See Certain, and cf. Decreet, Decretal.]

senses.d: To determine judicially by authority, or by decree; to constitute by edict; to appoint by decree or law; to determine; to order; to ordain; as, a court decrees a restoration of property.
q: Thou shalt also decree a thing, and it shall be established unto thee.

senses.d: To ordain by fate.
To make decrees; — used absolutely.
q: Father eternal! thine is to decree; Mine, both in heaven and earth to do thy will.

senses.d: Dedicated; set apart; devoted; consecrated.

Dedicate.etym: [L. dedicatus, p. p. of dedicare to affirm, to dedicate; de- + dicare to declare, dedicate; akin to dicere to say. See Diction.]

senses.d: To set apart and consecrate, as to a divinity, or for sacred uses; to devote formally and solemnly; as, to dedicate vessels, treasures, a temple, or a church, to a religious use.
q: Vessels of silver, and vessels of gold, . . . which also king David did dedicate unto the Lord.

We have come to dedicate a portion of that field as a final resting place for those who here gave their lives that that nation might live. . . . But in a larger sense we can not dedicate, we can not consecrate, we can not hallow this ground.

senses.d: To devote, set apart, or give up, as one's self, to a duty or service.
q: The profession of a soldier, to which he had dedicated himself.

senses.d: To inscribe or address, as to a patron.
q: He complied ten elegant books, and dedicated them to the Lord Burghley.

senses.d: The act of setting apart or consecrating to a divine Being, or to a sacred use, often with religious solemnities; solemn appropriation; as, the dedication of Solomon's temple.
A devoting or setting aside for any particular purpose; as, a dedication of lands to public use.
An address to a patron or friend, prefixed to a book, testifying respect, and often recommending the work to his special protection and favor.
Dead.
That which is done or effected by a responsible agent; an act; an action; a thing done; — a word of extensive application, including, whatever is done, good or bad, great or small.
q: And Joseph said to them, What deed is this which ye have done?
We receive the due reward of our deeds.
Would serve his kind in deed and word.

senses.d: Illustrious act; achievement; exploit.
q: Whose deeds some nobler poem shall adorn.

senses.d: Power of action; agency; efficiency.
q: To be, both will and deed, created free.

senses.d: Fact; reality; — whence we have indeed.
A sealed instrument in writing, on paper or parchment, duly executed and delivered, containing some transfer, bargain, or contract.
Performance; — followed by of.

Deed.etym: [AS. d�d; akin to OS. dād, D. & Dan. daad, G. thai, Sw. dåd, Goth. d�ds; fr. the root of do. See Do, v. t.]

senses.d: To convey or transfer by deed; as, he deeded all his estate to his eldest son.
To decide; to judge; to sentence; to condemn.
q: Claudius . . . Was demed for to hang upon a tree.

senses.d: To account; to esteem; to think; to judge; to hold in opinion; to regard.
q: For never can I deem him less him less than god.

Deem.etym: [OE. demen to judge, condemn, AS. dēman, fr. dōm doom; akin to OFries. dēma, OS. adōmian, D. doemen, OHG. tuommen, Icel. dæma, Sw. dömma, Dan. dömme, Goth. dōmjan. See Doom, n., and cf. Doom, v.]

senses.d: To be of opinion; to think; to estimate; to opine; to suppose.
q: And deemest thou as those who pore, With aged eyes, short way before?

senses.d: To pass judgment.
Opinion; judgment.

Extending far below the surface; of great perpendicular dimension (measured from the surface downward, and distinguished from high, which is measured upward); far to the bottom; having a certain depth; as, a deep sea.
q: The water where the brook is deep.

senses.d: Extending far back from the front or outer part; of great horizontal dimension (measured backward from the front or nearer part, mouth, etc.); as, a deep cave or recess or wound; a gallery ten seats deep; a company of soldiers six files deep.
q: Shadowing squadrons deep.
Safely in harbor Is the king's ship in the deep nook.

senses.d: Low in situation; lying far below the general surface; as, a deep valley.
Hard to penetrate or comprehend; profound; — opposed to shallow or superficial; intricate; mysterious; not obvious; obscure; as, a deep subject or plot.
q: Speculations high or deep.
A question deep almost as the mystery of life.
O Lord, . . . thy thoughts are very deep.

senses.d: Of penetrating or far-reaching intellect; not superficial; thoroughly skilled; sagacious; cunning.
q: Deep clerks she dumbs.

senses.d: Profound; thorough; complete; unmixed; intense; heavy; heartfelt; as, deep distress; deep melancholy; deep horror.
q: An attitude of deep respect.

senses.d: Strongly colored; dark; intense; not light or thin; as, deep blue or crimson.
Of low tone; full-toned; not high or sharp; grave; heavy.
q: The bass of heaven's deep organ.

senses.d: Muddy; boggy; sandy; — said of roads.
q: The ways in that vale were very deep.

Deep.etym: [OE. dep, deop, AS. deóp; akin to D. diep, G. tief, Icel. djūpr, Sw. diup, Dan. dyb, Goth. diups; fr. the root of E. dip, dive. See Dip, Dive.]

senses.d: To a great depth; with depth; far down; profoundly; deeply.
q: Deep-versed in books, and shallow in himself.
Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring.

senses.d: That which is deep, especially deep water, as the sea or ocean; an abyss; a great depth.
q: Courage from the deeps of knowledge springs.
The hollow deep of hell resounded.
Blue Neptune storms, the bellowing deeps resound.

senses.d: That which is profound, not easily fathomed, or incomprehensible; a moral or spiritual depth or abyss.
q: Thy judgments are a great deep.
The deep of night is crept upon our talk.

senses.d: At or to a great depth; far below the surface; as, to sink deeply.
Profoundly; thoroughly; not superficially; in a high degree; intensely; as, deeply skilled in ethics.
q: He had deeply offended both his nobles and people.
He sighed deeply in his spirit.

senses.d: Very; with a tendency to darkness of color.
q: The deeply red juice of buckthorn berries.

senses.d: Gravely; with low or deep tone; as, a deeply toned instrument.
With profound skill; with art or intricacy; as, a deeply laid plot or intrigue.
The state or quality of being deep, profound, mysterious, secretive, etc.; depth; profundity; — opposed to shallowness.
q: Because they had no deepness of earth.

senses.d: Craft; insidiousness.
Any animal; especially, a wild animal.
q: Mice and rats, and such small deer.
The camel, that great deer.

senses.d: A ruminant of the genus Cervus, of many species, and of related genera of the family Cervidæ. The males, and in some species the females, have solid antlers, often much branched, which are shed annually. Their flesh, for which they are hunted, is called venison.

Deer.etym: [OE. der, deor, animal, wild animal, AS. deór; akin to D. dier, OFries. diar, G. thier, tier, Icel. dȳr, Dan. dyr, Sw. djur, Goth. dius; of unknown origin. √71.]

senses.d: To harm or destroy the good fame or reputation of; to disgrace; especially, to speak evil of maliciously; to dishonor by slanderous reports; to calumniate; to asperse.
To render infamous; to bring into disrepute.
q: My guilt thy growing virtues did defame; My blackness blotted thy unblemish'd name.

senses.d: To charge; to accuse.
q: Rebecca is . . . defamed of sorcery practiced on the person of a noble knight.

Defame.syn: To asperse; slander; calumniate; vilify. See Asperse.
Defame.etym: [OE. defamen, diffamen, from F. diffamer, or OF. perh. defamer, fr. L. diffamare (cf. defamatus infamous); dis- (in this word confused with de) + fama a report. See Fame.]

senses.d: Dishonor.
To undo; to disfigure; to destroy.
q: His unkindness may defeat my life.

senses.d: To render null and void, as a title; to frustrate, as hope; to deprive, as of an estate.
q: He finds himself naturally to dread a superior Being that can defeat all his designs, and disappoint all his hopes.
The escheators . . . defeated the right heir of his succession.
In one instance he defeated his own purpose.

senses.d: To overcome or vanquish, as an army; to check, disperse, or ruin by victory; to overthrow.
To resist with success; as, to defeat an assault.
q: Sharp reasons to defeat the law.

Defeat.etym: [From F. défait, OF. desfait, p. p. ofe défaire, OF. desfaire, to undo; L. dis- + facere to do. See Feat, Fact, and cf. Disfashion.]

senses.d: An undoing or annulling; destruction.
q: Upon whose property and most dear life A damned defeat was made.

senses.d: Frustration by rendering null and void, or by prevention of success; as, the defeat of a plan or design.
An overthrow, as of an army in battle; loss of a battle; repulse suffered; discomfiture; — opposed to victory.

Defeat.etym: [Cf. F. défaite, fr. défaire. See Defeat, v.]

senses.d: To ward or fend off; to drive back or away; to repel.
q: Th' other strove for to defend The force of Vulcan with his might and main.

senses.d: To prohibit; to forbid.
q: Which God defend that I should wring from him.

senses.d: To repel danger or harm from; to protect; to secure against attack; to maintain against force or argument; to uphold; to guard; as, to defend a town; to defend a cause; to defend character; to defend the absent; — sometimes followed by from or against; as, to defend one's self from, or against, one's enemies.
q: The lord mayor craves aid . . . to defend the city.
God defend the right!
A village near it was defended by the river.

senses.d: To deny the right of the plaintiff in regard to (the suit, or the wrong charged); to oppose or resist, as a claim at law; to contest, as a suit.
q: As birds flying, so will the Lord of hosts defend Jerusalem; defending also he will deliver it.
Leave not the faithful side That gave thee being, still shades thee and protects.

Defend.etym: [F. défendre, L. defendere; de- + fendere (only in comp.) to strike; perh. akin to Gr. θείνειν to strike, and E. dint. Cf. Dint, Defense, Fend.]

senses.d: To put off; to postpone to a future time; to delay the execution of; to delay; to withhold.
q: Defer the spoil of the city until night.
God . . . will not long defer To vindicate the glory of his name.

Defer.etym: [OE. differren, F. différer, fr. L. differre to delay, bear different ways; dis- + ferre to bear. See Bear to support, and cf. Differ, Defer to offer.]

senses.d: To put off; to delay to act; to wait.
q: Pius was able to defer and temporize at leisure.

senses.d: To render or offer.
q: Worship deferred to the Virgin.

senses.d: To lay before; to submit in a respectful manner; to refer; — with to.
q: Hereupon the commissioners . . . deferred the matter to the Earl of Northumberland.

Defer.etym: [F. déférer to pay deference, to yield, to bring before a judge, fr. L. deferre to bring down; de- + ferre to bear. See Bear to support, and cf. Defer to delay, Delate.]

senses.d: To yield deference to the wishes of another; to submit to the opinion of another, or to authority; — with to.
q: The house, deferring to legal right, acquiesced.

senses.d: To march off in a line, file by file; to file off.

Defile.etym: [F. défiler; pref. dé-, for des- (L. dis-) + file a row or line. See File a row.]

senses.d: Same as Defilade.
Any narrow passage or gorge in which troops can march only in a file, or with a narrow front; a long, narrow pass between hills, rocks, etc.
The act of defilading a fortress, or of raising the exterior works in order to protect the interior. See Defilade.

Defile.etym: [Cf. F. défilé, fr. défiler to defile.]

senses.d: To make foul or impure; to make filthy; to dirty; to befoul; to pollute.
q: They that touch pitch will be defiled.

senses.d: To soil or sully; to tarnish, as reputation; to taint.
q: He is . . . among the greatest prelates of this age, however his character may be defiled by . . . dirty hands.

senses.d: To injure in purity of character; to corrupt.
q: Defile not yourselves with the idols of Egypt.

senses.d: To corrupt the chastity of; to debauch; to violate.
q: The husband murder'd and the wife defiled.

senses.d: To make ceremonially unclean; to pollute.
q: That which dieth of itself, or is torn with beasts, he shall not eat to defile therewith.

Defile.etym: [OE. defoulen, -foilen, to tread down, OF. defouler; de- + fouler to trample (see Full, v. t.), and OE. defoulen to foul (influenced in form by the older verb defoilen). See File to defile, Foul, Defoul.]

senses.d: To deprive of some right, interest, or property, by a deceitful device; to withhold from wrongfully; to injure by embezzlement; to cheat; to overreach; as, to defraud a servant, or a creditor, or the state; — with of before the thing taken or withheld.
q: We have defrauded no man.
Churches seem injured and defrauded of their rights.

Defraud.etym: [L. defraudare; de- + fraudare to cheat, fr. fraus, fraudis, fraud: cf. OF. defrauder. See Fraud.]

senses.d: To renounce or dissolve all bonds of affiance, faith, or obligation with; to reject, refuse, or renounce.
q: I defy the surety and the bond.
For thee I have defied my constant mistress.

senses.d: To provoke to combat or strife; to call out to combat; to challenge; to dare; to brave; to set at defiance; to treat with contempt; as, to defy an enemy; to defy the power of a magistrate; to defy the arguments of an opponent; to defy public opinion.
q: I once again Defy thee to the trial of mortal fight.
I defy the enemies of our constitution to show the contrary.

Defy.etym: [F. défier, OF. deffier, desfier, LL. disfidare to disown faith or fidelity, to dissolve the bond of allegiance, as between the vassal and his lord; hence, to challenge, defy; fr. L. dis- + fides faith. See Faith, and cf. Diffident, Affiance.]

senses.d: A challenge.
Having become worse than one's kind, or one's former state; having declined in worth; having lost in goodness; deteriorated; degraded; unworthy; base; low.
q: Faint-hearted and degenerate king.
A degenerate and degraded state.
Degenerate from their ancient blood.
These degenerate days.
I had planted thee a noble vine . . . : how then art thou turned into the degenerate plant of a strange vine unto me?

Degenerate.etym: [L. degeneratus, p. p. of degenerare to degenerate, cause to degenerate, fr. degener base, degenerate, that departs from its race or kind; de- + genus race, kind. See Kin relationship.]

senses.d: To be or grow worse than one's kind, or than one was originally; hence, to be inferior; to grow poorer, meaner, or more vicious; to decline in good qualities; to deteriorate.
q: When wit transgresseth decency, it degenerates into insolence and impiety.

senses.d: To fall off from the normal quality or the healthy structure of its kind; to become of a lower type.
A step, stair, or staircase.
q: By ladders, or else by degree.

senses.d: One of a series of progressive steps upward or downward, in quality, rank, acquirement, and the like; a stage in progression; grade; gradation; as, degrees of vice and virtue; to advance by slow degrees; degree of comparison.
The point or step of progression to which a person has arrived; rank or station in life; position.
Measure of advancement; quality; extent; as, tastes differ in kind as well as in degree.
q: The degree of excellence which proclaims genius, is different in different times and different places.

senses.d: Grade or rank to which scholars are admitted by a college or university, in recognition of their attainments; as, the degree of bachelor of arts, master, doctor, etc.
q: The youth attained his bachelor's degree, and left the university.

senses.d: A certain distance or remove in the line of descent, determining the proximity of blood; one remove in the chain of relationship; as, a relation in the third or fourth degree.
q: In the 11th century an opinion began to gain ground in Italy, that third cousins might marry, being in the seventh degree according to the civil law.

senses.d: Three figures taken together in numeration; thus, 140 is one degree, 222,140 two degrees.

State as indicated by sum of exponents; more particularly, the degree of a term is indicated by the sum of the exponents of its literal factors; thus, a2b3c is a term of the sixth degree. The degree of a power, or radical, is denoted by its index, that of an equation by the greatest sum of the exponents of the unknown quantities in any term; thus, ax4 + bx2 = c, and mx2y2 + nyx = p, are both equations of the fourth degree.
A 360th part of the circumference of a circle, which part is taken as the principal unit of measure for arcs and angles. The degree is divided into 60 minutes and the minute into 60 seconds.
A division, space, or interval, marked on a mathematical or other instrument, as on a thermometer.
A line or space of the staff.
q: It has been said that Scotsmen . . . are . . . grave to a degree on occasions when races more favored by nature are gladsome to excess.

Degree.etym: [F. degré, OF. degret, fr. LL. degradare. See Degrade.]

senses.d: A putting off or deferring; procrastination; lingering inactivity; stop; detention; hindrance.
q: Without any delay, on the morrow I sat on the judgment seat.
The government ought to be settled without the delay of a day.

Delay.etym: [F. délai, fr. OF. deleer to delay, or fr. L. dilatum, which, though really from a different root, is used in Latin only as a p. p. neut. of differre to carry apart, defer, delay. See Tolerate, and cf. Differ, Delay, v.]

senses.d: To put off; to defer; to procrastinate; to prolong the time of or before.
q: My lord delayeth his coming.

senses.d: To retard; to stop, detain, or hinder, for a time; to retard the motion, or time of arrival, of; as, the mail is delayed by a heavy fall of snow.
q: Thyrsis! whose artful strains have oft delayed The huddling brook to hear his madrigal.

senses.d: To allay; to temper.
q: The watery showers delay the raging wind.

Delay.etym: [OF. deleer, delaier, fr. the noun délai, or directly fr. L. dilatare to enlarge, dilate, in LL., to put off. See Delay, n., and cf. Delate, 1st Defer, Dilate.]

senses.d: To move slowly; to stop for a time; to linger; to tarry.
q: There seem to be certain bounds to the quickness and slowness of the succession of those ideas, . . . beyond which they can neither delay nor hasten.

senses.d: Highly pleasing; delightful.
q: Delectable both to behold and taste.

Delectable.etym: [OF. delitable, OF. delitable, F. délectable, fr. L. delectabilis, fr. delectare to delight. See Delight.]

senses.d: The state or condition of being delicate; agreeableness to the senses; delightfulness; as, delicacy of flavor, of odor, and the like.
q: What choice to choose for delicacy best.

senses.d: Nicety or fineness of form, texture, or constitution; softness; elegance; smoothness; tenderness; and hence, frailty or weakness; as, the delicacy of a fiber or a thread; delicacy of a hand or of the human form; delicacy of the skin; delicacy of frame.

Nice propriety of manners or conduct; susceptibility or tenderness of feeling; refinement; fastidiousness; and hence, in an exaggerated sense, effeminacy; as, great delicacy of behavior; delicacy in doing a kindness; delicacy of character that unfits for earnest action.
q: You know your mother's delicacy in this point.

senses.d: Addiction to pleasure; luxury; daintiness; indulgence; luxurious or voluptuous treatment.
q: And to those dainty limbs which Nature lent For gentle usage and soft delicacy?

senses.d: Nice and refined perception and discrimination; critical niceness; fastidious accuracy.
q: That Augustan delicacy of taste which is the boast of the great public schools of England.

senses.d: The state of being affected by slight causes; sensitiveness; as, the delicacy of a chemist's balance.
That which is alluring, delicate, or refined; a luxury or pleasure; something pleasant to the senses, especially to the sense of taste; a dainty; as, delicacies of the table.
q: The merchants of the earth are waxed rich through the abundance of her delicacies.

senses.d: Pleasure; gratification; delight.
q: He Rome brent for his delicacie.

senses.d: Addicted to pleasure; luxurious; voluptuous; alluring.
q: Dives, for his delicate life, to the devil went.
Haarlem is a very delicate town.

senses.d: Pleasing to the senses; refinedly agreeable; hence, adapted to please a nice or cultivated taste; nice; fine; elegant; as, a delicate dish; delicate flavor.
Slight and shapely; lovely; graceful; as, “a delicate creature.”
Fine or slender; minute; not coarse; — said of a thread, or the like; as, delicate cotton.
Slight or smooth; light and yielding; — said of texture; as, delicate lace or silk.
Soft and fair; — said of the skin or a surface; as, a delicate cheek; a delicate complexion.
Light, or softly tinted; — said of a color; as, a delicate blue.
Refined; gentle; scrupulous not to trespass or offend; considerate; — said of manners, conduct, or feelings; as, delicate behavior; delicate attentions; delicate thoughtfulness.
Tender; not able to endure hardship; feeble; frail; effeminate; — said of constitution, health, etc.; as, a delicate child; delicate health.
q: A delicate and tender prince.

senses.d: Requiring careful handling; not to be rudely or hastily dealt with; nice; critical; as, a delicate subject or question.
q: There are some things too delicate and too sacred to be handled rudely without injury to truth.

senses.d: Of exacting tastes and habits; dainty; fastidious.
Nicely discriminating or perceptive; refinedly critical; sensitive; exquisite; as, a delicate taste; a delicate ear for music.

Delicate.etym: [L. delicatus pleasing the senses, voluptuous, soft and tender; akin to deliciae delight: cf. F. délicat. See Delight.]

senses.d: A choice dainty; a delicacy.
q: With abstinence all delicates he sees.

senses.d: A delicate, luxurious, or effeminate person.
q: All the vessels, then, which our delicates have, — those I mean that would seem to be more fine in their houses than their neighbors, — are only of the Corinth metal.

senses.d: In a delicate manner.
The quality of being delicate.
Affording exquisite pleasure; delightful; most sweet or grateful to the senses, especially to the taste; charming.
q: Some delicious landscape.
