One draught of spring's delicious air.
Were not his words delicious?

senses.d: Addicted to pleasure; seeking enjoyment; luxurious; effeminate.
q: Others, lastly, of a more delicious and airy spirit, retire themselves to the enjoyments of ease and luxury.
Like the rich fruit he sings, delicious in decay.
No spring, nor summer, on the mountain seen, Smiles with gay fruits or with delightful green.

Delicious.etym: [OF. delicieus, F. délicieux, L. deliciosus, fr. deliciae delight, fr. delicere to allure. See Delight.]

senses.d: Delightfully; as, to feed deliciously; to be deliciously entertained.
A high degree of gratification of mind; a high- wrought state of pleasurable feeling; lively pleasure; extreme satisfaction; joy.
q: Sounds and sweet airs, that give delight and hurt not.
A fool hath no delight in understanding.

senses.d: That which gives great pleasure or delight.
q: Heaven's last, best gift, my ever new delight.

senses.d: Licentious pleasure; lust.

Delight.etym: [OE. delit, OF. delit, deleit, fr. delitier, to delight. See Delight, v. t.]

senses.d: To give delight to; to affect with great pleasure; to please highly; as, a beautiful landscape delights the eye; harmony delights the ear.
q: Inventions to delight the taste.
Delight our souls with talk of knightly deeds.

Delight.etym: [OE. deliten, OF. delitier, deleitier, F. délecter, fr. L. delectare to entice away, to delight (sc. by attracting or alluring), intens. of delicere to allure, delight; de- + lacere to entice, allure; cf. laqueus a snare. Cf. Delectate, Delicate, Delicious, Dilettante, Elicit, Lace.]

senses.d: To have or take great delight or pleasure; to be greatly pleased or rejoiced; — followed by an infinitive, or by in.
q: Love delights in praises.
I delight to do thy will, O my God.

senses.d: Endowed with delight.
q: If virtue no delighted beauty lack.

senses.d: Very pleasing; delightful.
q: Ye shall be a delightsome land, . . . saith the Lord.

senses.d: The mistress of Samson, who betrayed him (Judges xvi.); hence, a harlot; a temptress.
q: Other Delilahs on a smaller scale Burns met with during his Dumfries sojourn.

senses.d: To set free from restraint; to set at liberty; to release; to liberate, as from control; to give up; to free; to save; to rescue from evil actual or feared; — often with from or out of; as, to deliver one from captivity, or from fear of death.
q: He that taketh warning shall deliver his soul.
Promise was that I Should Israel from Philistian yoke deliver.

senses.d: To give or transfer; to yield possession or control of; to part with (to); to make over; to commit; to surrender; to resign; — often with up or over, to or into.
q: Thou shalt deliver Pharaoh's cup into his hand.
The constables have delivered her over.
The exalted mind All sense of woe delivers to the wind.

senses.d: To make over to the knowledge of another; to communicate; to utter; to speak; to impart.
q: Till he these words to him deliver might.
Whereof the former delivers the precepts of the art, and the latter the perfection.

senses.d: To give forth in action or exercise; to discharge; as, to deliver a blow; to deliver a broadside, or a ball.
q: Shaking his head and delivering some show of tears.
An uninstructed bowler . . . thinks to attain the jack by delivering his bowl straightforward upon it.

senses.d: To free from, or disburden of, young; to relieve of a child in childbirth; to bring forth; — often with of.
q: She was delivered safe and soon.
Tully was long ere he could be delivered of a few verses, and those poor ones.

senses.d: To discover; to show.
q: I 'll deliver Myself your loyal servant.

senses.d: To deliberate.
To admit; to allow to pass.

Deliver.syn: To Deliver, Give Forth, Discharge, Liberate, Pronounce, Utter.
Deliver.etym: [F. délivrer, LL. deliberare to liberate, give over, fr. L. de + liberare to set free. See Liberate.]

senses.d: Free; nimble; sprightly; active.
q: Wonderly deliver and great of strength.

Deliver.etym: [OF. delivre free, unfettered. See Deliver, v. t.]

senses.d: The act of delivering or freeing from restraint, captivity, peril, and the like; rescue; as, the deliverance of a captive.
q: He hath sent me to heal the broken-hearted, to preach deliverance to the captives.
One death or one deliverance we will share.

senses.d: Act of bringing forth children.
Act of speaking; utterance.
The state of being delivered, or freed from restraint.
q: I do desire deliverance from these officers.

senses.d: Anything delivered or communicated; esp., an opinion or decision expressed publicly.
Any fact or truth which is decisively attested or intuitively known as a psychological or philosophical datum; as, the deliverance of consciousness.
One who delivers or rescues; a preserver.
One who relates or communicates.
The act of delivering from restraint; rescue; release; liberation; as, the delivery of a captive from his dungeon.
The act of delivering up or over; surrender; transfer of the body or substance of a thing; distribution; as, the delivery of a fort, of hostages, of a criminal, of goods, of letters.
The act or style of utterance; manner of speaking; as, a good delivery; a clear delivery.
The act of giving birth; parturition; the expulsion or extraction of a fetus and its membranes.
The act of exerting one's strength or limbs.
q: Neater limbs and freer delivery.

senses.d: The act or manner of delivering a ball; as, the pitcher has a swift delivery.
The act of deluding; deception; a misleading of the mind.
The state of being deluded or misled.
That which is falsely or delusively believed or propagated; false belief; error in belief.
q: And fondly mourned the dear delusion gone.

senses.d: To ask or call for with authority; to claim or seek from, as by authority or right; to claim, as something due; to call for urgently or peremptorily; as, to demand a debt; to demand obedience.
q: This, in our foresaid holy father's name, Pope Innocent, I do demand of thee.

senses.d: To inquire authoritatively or earnestly; to ask, esp. in a peremptory manner; to question.
q: I did demand what news from Shrewsbury.

senses.d: To require as necessary or useful; to be in urgent need of; hence, to call for; as, the case demands care.
To call into court; to summon.

Demand.etym: [F. demander, LL. demandare to demand, summon, send word, fr. L. demandare to give in charge, intrust; de- + mandare to commit to one's charge, commission, order, command. Cf. Mandate, Commend.]

senses.d: To make a demand; to inquire.
q: The soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do?

senses.d: The act of demanding; an asking with authority; a peremptory urging of a claim; a claiming or challenging as due; requisition; as, the demand of a creditor; a note payable on demand.
q: The demand by the word of the holy ones.
He that has confidence to turn his wishes into demands will be but a little way from thinking he ought to obtain them.

senses.d: Earnest inquiry; question; query.
A diligent seeking or search; manifested want; desire to possess; request; as, a demand for certain goods; a person's company is in great demand.
q: In 1678 came forth a second edition with additions; and then the demand became immense.

senses.d: That which one demands or has a right to demand; thing claimed as due; claim; as, demands on an estate.
The asking or seeking for what is due or claimed as due.

Demand.etym: [F. demande, fr. demander. See Demand, v. t.]

senses.d: The act of demonstrating; an exhibition; proof; especially, proof beyond the possibility of doubt; indubitable evidence, to the senses or reason.
q: Those intervening ideas which serve to show the agreement of any two others are called “proofs;” and where agreement or disagreement is by this means plainly and clearly perceived, it is called demonstration.

senses.d: An expression, as of the feelings, by outward signs; a manifestation; a show.
q: Did your letters pierce the queen to any demonstration of grief?
Loyal demonstrations toward the prince.

senses.d: The exhibition and explanation of a dissection or other anatomical preparation.
(Mil.) a decisive exhibition of force, or a movement indicating an attack.
The act of proving by the syllogistic process, or the proof itself.
A course of reasoning showing that a certain result is a necessary consequence of assumed premises; — these premises being definitions, axioms, and previously established propositions.
A small cavern or hollow place in the side of a hill, or among rocks; esp., a cave used by a wild beast for shelter or concealment; as, a lion's den; a den of robbers.
A squalid place of resort; a wretched dwelling place; a haunt; as, a den of vice.
Any snug or close retreat where one goes to be alone.
A narrow glen; a ravine; a dell.

Den.etym: [AS. denn; perh. akin to G. tenne floor, thrashing floor, and to AS. denu valley.]

senses.d: To live in, or as in, a den.
q: The sluggish salvages that den below.

senses.d: To make known in a solemn or official manner; to declare; to proclaim (especially an evil).
q: Denouncing wrath to come.
I denounce unto you this day, that ye shall surely perish.

senses.d: To proclaim in a threatening manner; to threaten by some outward sign or expression.
q: His look denounced desperate.

senses.d: To point out as deserving of reprehension or punishment, etc.; to accuse in a threatening manner; to invoke censure upon; to stigmatize.
q: Denounced for a heretic.
To denounce the immoralities of Julius Cæsar.

Denounce.etym: [F. dénoncer, OF. denoncier, fr. L. denuntiare, denunciare; de- + nunciare, nuntiare, to announce, report, nuntius a messenger, message. See Nuncio, and cf. Denunciate.]

senses.d: To declare not to be true; to gainsay; to contradict; — opposed to affirm, allow, or admit.
To refuse (to do something or to accept something); to reject; to decline; to renounce.
To refuse to grant; to withhold; to refuse to gratify or yield to; as, to deny a request.
q: Who finds not Providence all good and wise, Alike in what it gives, and what denies?
To some men, it is more agreeable to deny a vicious inclination, than to gratify it.

senses.d: To disclaim connection with, responsibility for, and the like; to refuse to acknowledge; to disown; to abjure; to disavow.
q: The falsehood of denying his opinion.
Thou thrice denied, yet thrice beloved.
Let him deny himself, and take up his cross.

Deny.etym: [OE. denien, denaien, OF. denier, deneer, F. dénier, fr. L. denegare; de- + negare to say no, deny. See Negation.]

senses.d: To answer in ��� negative; to declare an assertion not to be true.
q: Then Sarah denied, saying, I laughed not; for she was afraid.

senses.d: To part; to divide; to separate.

To go forth or away; to quit, leave, or separate, as from a place or a person; to withdraw; — opposed to arrive; — often with from before the place, person, or thing left, and for or to before the destination.
q: I will depart to mine own land.
Ere thou from hence depart.
He which hath no stomach to this fight, Let him depart.

senses.d: To forsake; to abandon; to desist or deviate (from); not to adhere to; — with from; as, we can not depart from our rules; to depart from a title or defense in legal pleading.
q: If the plan of the convention be found to depart from republican principles.

senses.d: To pass away; to perish.
q: The glory is departed from Israel.

senses.d: To quit this world; to die.
q: Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace.

Depart.etym: [OE. departen to divide, part, depart, F. départir to divide, distribute, se départir to separate one's self, depart; pref. dé- (L. de) + partir to part, depart, fr. L. partire, partiri, to divide, fr. pars part. See Part.]

senses.d: To part thoroughly; to dispart; to divide; to separate.
q: Till death departed them, this life they lead.

senses.d: To divide in order to share; to apportion.
q: And here is gold, and that full great plentee, That shall departed been among us three.

senses.d: To leave; to depart from.
Division; separation, as of compound substances into their ingredients.
q: The chymists have a liquor called water of depart.

senses.d: A going away; departure; hence, death.
q: At my depart for France.
Your loss and his depart.

senses.d: Division; separation; putting away.
q: No other remedy . . . but absolute departure.

senses.d: Separation or removal from a place; the act or process of departing or going away.
q: Departure from this happy place.

senses.d: Removal from the present life; death; decease.
q: The time of my departure is at hand.
His timely departure . . . barred him from the knowledge of his son's miseries.

senses.d: Deviation or abandonment, as from or of a rule or course of action, a plan, or a purpose.
q: Any departure from a national standard.

senses.d: The desertion by a party to any pleading of the ground taken by him in his last antecedent pleading, and the adoption of another.
The distance due east or west which a person or ship passes over in going along an oblique line.
To lay down; to divest one's self of; to lay aside.
q: Thus when the state one Edward did depose, A greater Edward in his room arose.

senses.d: To let fall; to deposit.
q: Additional mud deposed upon it.

senses.d: To remove from a throne or other high station; to dethrone; to divest or deprive of office.
q: A tyrant over his subjects, and therefore worthy to be deposed.

senses.d: To testify under oath; to bear testimony to; — now usually said of bearing testimony which is officially written down for future use.
q: To depose the yearly rent or valuation of lands.

senses.d: To put under oath.
q: Depose him in the justice of his cause.

Depose.etym: [FF. déposer, in the sense of L. deponere to put down; but from pref. dé- (L. de) + poser to place. See Pose, Pause.]

senses.d: To bear witness; to testify under oath; to make deposition.
q: Then, seeing't was he that made you to despose, Your oath, my lord, is vain and frivolous.

senses.d: To take away; to put an end; to destroy.
q: 'Tis honor to deprive dishonored life.

senses.d: To dispossess; to bereave; to divest; to hinder from possessing; to debar; to shut out from; — with a remoter object, usually preceded by of.
q: God hath deprived her of wisdom.
It was seldom that anger deprived him of power over himself.

senses.d: To divest of office; to depose; to dispossess of dignity, especially ecclesiastical.
q: A minister deprived for inconformity.

Deprive.etym: [LL. deprivare, deprivatium, to divest of office; L. de- + privare to bereave, deprive: cf. OF. depriver. See Private.]

senses.d: The quality of being deep; deepness; perpendicular measurement downward from the surface, or horizontal measurement backward from the front; as, the depth of a river; the depth of a body of troops.
Profoundness; extent or degree of intensity; abundance; completeness; as, depth of knowledge, or color.
q: Mindful of that heavenly love Which knows no end in depth or height.

senses.d: Lowness; as, depth of sound.
That which is deep; a deep, or the deepest, part or place; the deep; the middle part; as, the depth of night, or of winter.
q: From you unclouded depth above.
The depth closed me round about.

senses.d: The number of simple elements which an abstract conception or notion includes; the comprehension or content.
A pair of toothed wheels which work together.

Depth.etym: [From Deep; akin to D. diepte, Icel. dȳpt, dȳpð, Goth. diupiþa.]

senses.d: The perpendicular distance from the chord to the farthest point of an arched surface.
To appoint as deputy or agent; to commission to act in one's place; to delegate.
q: There is no man deputed of the king to hear thee.
Some persons, deputed by a meeting.

senses.d: To appoint; to assign; to choose.
q: The most conspicuous places in cities are usually deputed for the erection of statues.

Depute.etym: [F. députer, fr. L. deputare to esteem, consider, in LL., to destine, allot; de- + putare to clean, prune, clear up, set in order, reckon, think. See Pure.]

senses.d: A person deputed; a deputy.

One appointed as the substitute of another, and empowered to act for him, in his name or his behalf; a substitute in office; a lieutenant; a representative; a delegate; a vicegerent; as, the deputy of a prince, of a sheriff, of a township, etc.
q: There was then no king in Edom; a deputy was king.
God's substitute, His deputy anointed in His sight.

senses.d: A member of the Chamber of Deputies.

Deputy.syn: Substitute; representative; legate; delegate; envoy; agent; factor.
Deputy.etym: [F. député, fr. LL. deputatus. See Depute.]

senses.d: To laugh at with contempt; to laugh to scorn; to turn to ridicule or make sport of; to mock; to scoff at.
q: And the Pharisees, also, . . . derided him.
Sport that wrinkled Care derides. And Laughter holding both his sides.

Deride.syn: To mock; laugh at; ridicule; insult; taunt; jeer; banter; rally.
Deride.etym: [L. deridere, derisum; de- + rid�re to laugh. See Ridicule.]

senses.d: The act of deriding, or the state of being derided; mockery; scornful or contemptuous treatment which holds one up to ridicule.
q: He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh; the Lord shall have them in derision.
Satan beheld their plight, And to his mates thus in derision called.

senses.d: An object of derision or scorn; a laughing-stock.
q: I was a derision to all my people.

Derision.etym: [L. derisio: cf. F. dérision. See Deride.]

senses.d: To pass from a higher to a lower place; to move downwards; to come or go down in any way, as by falling, flowing, walking, etc.; to plunge; to fall; to incline downward; — the opposite of ascend.
q: The rain descended, and the floods came.
We will here descend to matters of later date.

senses.d: To enter mentally; to retire.
q: with holiest meditations fed, Into himself descended.

senses.d: To make an attack, or incursion, as if from a vantage ground; to come suddenly and with violence; — with on or upon.
q: And on the suitors let thy wrath descend.

senses.d: To come down to a lower, less fortunate, humbler, less virtuous, or worse, state or station; to lower or abase one's self; as, he descended from his high estate.
To pass from the more general or important to the particular or less important matters to be considered.

To come down, as from a source, original, or stock; to be derived; to proceed by generation or by transmission; to fall or pass by inheritance; as, the beggar may descend from a prince; a crown descends to the heir.
To move toward the south, or to the southward.
To fall in pitch; to pass from a higher to a lower tone.

Descend.etym: [F. descendre, L. descendere, descensum; de- + scandere to climb. See Scan.]

senses.d: To go down upon or along; to pass from a higher to a lower part of; as, they descended the river in boats; to descend a ladder.
q: But never tears his cheek descended.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to descent; moving downwards.
The act of descending, or passing downward; change of place from higher to lower.
Incursion; sudden attack; especially, hostile invasion from sea; — often followed by upon or on; as, to make a descent upon the enemy.
q: The United Provinces . . . ordered public prayer to God, when they feared that the French and English fleets would make a descent upon their coasts.

senses.d: Progress downward, as in station, virtue, as in station, virtue, and the like, from a higher to a lower state, from a higher to a lower state, from the more to the less important, from the better to the worse, etc.
Derivation, as from an ancestor; procedure by generation; lineage; birth; extraction.
Transmission of an estate by inheritance, usually, but not necessarily, in the descending line; title to inherit an estate by reason of consanguinity.
Inclination downward; a descending way; inclined or sloping surface; declivity; slope; as, a steep descent.
That which is descended; descendants; issue.
q: If care of our descent perplex us most, Which must be born to certain woe.

senses.d: A step or remove downward in any scale of gradation; a degree in the scale of genealogy; a generation.
q: No man living is a thousand descents removed from Adam himself.

senses.d: Lowest place; extreme downward place.
q: And from the extremest upward of thy head, To the descent and dust below thy foot.

senses.d: A passing from a higher to a lower tone.

Descent.syn: Declivity; slope; degradation; extraction; lineage; assault; invasion; attack.
Descent.etym: [F. descente, fr. descendre; like vente, from vendre. See Descend.]

senses.d: To represent by drawing; to draw a plan of; to delineate; to trace or mark out; as, to describe a circle by the compasses; a torch waved about the head in such a way as to describe a circle.
To represent by words written or spoken; to give an account of; to make known to others by words or signs; as, the geographer describes countries and cities.
To distribute into parts, groups, or classes; to mark off; to class.
q: Passed through the land, and described it by cities into seven parts in a book.

Describe.syn: To set forth; represent; delineate; relate; recount; narrate; express; explain; depict; portray; chracterize.
Describe.etym: [L. describere, descriptum; de- + scribere to write: cf. OE. descriven, OF. descrivre, F. décrire. See Scribe, and cf. Descry.]

senses.d: To use the faculty of describing; to give a description; as, Milton describes with uncommon force and beauty.
The act of describing; a delineation by marks or signs.
A sketch or account of anything in words; a portraiture or representation in language; an enumeration of the essential qualities of a thing or species.
q: Milton has descriptions of morning.

senses.d: A class to which a certain representation is applicable; kind; sort.
q: A difference . . . between them and another description of public creditors.
The plates were all of the meanest description.

Description.syn: Account; definition; recital; relation; detail; narrative; narration; explanation; delineation; representation; kind; sort. See Definition.

senses.d: To spy out or discover by the eye, as objects distant or obscure; to espy; to recognize; to discern; to discover.
q: And the house of Joseph sent to descry Bethel.
Edmund, I think, is gone . . . to descry The strength o' the enemy.
And now their way to earth they had descried.

senses.d: To discover; to disclose; to reveal.
q: His purple robe he had thrown aside, lest it should descry him.

Descry.syn: To see; behold; espy; discover; discern.
Descry.etym: [OE. descrien, discrien, to espy, prob. from the proclaiming of what was espied, fr. OF. descrier to proclaim, cry down, decry, F. décrier. The word was confused somewhat with OF. descriven, E. describe, OF. descrivre, from L. describere. See Decry.]

senses.d: Discovery or view, as of an army seen at a distance.
q: Near, and on speedy foot; the main descry Stands on the hourly thought.

senses.d: That which is deserved; the reward or the punishment justly due; claim to recompense, usually in a good sense; right to reward; merit.
q: According to their deserts will I judge them.
Andronicus, surnamed Pius For many good and great deserts to Rome.
His reputation falls far below his desert.

Desert.etym: [OF. deserte, desserte, merit, recompense, fr. deservir, desservir, to merit. See Deserve.]

senses.d: A deserted or forsaken region; a barren tract incapable of supporting population, as the vast sand plains of Asia and Africa which are destitute of moisture and vegetation.
q: A dreary desert and a gloomy waste.

senses.d: A tract, which may be capable of sustaining a population, but has been left unoccupied and uncultivated; a wilderness; a solitary place.
q: He will make her wilderness like Eden, and her desert like the garden of the Lord.
Before her extended Dreary and vast and silent, the desert of life.

Desert.etym: [F. désert, L. desertum, from desertus solitary, desert, pp. of deserere to desert; de- + serere to join together. See Series.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to a desert; forsaken; without life or cultivation; unproductive; waste; barren; wild; desolate; solitary; as, they landed on a desert island.
q: He . . . went aside privately into a desert place.
Full many a flower is born to blush unseen, And waste its sweetness on the desert air.

Desert.etym: [Cf. L. desertus, p. p. of deserere, and F. désert. See 2d Desert.]

senses.d: To leave (especially something which one should stay by and support); to leave in the lurch; to abandon; to forsake; — implying blame, except sometimes when used of localities; as, to desert a friend, a principle, a cause, one's country.
To abandon (the service) without leave; to forsake in violation of duty; to abscond from; as, to desert the army; to desert one's colors.

Desert.etym: [Cf. L. desertus, p. p. of deserere to desert, F. déserter. See 2d Desert.]

senses.d: To abandon a service without leave; to quit military service without permission, before the expiration of one's term; to abscond.
q: The soldiers . . . deserted in numbers.

Desert.syn: To abandon; forsake; leave; relinquish; renounce; quit; depart from; abdicate. See Abandon.

senses.d: To earn by service; to be worthy of (something due, either good or evil); to merit; to be entitled to; as, the laborer deserves his wages; a work of value deserves praise.
q: God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth.
John Gay deserved to be a favorite.
Encouragement is not held out to things that deserve reprehension.

senses.d: To serve; to treat; to benefit.
q: A man that hath So well deserved me.

Deserve.etym: [OF. deservir, desservir, to merit, L. deservire to serve zealously, be devoted to; de- + servire to serve. See Serve.]

senses.d: To be worthy of recompense; — usually with ill or with well.
q: One man may merit or deserve of another.

senses.d: Desert; merit.
q: A person of great deservings from the republic.

senses.d: Meritorious; worthy; as, a deserving person or act.
Worthy of desire or longing; fitted to excite desire or a wish to possess; pleasing; agreeable.
q: All of them desirable young men.
As things desirable excite Desire, and objects move the appetite.

Desirable.etym: [F. désirable, fr. L. desiderabilis. See Desire, v. t.]

senses.d: To long for; to wish for earnestly; to covet.
q: Neither shall any man desire thy land.
Ye desire your child to live.

senses.d: To express a wish for; to entreat; to request.
q: Then she said, Did I desire a son of my lord?
Desire him to go in; trouble him no more.

senses.d: To require; to demand; to claim.
q: A doleful case desires a doleful song.

senses.d: To miss; to regret.
q: She shall be pleasant while she lives, and desired when she dies.

Desire.syn: To long for; hanker after; covet; wish; ask; request; solicit; entreat; beg.
Desire.etym: [F. désirer, L. desiderare, origin uncertain, perh. fr. de- + sidus star, constellation, and hence orig., to turn the eyes from the stars. Cf. Consider, and Desiderate, and see Sidereal.]

senses.d: The natural longing that is excited by the enjoyment or the thought of any good, and impels to action or effort its continuance or possession; an eager wish to obtain or enjoy.
q: Unspeakable desire to see and know.

senses.d: An expressed wish; a request; petition.
q: And slowly was my mother brought To yield consent to my desire.

senses.d: Anything which is desired; an object of longing.
q: The Desire of all nations shall come.

senses.d: Excessive or morbid longing; lust; appetite.
Grief; regret.

Desire.syn: Wish; appetency; craving; inclination; eagerness; aspiration; longing.
Desire.etym: [F. désir, fr. désirer. See Desire, v. t.]

senses.d: Feeling desire; eagerly wishing; solicitous; eager to obtain; covetous.
q: Jesus knew that they were desirous to ask him.
Be not desirous of his dainties.

Desirous.etym: [F. désireux, OF. desiros, fr. desir. See Desire, n.]

senses.d: Destitute or deprived of inhabitants; deserted; uninhabited; hence, gloomy; as, a desolate isle; a desolate wilderness; a desolate house.
q: I will make Jerusalem . . . a den of dragons, and I will make the cities of Judah desolate, without an inhabitant.
And the silvery marish flowers that throng The desolate creeks and pools among.

senses.d: Laid waste; in a ruinous condition; neglected; destroyed; as, desolate altars.
Left alone; forsaken; lonely; comfortless.
q: Have mercy upon, for I am desolate.
Voice of the poor and desolate.

senses.d: Lost to shame; dissolute.
Destitute of; lacking in.
q: I were right now of tales desolate.

Desolate.etym: [L. desolatus, p. p. of desolare to leave alone, forsake; de- + solare to make lonely, solus alone. See Sole, a.]

senses.d: To make desolate; to leave alone; to deprive of inhabitants; as, the earth was nearly desolated by the flood.
To lay waste; to ruin; to ravage; as, a fire desolates a city.
q: Constructed in the very heart of a desolating war.

senses.d: The act of desolating or laying waste; destruction of inhabitants; depopulation.
q: Unto the end of the war desolations are determined.

senses.d: The state of being desolated or laid waste; ruin; solitariness; destitution; gloominess.
q: You would have sold your king to slaughter, . . . And his whole kingdom into desolation.

senses.d: A place or country wasted and forsaken.
q: How is Babylon become a desolation!

Desolation.syn: Waste; ruin; destruction; havoc; devastation; ravage; sadness; destitution; melancholy; gloom; gloominess.

senses.d: To be hopeless; to have no hope; to give up all hope or expectation; — often with of.
q: We despaired even of life.
Never despair of God's blessings here.

Despair.etym: [OE. despeiren, dispeiren, OF. desperer, fr. L. desperare; de- + sperare to hope; akin to spes hope, and perh. to spatium space, E. space, speed; cf. OF. espeir hope, F. espoir. Cf. Prosper, Desperate.]

senses.d: To give up as beyond hope or expectation; to despair of.
q: I would not despair the greatest design that could be attempted.

senses.d: To cause to despair.
Loss of hope; utter hopelessness; complete despondency.
q: We in dark dreams are tossing to and fro, Pine with regret, or sicken with despair.
Before he was ten, his sports were interrupted by fits of remorse and despair.

senses.d: That which is despaired of.
Without hope; given to despair; hopeless.
q: I am desperate of obtaining her.

senses.d: Beyond hope; causing despair; extremely perilous; irretrievable; past cure, or, at least, extremely dangerous; as, a desperate disease; desperate fortune.
Proceeding from, or suggested by, despair; without regard to danger or safety; reckless; furious; as, a desperate effort.
Extreme, in a bad sense; outrageous; — used to mark the extreme predominance of a bad quality.
q: A desperate offendress against nature.
The most desperate of reprobates.

Desperate.syn: Hopeless; despairing; desponding; rash; headlong; precipitate; irretrievable; irrecoverable; forlorn; mad; furious; frantic.
Desperate.etym: [L. desperatus, p. p. of desperare. See Despair, and cf. Desperado.]

senses.d: One desperate or hopeless.
In a desperate manner; without regard to danger or safety; recklessly; extremely; as, the troops fought desperately.
q: She fell desperately in love with him.

senses.d: To look down upon with disfavor or contempt; to contemn; to scorn; to disdain; to have a low opinion or contemptuous dislike of.
q: Fools despise wisdom and instruction.
Men naturally despise those who court them, but respect those who do not give way to them.

Despise.syn: To contemn; scorn; disdain; slight; undervalue. See Contemn.
Despise.etym: [OF. despis-, in some forms of despire to despise, fr. L. despicere, despectum, to look down upon, despise; de- + spicere, specere, to look. See Spy, and cf. Despicable, Despite.]

senses.d: One who despises; a contemner; a scorner.
Malice; malignity; spite; malicious anger; contemptuous hate.
q: With all thy despite against the land of Israel.

senses.d: An act of malice, hatred, or defiance; contemptuous defiance; a deed of contempt.
q: A despite done against the Most High.

Despite.etym: [OF. despit, F. dépit, fr. L. despectus contempt, fr. despicere. See Despise, and cf. Spite, Despect.]

senses.d: To vex; to annoy; to offend contemptuously.

Despite.etym: [OF. despitier, fr. L. despectare, intens. of despicere. See Despite, n.]

senses.d: In spite of; against, or in defiance of; notwithstanding; as, despite his prejudices.
Full of despite; expressing malice or contemptuous hate; malicious.
q: Haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters.
Pray for them which despitefully use you.
Let us examine him with despitefulness and fortune.

senses.d: Forsaken; not having in possession (something necessary, or desirable); deficient; lacking; devoid; — often followed by of.
q: In thee is my trust; leave not my soul destitute.
Totally destitute of all shadow of influence.

senses.d: Not possessing the necessaries of life; in a condition of want; needy; without possessions or resources; very poor.
q: They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented.

Destitute.etym: [L. destitutus, p. p. of destituere to set away, leave alone, forsake; de + statuere to set. See Statute.]

senses.d: To leave destitute; to forsake; to abandon.
q: To forsake or destitute a plantation.

senses.d: To make destitute; to cause to be in want; to deprive; — followed by of.
q: Destituted of all honor and livings.

senses.d: To disappoint.
q: When his expectation is destituted.

senses.d: To unbuild; to pull or tear down; to separate virulently into its constituent parts; to break up the structure and organic existence of; to demolish.
q: But ye shall destroy their altars, break their images, and cut down their groves.

senses.d: To ruin; to bring to naught; to put an end to; to annihilate; to consume.
q: I will utterly pluck up and destroy that nation.

senses.d: To put an end to the existence, prosperity, or beauty of; to kill.
q: If him by force he can destroy, or, worse, By some false guile pervert.

Destroy.syn: To demolish; lay waste; consume; raze; dismantle; ruin; throw down; overthrow; subvert; desolate; devastate; deface; extirpate; extinguish; kill; slay. See Demolish.
Destroy.etym: [OE. destroien, destruien, destrien, OF. destruire, F. détruire, fr. L. destruere, destructum; de + struere to pile up, build. See Structure.]

senses.d: One who destroys, ruins, kills, or desolates.
= Torpedo-boat destroyer.
The act of destroying; a tearing down; a bringing to naught; subversion; demolition; ruin; slaying; devastation.
q: The Jews smote all their enemies with the stroke of the sword, and slaughter, and destruction.
'Tis safer to be that which we destroy Than by destruction dwell in doubtful joy.
Destruction of venerable establishment.

senses.d: The state of being destroyed, demolished, ruined, slain, or devastated.
q: This town came to destruction.
Thou castedst them down into destruction.

senses.d: A destroying agency; a cause of ruin or of devastation; a destroyer.
q: The destruction that wasteth at noonday.

Destruction.syn: Demolition; subversion; overthrow; desolation; extirpation; extinction; devastation; downfall; extermination; havoc; ruin.
Destruction.etym: [L. destructio: cf. F. destruction. See Destroy.]

senses.d: To keep back or from; to withhold.
q: Detain not the wages of the hireling.

senses.d: To restrain from proceeding; to stay or stop; to delay; as, we were detained by an accident.
q: Let us detain thee, until we shall have made ready a kid for thee.

senses.d: To hold or keep in custody.

Detain.syn: To withhold; retain; stop; stay; arrest; check; retard; delay; hinder.
Detain.etym: [F. détenir, L. detinere, detentum; de + tenere to hold. See Tenable.]

senses.d: Detention.
Having defined limits; not uncertain or arbitrary; fixed; established; definite.
q: Quantity of words and a determinate number of feet.

senses.d: Conclusive; decisive; positive.
q: The determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God.

senses.d: Determined or resolved upon.
q: My determinate voyage.

senses.d: Of determined purpose; resolute.
q: More determinate to do than skillful how to do.

Determinate.etym: [L. determinatus, p. p. of determinare. See Determine.]

senses.d: To bring to an end; to determine. See Determine.
q: The sly, slow hours shall not determinate The dateless limit of thy dear exile.

senses.d: The act of determining, or the state of being determined.
Bringing to an end; termination; limit.
q: A speedy determination of that war.

senses.d: Direction or tendency to a certain end; impulsion.
q: Remissness can by no means consist with a constant determination of the will . . . to the greatest apparent good.

senses.d: The quality of mind which reaches definite conclusions; decision of character; resoluteness.
q: He only is a well-made man who has a good determination.

senses.d: The state of decision; a judicial decision, or ending of controversy.
That which is determined upon; result of deliberation; purpose; conclusion formed; fixed resolution.
q: So bloodthirsty a determination to obtain convictions.

senses.d: A flow, rush, or tendency to a particular part; as, a determination of blood to the head.

The act, process, or result of any accurate measurement, as of length, volume, weight, intensity, etc.; as, the determination of the ohm or of the wave length of light; the determination of the salt in sea water, or the oxygen in the air.
The act of defining a concept or notion by giving its essential constituents.

The act of determining the relations of an object, as regards genus and species; the referring of minerals, plants, or animals, to the species to which they belong; classification; as, I am indebted to a friend for the determination of most of these shells.

Determination.syn: Decision; conclusion; judgment; purpose; resolution; resolve; firmness. See Decision.
Determination.etym: [L. determinatio boundary, end: cf. F. détermination.]

senses.d: To fix the boundaries of; to mark off and separate.
q: hath determined the times before appointed.

senses.d: To set bounds to; to fix the determination of; to limit; to bound; to bring to an end; to finish.
q: The knowledge of men hitherto hath been determined by the view or sight.
Now, where is he that will not stay so long Till his friend sickness hath determined me?

senses.d: To fix the form or character of; to shape; to prescribe imperatively; to regulate; to settle.
q: The character of the soul is determined by the character of its God.
Something divinely beautiful . . . that at some time or other might influence or even determine her course of life.

senses.d: To fix the course of; to impel and direct; — with a remoter object preceded by to; as, another's will determined me to this course.
To ascertain definitely; to find out the specific character or name of; to assign to its true place in a system; as, to determine an unknown or a newly discovered plant or its name.
To bring to a conclusion, as a question or controversy; to settle authoritative or judicial sentence; to decide; as, the court has determined the cause.
To resolve on; to have a fixed intention of; also, to cause to come to a conclusion or decision; to lead; as, this determined him to go immediately.
To define or limit by adding a differentia.
To ascertain the presence, quantity, or amount of; as, to determine the parallax; to determine the salt in sea water.

Determine.etym: [F. déterminer, L. determinare, determinatum; de + terminare limit, terminus limit. See Term.]

senses.d: To come to an end; to end; to terminate.
q: He who has vented a pernicious doctrine or published an ill book must know that his life determine not together.
Estates may determine on future contingencies.

senses.d: To come to a decision; to decide; to resolve; — often with on.
q: He shall pay as the judges determine.

senses.d: Decided; resolute.
To witness against; to denounce; to condemn.
q: The heresy of Nestorius . . . was detested in the Eastern churches.
God hath detested them with his own mouth.

senses.d: To hate intensely; to abhor; to abominate; to loathe; as, we detest what is contemptible or evil.
q: Who dares think one thing, and another tell, My heart detests him as the gates of hell.

Detest.syn: To abhor; abominate; execrate. See Hate.
Detest.etym: [L. detestare, detestatum, and detestari, to curse while calling a deity to witness, to execrate, detest; de + testari to be a witness, testify, testis a witness: cf. F. détester. See Testify.]

senses.d: Worthy of being detested; abominable; extremely hateful; very odious; deserving abhorrence; as, detestable vices.
q: Thou hast defiled my sanctuary will all thy detestable things, and with all thine abominations.

senses.d: That which is devised, or formed by design; a contrivance; an invention; a project; a scheme; often, a scheme to deceive; a stratagem; an artifice.
q: His device in against Babylon, to destroy it.
Their recent device of demanding benevolences.
He disappointeth the devices of the crafty.

senses.d: Power of devising; invention; contrivance.
q: I must have instruments of my own device.

senses.d: An emblematic design, generally consisting of one or more figures with a motto, used apart from heraldic bearings to denote the historical situation, the ambition, or the desire of the person adopting it. See Cognizance.
q: Knights-errant used to distinguish themselves by devices on their shields.
A banner with this strange device - Excelsior.

senses.d: Anything fancifully conceived.
A spectacle or show.
Opinion; decision.

Device.syn: Contrivance; invention; design; scheme; project; stratagem; shift.
Device.etym: [OE. devis, devise, will, intention, opinion, invention, fr. F. devis architect's plan and estimates (in OF., division, plan, wish), devise device (in sense 3), in OF. also, division, wish, last will, fr. deviser. See Devise, v. t., and cf. Devise, n.]

senses.d: The Evil One; Satan, represented as the tempter and spiritual of mankind.
q: being forty days tempted of the devil.
That old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world.

senses.d: An evil spirit; a demon.
q: A dumb man possessed with a devil.

senses.d: A very wicked person; hence, any great evil.
q: Have not I chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?

senses.d: An expletive of surprise, vexation, or emphasis, or, ironically, of negation.
q: The devil a puritan that he is, . . . but a timepleaser.
The things, we know, are neither rich nor rare, But wonder how the devil they got there.

senses.d: A dish, as a bone with the meat, broiled and excessively peppered; a grill with Cayenne pepper.
q: Men and women busy in baking, broiling, roasting oysters, and preparing devils on the gridiron.

senses.d: A machine for tearing or cutting rags, cotton, etc.

Devil.etym: [AS. deófol, deóful; akin to G. �eufel, Goth. diabaúlus; all fr. L. diabolus the devil, Gr. � the devil, the slanderer, fr. � to slander, calumniate, orig., to throw across; � across + � to throw, let fall, fall; cf. Skr. gal to fall. Cf. Diabolic.]

senses.d: To make like a devil; to invest with the character of a devil.
To grill with Cayenne pepper; to season highly in cooking, as with pepper.
q: A deviled leg of turkey.

senses.d: Resembling, characteristic of, or pertaining to, the devil; diabolical; wicked in the extreme.
q: This wisdom descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish.

senses.d: Extreme; excessive.

Devilish.syn: Diabolical; infernal; hellish; satanic; wicked; malicious; detestable; destructive.

senses.d: To form in the mind by new combinations of ideas, new applications of principles, or new arrangement of parts; to formulate by thought; to contrive; to excogitate; to invent; to plan; to scheme; as, to devise an engine, a new mode of writing, a plan of defense, or an argument.
q: To devise curious works.
Devising schemes to realize his ambitious views.

senses.d: To plan or scheme for; to purpose to obtain.
q: For wisdom is most riches; fools therefore They are which fortunes do by vows devise.

senses.d: To say; to relate; to describe.
To imagine; to guess.
To give by will; — used of real estate; formerly, also, of chattels.

Devise.syn: To bequeath; invent; discover; contrive; excogitate; imagine; plan; scheme. See Bequeath.
Devise.etym: [OF. deviser to distribute, regulate, direct, relate, F., to chat, fr. L. divisus divided, distributed, p. p. of dividere. See Divide, and cf. Device.]

senses.d: To form a scheme; to lay a plan; to contrive; to consider.
q: I thought, devised, and Pallas heard my prayer.

senses.d: The act of giving or disposing of real estate by will; — sometimes improperly applied to a bequest of personal estate.
A will or testament, conveying real estate; the clause of a will making a gift of real property.
q: Fines upon devises were still exacted.

senses.d: Property devised, or given by will.

Devise.etym: [OF. devise division, deliberation, wish, will, testament. See Device.]

senses.d: Device. See Device.
To appropriate by vow; to set apart or dedicate by a solemn act; to consecrate; also, to consign over; to doom; to evil; to devote one to destruction; the city was devoted to the flames.
q: No devoted thing that a man shall devote unto the Lord . . . shall be sold or redeemed.

senses.d: To execrate; to curse.
To give up wholly; to addict; to direct the attention of wholly or compound; to attach; — often with a reflexive pronoun; as, to devote one's self to science, to one's friends, to piety, etc.
q: Thy servant who is devoted to thy fear.
They devoted themselves unto all wickedness.
A leafless and simple branch . . . devoted to the purpose of climbing.

Devote.syn: To addict; apply; dedicate; consecrate; resign; destine; doom; consign. See Addict.
Devote.etym: [L. devotus, p. p. of devovere; de + vovere to vow. See Vow, and cf. Devout, Devow.]

senses.d: Devoted; addicted; devout.
A devotee.
Consecrated to a purpose; strongly attached; zealous; devout; as, a devoted admirer.
The act of devoting; consecration.
The state of being devoted; addiction; eager inclination; strong attachment love or affection; zeal; especially, feelings toward God appropriately expressed by acts of worship; devoutness.
q: Genius animated by a fervent spirit of devotion.

senses.d: Act of devotedness or devoutness; manifestation of strong attachment; act of worship; prayer.
Disposal; power of disposal.
q: They are entirely at our devotion, and may be turned backward and forward, as we please.

senses.d: A thing consecrated; an object of devotion.
q: Churches and altars, priests and all devotions, Tumbled together into rude chaos.

Devotion.syn: Consecration; devoutness; religiousness; piety; attachment; devotedness; ardor; earnestness.

senses.d: To eat up with greediness; to consume ravenously; to feast upon like a wild beast or a glutton; to prey upon.
q: Some evil beast hath devoured him.

senses.d: To seize upon and destroy or appropriate greedily, selfishly, or wantonly; to consume; to swallow up; to use up; to waste; to annihilate.
q: Famine and pestilence shall devour him.
I waste my life and do my days devour.

senses.d: To enjoy with avidity; to appropriate or take in eagerly by the senses.
q: Longing they look, and gaping at the sight, Devour her o'er with vast delight.

Devour.etym: [F. dévorer, fr. L. devorare; de + vorare to eat greedily, swallow up. See Voracious.]

senses.d: One who, or that which, devours.
Devoted to religion or to religious feelings and duties; absorbed in religious exercises; given to devotion; pious; reverent; religious.
q: A devout man, and one that feared God.
We must be constant and devout in the worship of God.

senses.d: Expressing devotion or piety; as, eyes devout; sighs devout; a devout posture.
Warmly devoted; hearty; sincere; earnest; as, devout wishes for one's welfare.

Devout.syn: Holy; pure; religious; prayerful; pious; earnest; reverent; solemn; sincere.
Devout.etym: [OE. devot, devout, F. dévot, from L. devotus devoted, p. p. of devovere. See Devote, v. t.]

senses.d: A devotee.
A devotional composition, or part of a composition; devotion.
Moisture from the atmosphere condensed by cool bodies upon their surfaces, particularly at night.
q: Her tears fell with the dews at even.

senses.d: Figuratively, anything which falls lightly and in a refreshing manner.
An emblem of morning, or fresh vigor.

Dew.etym: [AS. deáw; akin to D. dauw, G. thau, tau, Icel. dögg, Sw. dagg, Dan. dug; cf. Skr. dhav, dhāv, to flow. √72. Cf. Dag dew.]

senses.d: To wet with dew or as with dew; to bedew; to moisten; as with dew.
q: The grasses grew A little ranker since they dewed them so.

senses.d: Same as Due, or Duty.
Originally, an ornamental head band or fillet, worn by Eastern monarchs as a badge of royalty; hence (later), also, a crown, in general.
Regal power; sovereignty; empire; — considered as symbolized by the crown.
An arch rising from the rim of a crown (rarely also of a coronet), and uniting with others over its center.

Diadem.etym: [F. diadème, L. diadema, fr. Gr. �, fr. � to bind round; διά through, across + � to bind; cf. Skr. dā to bind.]

senses.d: To adorn with a diadem; to crown.
q: Not so, when diadem'd with rays divine.
To terminate the evil, To diadem the right.

senses.d: An instrument, formerly much used for showing the time of day from the shadow of a style or gnomon on a graduated arc or surface; esp., a sundial; but there are lunar and astral dials. The style or gnomon is usually parallel to the earth's axis, but the dial plate may be either horizontal or vertical.
The graduated face of a timepiece, on which the time of day is shown by pointers or hands.
A miner's compass.

Dial.etym: [LL. dialis daily, fr. L. dies day. See Deity.]

senses.d: To measure with a dial.
q: Hours of that true time which is dialed in heaven.

senses.d: To survey with a dial.
A precious stone or gem excelling in brilliancy and beautiful play of prismatic colors, and remarkable for extreme hardness.
A geometrical figure, consisting of four equal straight lines, and having two of the interior angles acute and two obtuse; a rhombus; a lozenge.
One of a suit of playing cards, stamped with the figure of a diamond.
A pointed projection, like a four-sided pyramid, used for ornament in lines or groups.
The infield; the square space, 90 feet on a side, having the bases at its angles.
The smallest kind of type in English printing, except that called brilliant, which is seldom seen.

Diamond.etym: [OE. diamaund, diamaunt, F. diamant, corrupted, fr. L. adamas, the hardest iron, steel, diamond, Gr. �. Perh. the corruption is due to the influence of Gr. � transparent. See Adamant, Tame.]

senses.d: Resembling a diamond; made of, or abounding in, diamonds; as, a diamond chain; a diamond field.
The daughter of Jupiter and Latona; a virgin goddess who presided over hunting, chastity, and marriage; — identified with the Greek goddess Artemis.
q: And chaste Diana haunts the forest shade.

senses.d: the 2d pers. sing. imp. of Do.

To pass from an animate to a lifeless state; to cease to live; to suffer a total and irreparable loss of action of the vital functions; to become dead; to expire; to perish; — said of animals and vegetables; often with of, by, with, from, and rarely for, before the cause or occasion of death; as, to die of disease or hardships; to die by fire or the sword; to die with horror at the thought.
q: To die by the roadside of grief and hunger.
She will die from want of care.

senses.d: To suffer death; to lose life.
q: In due time Christ died for the ungodly.

senses.d: To perish in any manner; to cease; to become lost or extinct; to be extinguished.
q: Letting the secret die within his own breast.
Great deeds can not die.

senses.d: To sink; to faint; to pine; to languish, with weakness, discouragement, love, etc.
q: His heart died within, and he became as a stone.
The young men acknowledged, in love letters, that they died for Rebecca.

senses.d: To become indifferent; to cease to be subject; as, to die to pleasure or to sin.
To recede and grow fainter; to become imperceptible; to vanish; — often with out or away.
q: Blemishes may die away and disappear amidst the brightness.

senses.d: To disappear gradually in another surface, as where moldings are lost in a sloped or curved face.
To become vapid, flat, or spiritless, as liquor.

Die.syn: To expire; decease; perish; depart; vanish.
Die.etym: [OE. deyen, dien, of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. deyja; akin to Dan. döe, Sw. dö, Goth. diwan (cf. Goth. afd�jan to harass), OFries. d�ia to kill, OS. doian to die, OHG. touwen, OSlav. daviti to choke, Lith. dovyti to torment. Cf. Dead, Death.]

senses.d: A small cube, marked on its faces with spots from one to six, and used in playing games by being shaken in a box and thrown from it. See Dice.
Any small cubical or square body.
q: Words . . . pasted upon little flat tablets or dies.

senses.d: That which is, or might be, determined, by a throw of the die; hazard; chance.
q: Such is the die of war.

senses.d: That part of a pedestal included between base and cornice; the dado.

A metal or plate (often one of a pair) so cut or shaped as to give a certain desired form to, or impress any desired device on, an object or surface, by pressure or by a blow; used in forging metals, coining, striking up sheet metal, etc.

Die.etym: [OE. dee, die, F. dé, fr. L. datus given, thrown, p. p. of dare to give, throw. See Date a point of time.]

senses.d: Course of living or nourishment; what is eaten and drunk habitually; food; victuals; fare.
A course of food selected with reference to a particular state of health; prescribed allowance of food; regimen prescribed.
q: To fast like one that takes diet.

Diet.etym: [F. diète, L. diaeta, fr. Gr. � manner of living.]

senses.d: To cause to take food; to feed.
To cause to eat and drink sparingly, or by prescribed rules; to regulate medicinally the food of.
q: She diets him with fasting every day.

senses.d: To eat; to take one's meals.
q: Let him . . . diet in such places, where there is good company of the nation, where he traveleth.

senses.d: To eat according to prescribed rules; to ear sparingly; as, the doctor says he must diet.
A legislative or administrative assembly in Germany, Poland, and some other countries of Europe; a deliberative convention; a council; as, the Diet of Worms, held in 1521.

Diet.etym: [F. diète, LL. dieta, diaeta, an assembly, a day's journey; the same word as diet course of living, but with the sense changed by L. dies day: cf. G. tag day� and Reichstag.]

senses.d: Any of various national or local assemblies;
Occasionally, the Reichstag of the German Empire, Reichsrath of the Austrian Empire, the federal legislature of Switzerland, etc.
The legislature of Denmark, Sweden, Japan, or Hungary.

The state assembly or any of various local assemblies in the states of the German Empire, as the legislature (Landtag) of the kingdom of Prussia, and the Diet of the Circle (Kreistag) in its local government.
The local legislature (Landtag) of an Austrian province.
The federative assembly of the old Germanic Confederation (1815 — 66).
In the old German or Holy Roman Empire, the great formal assembly of counselors (the Imperial Diet or Reichstag) or a small, local, or informal assembly of a similar kind (the Court Diet, or Hoftag).
To be or stand apart; to disagree; to be unlike; to be distinguished; — with from.
q: One star differeth from another star in glory.
Minds differ, as rivers differ.

senses.d: To be of unlike or opposite opinion; to disagree in sentiment; — often with from or with.
To have a difference, cause of variance, or quarrel; to dispute; to contend.
q: We 'll never differ with a crowded pit.
Severely punished, not for differing from us in opinion, but for committing a nuisance.
Davidson, whom on a former occasion we quoted, to differ from him.
Much as I differ from him concerning an essential part of the historic basis of religion.
I differ with the honorable gentleman on that point.
If the honorable gentleman differs with me on that subject, I differ as heartily with him, and shall always rejoice to differ.

Differ.syn: To vary; disagree; dissent; dispute; contend; oppose; wrangle.
Differ.etym: [L. differre; dif- = dis- + ferre to bear, carry: cf. F. différer. See 1st Bear, and cf. Defer, Delay.]

senses.d: To cause to be different or unlike; to set at variance.
q: But something 'ts that differs thee and me.

senses.d: The act of differing; the state or measure of being different or unlike; distinction; dissimilarity; unlikeness; variation; as, a difference of quality in paper; a difference in degrees of heat, or of light; what is the difference between the innocent and the guilty?
q: Differencies of administration, but the same Lord.

senses.d: Disagreement in opinion; dissension; controversy; quarrel; hence, cause of dissension; matter in controversy.
q: What was the difference? It was a contention in public.
Away therefore went I with the constable, leaving the old warden and the young constable to compose their difference as they could.

senses.d: That by which one thing differs from another; that which distinguishes or causes to differ; mark of distinction; characteristic quality; specific attribute.
q: The marks and differences of sovereignty.

senses.d: Choice; preference.
q: That now he chooseth with vile difference To be a beast, and lack intelligence.

senses.d: An addition to a coat of arms to distinguish the bearings of two persons, which would otherwise be the same. See Augmentation, and Marks of cadency, under Cadency.
The quality or attribute which is added to those of the genus to constitute a species; a differentia.
The quantity by which one quantity differs from another, or the remainder left after subtracting the one from the other.

Difference.syn: Distinction; dissimilarity; dissimilitude; variation; diversity; variety; contrariety; disagreement; variance; contest; contention; dispute; controversy; debate; quarrel; wrangle; strife.

senses.d: To cause to differ; to make different; to mark as different; to distinguish.
q: Thou mayest difference gods from men.
Kings, in receiving justice and undergoing trial, are not differenced from the meanest subject.
So completely differenced by their separate and individual characters that we at once acknowledge them as distinct persons.

senses.d: To turn up, or delve in, (earth) with a spade or a hoe; to open, loosen, or break up (the soil) with a spade, or other sharp instrument; to pierce, open, or loosen, as if with a spade.
q: Be first to dig the ground.

senses.d: To get by digging; as, to dig potatoes, or gold.
To hollow out, as a well; to form, as a ditch, by removing earth; to excavate; as, to dig a ditch or a well.
To thrust; to poke.
q: You should have seen children . . . dig and push their mothers under the sides, saying thus to them: Look, mother, how great a lubber doth yet wear pearls.

Dig.etym: [OE. diggen, perh. the same word as diken, dichen (see Dike, Ditch); cf. Dan. dige to dig, dige a ditch; or (?) akin to E. 1st dag. √67.]

senses.d: To work with a spade or other like implement; to do servile work; to delve.
q: Dig for it more than for hid treasures.
I can not dig; to beg I am ashamed.

senses.d: To take ore from its bed, in distinction from making excavations in search of ore.
To work like a digger; to study ploddingly and laboriously.
A thrust; a punch; a poke; as, a dig in the side or the ribs. See Dig, v. t., 4.
A plodding and laborious student.
To work hard or drudge;
q: Peter dug at his books all the harder.

senses.d: Of a tool: To cut deeply into the work because ill set, held at a wrong angle, or the like, as when a lathe tool is set too low and so sprung into the work.
A tool for digging.
An act of digging.
An amount to be dug.
= Gouge.
The state of being worthy or honorable; elevation of mind or character; true worth; excellence.
Elevation; grandeur.
q: The dignity of this act was worth the audience of kings.

senses.d: Elevated rank; honorable station; high office, political or ecclesiastical; degree of excellence; preferment; exaltation.
q: And the king said, What honor and dignity hath been done to Mordecai for this?
Reuben, thou art my firstborn, . . . the excellency of dignity, and the excellency of power.

senses.d: Quality suited to inspire respect or reverence; loftiness and grace; impressiveness; stateliness; — said of mien, manner, style, etc.
q: A letter written with singular energy and dignity of thought and language.

senses.d: One holding high rank; a dignitary.
q: These filthy dreamers . . . speak evil of dignities.

senses.d: Fundamental principle; axiom; maxim.
q: Sciences concluding from dignities, and principles known by themselves.
They did not stand upon their dignity, nor give their minds to being or to seeming as elegant and as fine as anybody else.

Dignity.etym: [OE. dignete, dignite, OF. digneté, dignité, F. dignité, fr. L. dignitas, from dignus worthy. See Dainty, Deign.]

senses.d: The quality of being diligent; carefulness; careful attention; — the opposite of negligence.
Interested and persevering application; devoted and painstaking effort to accomplish what is undertaken; assiduity in service.
q: That which ordinary men are fit for, I am qualified in; and the best of me is diligence.

senses.d: Process by which persons, lands, or effects are seized for debt; process for enforcing the attendance of witnesses or the production of writings.
q: And each of them doth all his diligence To do unto the festé reverence.
The sweat of industry would dry and die, But for the end it works to.
Diligence and accuracy are the only merits which an historical writer ascribe to himself.

Diligence.syn: Attention; industry; assiduity; sedulousness; earnestness; constancy; heed; heedfulness; care; caution. — Diligence, Industry. Industry has the wider sense of the two, implying an habitual devotion to labor for some valuable end, as knowledge, property, etc. Diligence denotes earnest application to some specific object or pursuit, which more or less directly has a strong hold on one's interests or feelings. A man may be diligent for a time, or in seeking some favorite end, without meriting the title of industrious. Such was the case with Fox, while Burke was eminent not only for diligence, but

senses.d: A four-wheeled public stagecoach, used in France.
Prosecuted with careful attention and effort; careful; painstaking; not careless or negligent.
q: The judges shall make diligent inquisition.

senses.d: Interestedly and perseveringly attentive; steady and earnest in application to a subject or pursuit; assiduous; industrious.
q: Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings.
Diligent cultivation of elegant literature.

Diligent.syn: Active; assiduous; sedulous; laborious; persevering; attentive; industrious.
Diligent.etym: [F. diligent, L. diligens, -entis, p. pr. of diligere, dilectum, to esteem highly, prefer; di- = dis- + legere to choose. See Legend.]

senses.d: In a diligent manner; not carelessly; not negligently; with industry or assiduity.
q: Ye diligently keep commandments of the Lord your God.

senses.d: Not bright or distinct; wanting luminousness or clearness; obscure in luster or sound; dusky; darkish; obscure; indistinct; overcast; tarnished.
q: The dim magnificence of poetry.
How is the gold become dim!
I never saw The heavens so dim by day.
Three sleepless nights I passed in sounding on, Through words and things, a dim and perilous way.

senses.d: Of obscure vision; not seeing clearly; hence, dull of apprehension; of weak perception; obtuse.
q: Mine eye also is dim by reason of sorrow.
The understanding is dim.

Dim.syn: Obscure; dusky; dark; mysterious; imperfect; dull; sullied; tarnished.
Dim.etym: [AS. dim; akin to OFries. dim, Icel. dimmr: cf. MHG. timmer, timber; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: To render dim, obscure, or dark; to make less bright or distinct; to take away the luster of; to darken; to dull; to obscure; to eclipse.
q: A king among his courtiers, who dims all his attendants.
Now set the sun, and twilight dimmed the ways.

senses.d: To deprive of distinct vision; to hinder from seeing clearly, either by dazzling or clouding the eyes; to darken the senses or understanding of.
q: Her starry eyes were dimmed with streaming tears.

senses.d: To grow dim.
To make smaller in any manner; to reduce in bulk or amount; to lessen; — opposed to augment or increase.
q: Not diminish, but rather increase, the debt.

senses.d: To lessen the authority or dignity of; to put down; to degrade; to abase; to weaken.
q: This doth nothing diminish their opinion.
I will diminish them, that they shall no more rule over the nations.
O thou . . . at whose sight all the stars Hide their diminished heads.

senses.d: To make smaller by a half step; to make (an interval) less than minor; as, a diminished seventh.
To take away; to subtract.
q: Neither shall ye diminish aught from it.

Diminish.syn: To decrease; lessen; abate; reduce; contract; curtail; impair; degrade. See Decrease.
Diminish.etym: [Pref. di- (= L. dis-) + minish: cf. L. diminuere, F. diminuer, OE. diminuen. See Dis-, and Minish.]

senses.d: To become or appear less or smaller; to lessen; as, the apparent size of an object diminishes as we recede from it.
The state or quality � being dim; lack of brightness, clearness, or distinctness; dullness; obscurity.
Dullness, or want of clearness, of vision or of intellectual perception.
Loud, confused, harsh noise; a loud, continuous, rattling or clanging sound; clamor; roar.
q: Think you a little din can daunt mine ears?
He knew the battle's din afar.
The dust and din and steam of town.

Din.etym: [AS. dyne, dyn; akin to Icel. dynr, and to AS. dynian to resound, Icel. dynja to pour down like hail or rain; cf. Skr. dhuni roaring, a torrent, dhvan to sound. Cf. Dun to ask payment.]

senses.d: To strike with confused or clanging sound; to stun with loud and continued noise; to harass with clamor; as, to din the ears with cries.
To utter with a din; to repeat noisily; to ding.
q: This hath been often dinned in my ears.

senses.d: To sound with a din; a ding.
q: The gay viol dinning in the dale.

senses.d: To eat the principal regular meal of the day; to take dinner.
q: Now can I break my fast, dine, sup, and sleep.

Dine.etym: [F. dîner, OF. disner, LL. disnare, contr. fr. an assumed disjunare; dis- + an assumed junare (OF. juner) to fast, for L. jejunare, fr. jejunus fasting. See Jejune, and cf. Dinner, D�jeuner.]

senses.d: To give a dinner to; to furnish with the chief meal; to feed; as, to dine a hundred men.
q: A table massive enough to have dined Johnnie Armstrong and his merry men.

senses.d: To dine upon; to have to eat.
The principal meal of the day, eaten by most people about midday, but by many (especially in cities) at a later hour.
An entertainment; a feast.
q: A grand political dinner.

Dinner.etym: [F. dîner, fr. dîner to dine. See Dine.]

senses.d: To plunge or immerse; especially, to put for a moment into a liquid; to insert into a fluid and withdraw again.
q: The priest shall dip his finger in the blood.
now dip their pinions in the briny deep.
While the prime swallow dips his wing.

senses.d: To immerse for baptism; to baptize by immersion.
To wet, as if by immersing; to moisten.
q: A cold shuddering dew Dips me all o'er.

senses.d: To plunge or engage thoroughly in any affair.
q: He was . . . dipt in the rebellion of the Commons.

senses.d: To take out, by dipping a dipper, ladle, or other receptacle, into a fluid and removing a part; — often with out; as, to dip water from a boiler; to dip out water.
To engage as a pledge; to mortgage.
q: Live on the use and never dip thy lands.

Dip.etym: [OE. dippen, duppen, AS. dyppan; akin to Dan. dyppe, Sw. doppa, and to AS. d�pan to baptize, OS. d�pian, D. doopen, G. taufen, Sw. döpa, Goth. daupjan, Lith. dubus deep, hollow, OSlav. dupl� hollow, and to E. dive. Cf. Deep, Dive.]

senses.d: To immerse one's self; to become plunged in a liquid; to sink.
q: The sun's rim dips; the stars rush out.

senses.d: To perform the action of plunging some receptacle, as a dipper, ladle. etc.; into a liquid or a soft substance and removing a part.
q: Whoever dips too deep will find death in the pot.

senses.d: To pierce; to penetrate; — followed by in or into.
q: When I dipt into the future.

senses.d: To enter slightly or cursorily; to engage one's self desultorily or by the way; to partake limitedly; — followed by in or into.
To incline downward from the plane of the horizon; as, strata of rock dip.
To dip snuff.
The action of dipping or plunging for a moment into a liquid.
Inclination downward; direction below a horizontal line; slope; pitch.
A liquid, as a sauce or gravy, served at table with a ladle or spoon.
A dipped candle.

A gymnastic exercise on the parallel bars in which the performer, resting on his hands, lets his arms bend and his body sink until his chin is level with the bars, and then raises himself by straightening his arms.
In the turpentine industry, the viscid exudation, which is dipped out from incisions in the trees; as, virgin dip (the runnings of the first year), yellow dip (the runnings of subsequent years).
A sudden drop followed by a climb, usually to avoid obstacles or as the result of getting into an airhole.
Straight; not crooked, oblique, or circuitous; leading by the short or shortest way to a point or end; as, a direct line; direct means.
q: What is direct to, what slides by, the question.

senses.d: Straightforward; not of crooked ways, or swerving from truth and openness; sincere; outspoken.
q: Be even and direct with me.

senses.d: Immediate; express; plain; unambiguous.
q: He nowhere, that I know, says it in direct words.
A direct and avowed interference with elections.

senses.d: In the line of descent; not collateral; as, a descendant in the direct line.
In the direction of the general planetary motion, or from west to east; in the order of the signs; not retrograde; — said of the motion of a celestial body.

Direct.etym: [L. directus, p. p. of dirigere to direct: cf. F. direct. See Dress, and cf. Dirge.]

senses.d: To arrange in a direct or straight line, as against a mark, or towards a goal; to point; to aim; as, to direct an arrow or a piece of ordnance.
To point out or show to (any one), as the direct or right course or way; to guide, as by pointing out the way; as, he directed me to the left-hand road.
q: The Lord direct your into the love of God.
The next points to which I will direct your attention.

senses.d: To determine the direction or course of; to cause to go on in a particular manner; to order in the way to a certain end; to regulate; to govern; as, to direct the affairs of a nation or the movements of an army.
q: I will direct their work in truth.

senses.d: To point out to with authority; to instruct as a superior; to order; as, he directed them to go.
q: I 'll first direct my men what they shall do.

senses.d: To put a direction or address upon; to mark with the name and residence of the person to whom anything is sent; to superscribe; as, to direct a letter.

Direct.syn: To guide; lead; conduct; dispose; manage; regulate; order; instruct; command.

senses.d: To give direction; to point out a course; to act as guide.
q: Wisdom is profitable to direct.

senses.d: A character, thus , placed at the end of a staff on the line or space of the first note of the next staff, to apprise the performer of its situation.
Pertaining to, or effected immediately by, action of the people through their votes instead of through one or more representatives or delegates; as, direct nomination, direct legislation.
The act of directing, of aiming, regulating, guiding, or ordering; guidance; management; superintendence; administration; as, the direction o� public affairs or of a bank.
q: I do commit his youth To your direction.
All nature is but art, unknown to thee; ll chance, direction, which thou canst not see.

senses.d: That which is imposed by directing; a guiding or authoritative instruction; prescription; order; command; as, he grave directions to the servants.
q: The princes digged the well . . . by the direction of the law giver.

senses.d: The name and residence of a person to whom any thing is sent, written upon the thing sent; superscription; address; as, the direction of a letter.

The line or course upon which anything is moving or aimed to move, or in which anything is lying or pointing; aim; line or point of tendency; direct line or course; as, the ship sailed in a southeasterly direction.
The body of managers of a corporation or enterprise; board of directors.
The pointing of a piece with reference to an imaginary vertical axis; — distinguished from elevation. The direction is given when the plane of sight passes through the object.

Direction.syn: Administration; guidance; management; superintendence; oversight; government; order; command; guide; clew.

senses.d: In a direct manner; in a straight line or course.
q: Indirectly and directly too Thou hast contrived against the very life Of the defendant.

senses.d: In a straightforward way; without anything intervening; not by secondary, but by direct, means.
Without circumlocution or ambiguity; absolutely; in express terms.
q: No man hath hitherto been so impious as plainly and directly to condemn prayer.

senses.d: Exactly; just.
q: Stand you directly in Antonius' way.

senses.d: Straightforwardly; honestly.
q: I have dealt most directly in thy affair.

senses.d: Manifestly; openly.
q: Desdemona is directly in love with him.

senses.d: Straightway; next in order; without delay; immediately.
Immediately after; as soon as.
q: Directly he stopped, the coffin was removed.

Directly.syn: Immediately; forthwith; straightway; instantly; instantaneously; soon; promptly; openly; expressly.

senses.d: Any foul of filthy substance, as excrement, mud, dust, etc.; whatever, adhering to anything, renders it foul or unclean; earth; as, a wagonload of dirt.
q: Whose waters cast up mire and dirt.

senses.d: Meanness; sordidness.
q: Honors . . . thrown away upon dirt and infamy.

senses.d: In placer mining, earth, gravel, etc., before washing.

Dirt.etym: [OE. drit; kin to Icel. drit excrement, drīta to dung, OD. drijten to dung, AS. gedrītan.]

senses.d: To make foul of filthy; to dirty.
To refuse to allow; to deny the force or validity of; to disown and reject; as, the judge disallowed the executor's charge.
q: To whom coming, as unto a living stone, disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God.
That the edicts of Cæsar we may at all times disallow, but the statutes of God for no reason we may reject.

Disallow.etym: [Pref. dis- + allow: cf. OF. desalouer, desloer, to blame, dissuade.]

senses.d: To annul completely; to render void or of no effect.
q: For the Lord of hosts hath purposed, and who shall disannul it?

senses.d: To defeat of expectation or hope; to hinder from the attainment of that which was expected, hoped, or desired; to balk; as, a man is disappointed of his hopes or expectations, or his hopes, desires, intentions, expectations, or plans are disappointed; a bad season disappoints the farmer of his crops; a defeat disappoints an enemy of his spoil.
q: I was disappointed, but very agreeably.

senses.d: To frustrate; to fail; to hinder of result.
q: His retiring foe Shrinks from the wound, and disappoints the blow.

Disappoint.syn: To tantalize; fail; frustrate; balk; baffle; delude; foil; defeat. See Tantalize.
Disappoint.etym: [OF. desapointier, F. désappointer; pref. des- (L. dis-) + apointier, F. appointier, to appoint. See Appoint.]

senses.d: Defeated of expectation or hope; balked; as, a disappointed person or hope.
Unprepared; unequipped.
q: Cut off even in the blossoms of my sin, Unhouseled, disappointed, unaneled.

senses.d: To see and identify by noting a difference or differences; to note the distinctive character of; to discriminate; to distinguish.
q: To discern such buds as are fit to produce blossoms.
A counterfeit stone which thine eye can not discern from a right stone.

senses.d: To see by the eye or by the understanding; to perceive and recognize; as, to discern a difference.
q: And beheld among the simple ones, I discerned among the youths, a young man void of understanding.
Our unassisted sight . . . is not acute enough to discern the minute texture of visible objects.
I wake, and I discern the truth.

Discern.syn: To perceive; distinguish; discover; penetrate; discriminate; espy; descry; detect. See Perceive.
Discern.etym: [F. discerner, L. discernere, discretum; dis- + cernere to separate, distinguish. See Certain, and cf. Discreet.]

senses.d: To see or understand the difference; to make distinction; as, to discern between good and evil, truth and falsehood.
q: More than sixscore thousand that cannot discern between their right hand their left.

senses.d: To make cognizance.
One who, or that which, discerns, distinguishes, perceives, or judges; as, a discerner of truth, of right and wrong.
q: A great observer and discerner of men's natures.

senses.d: Acute; shrewd; sagacious; sharp-sighted.
To relieve of a charge, load, or burden; to empty of a load or cargo; to unburden; to unload; as, to discharge a vessel.

To free of the missile with which anything is charged or loaded; to let go the charge of; as, to discharge a bow, catapult, etc.; especially, said of firearms, — to fire off; to shoot off; also, to relieve from a state of tension, as a Leyden jar.
q: The galleys also did oftentimes, out of their prows, discharge their great pieces against the city.
Feeling in other cases discharges itself in indirect muscular actions.

senses.d: To of something weighing upon or impeding over one, as a debt, claim, obligation, responsibility, accusation, etc.; to absolve; to acquit; to clear.
q: Discharged of business, void of strife.
In one man's fault discharge another man of his duty.

senses.d: To relieve of an office or employment; to send away from service; to dismiss.
q: Discharge the common sort With pay and thanks.
Grindal . . . was discharged the government of his see.

senses.d: To release legally from confinement; to set at liberty; as, to discharge a prisoner.
To put forth, or remove, as a charge or burden; to take out, as that with which anything is loaded or filled; as, to discharge a cargo.
To let fly, as a missile; to shoot.
q: They do discharge their shot of courtesy.

senses.d: To set aside; to annul; to dismiss.
q: We say such an order was “discharged on appeal.”
The order for Daly's attendance was discharged.

senses.d: To throw off the obligation of, as a duty or debt; to relieve one's self of, by fulfilling conditions, performing duty, trust, and the like; hence, to perform or execute, as an office, or part.
q: Had I a hundred tongues, a wit so large As could their hundred offices discharge.

senses.d: To send away (a creditor) satisfied by payment; to pay one's debt or obligation to.
q: If he had The present money to discharge the Jew.

senses.d: To give forth; to emit or send out; as, a pipe discharges water; to let fly; to give expression to; to utter; as, to discharge a horrible oath.
To prohibit; to forbid.

Discharge.etym: [OE. deschargen, dischargen, OF. deschargier, F. décharger; pref. des- (L. dis) + chargier, F. charger. See Charge.]

senses.d: To throw off or deliver a load, charge, or burden; to unload; to emit or give vent to fluid or other contents; as, the water pipe discharges freely.
q: The cloud, if it were oily or fatty, would not discharge.

senses.d: The act of discharging; the act of relieving of a charge or load; removal of a load or burden; unloading; as, the discharge of a ship; discharge of a cargo.
