Firing off; explosive removal of a charge; explosion; letting off; as, a discharge of arrows, of artillery.
Act of relieving of something which oppresses or weighs upon one, as an obligation, liability, debt, accusation, etc.; acquittance; as, the discharge of a debtor.
Act of removing, or getting rid of, an obligation, liability, etc.; fulfillment, as by the payment of a debt, or the performance of a trust or duty.
q: Indefatigable in the discharge of business.
Nothing can absolve us from the discharge of those duties.

senses.d: Release or dismissal from an office, employment, etc.; dismission; as, the discharge of a workman by his employer.
Legal release from confinement; liberation; as, the discharge of a prisoner.
The state of being discharged or relieved of a debt, obligation, office, and the like; acquittal.
q: Too secure of our discharge From penalty.

senses.d: That which discharges or releases from an obligation, liability, penalty, etc., as a price of ransom, a legal document.
q: Death, who sets all free, Hath paid his ransom now and full discharge.

senses.d: A flowing or issuing out; emission; vent; evacuation; also, that which is discharged or emitted; as, a rapid discharge of water from the pipe.
q: The hemorrhage being stopped, the next occurrence is a thin serous discharge.

Discharge.etym: [Cf. F. décharge. See Discharge, v. t.]

senses.d: To bleach out or to remove or efface, as by a chemical process; as, to discharge the color from a dyed fabric in order to form light figures on a dark ground.

The equalization of a difference of electric potential between two points. The character of the discharge is mostly determined by the nature of the medium through which it takes place, the amount of the difference of potential, and the form of the terminal conductors on which the difference exists. The discharge may be alternating, continuous, brush, connective, disruptive, glow, oscillatory, stratified, etc.

One who receives instruction from another; a scholar; a learner; especially, a follower who has learned to believe in the truth of the doctrine of his teacher; an adherent in doctrine; as, the disciples of Plato; the disciples of our Savior.

Disciple.etym: [OE. disciple, deciple, OF. disciple, fr. L. discipulus, fr. discere to learn (akin to docere to teach; see Docile) + prob. a root meaning to turn or drive, as in L. pellere to drive (see Pulse).]

senses.d: To teach; to train.
q: That better were in virtues discipled.

senses.d: To punish; to discipline.
To make disciples of; to convert to doctrines or principles.
q: Sending missionaries to disciple all nations.

senses.d: The treatment suited to a disciple or learner; education; development of the faculties by instruction and exercise; training, whether physical, mental, or moral.
q: Wife and children are a kind of discipline of humanity.
Discipline aims at the removal of bad habits and the substitution of good ones, especially those of order, regularity, and obedience.

senses.d: Training to act in accordance with established rules; accustoming to systematic and regular action; drill.
q: Their wildness lose, and, quitting nature's part, Obey the rules and discipline of art.

senses.d: Subjection to rule; submissiveness to order and control; habit of obedience.
q: The most perfect, who have their passions in the best discipline, are yet obliged to be constantly on their guard.

senses.d: Severe training, corrective of faults; instruction by means of misfortune, suffering, punishment, etc.
q: A sharp discipline of half a century had sufficed to educate us.

senses.d: Correction; chastisement; punishment inflicted by way of correction and training.
q: Giving her the discipline of the strap.

senses.d: The subject matter of instruction; a branch of knowledge.
The enforcement of methods of correction against one guilty of ecclesiastical offenses; reformatory or penal action toward a church member.
Self-inflicted and voluntary corporal punishment, as penance, or otherwise; specifically, a penitential scourge.
A system of essential rules and duties; as, the Romish or Anglican discipline.

Discipline.syn: Education; instruction; training; culture; correction; chastisement; punishment.
Discipline.etym: [F. discipline, L. disciplina, from discipulus. See Disciple.]

senses.d: To educate; to develop by instruction and exercise; to train.

To accustom to regular and systematic action; to bring under control so as to act systematically; to train to act together under orders; to teach subordination to; to form a habit of obedience in; to drill.
q: Ill armed, and worse disciplined.
His mind . . . imperfectly disciplined by nature.

senses.d: To improve by corrective and penal methods; to chastise; to correct.
q: Has he disciplined Aufidius soundly?

senses.d: To inflict ecclesiastical censures and penalties upon.

Discipline.syn: To train; form; teach; instruct; bring up; regulate; correct; chasten; chastise; punish.
Discipline.etym: [Cf. LL. disciplinarian to flog, fr. L. disciplina discipline, and F. discipliner to discipline.]

senses.d: To unclose; to open; — applied esp. to eggs in the sense of to hatch.
q: The ostrich layeth her eggs under sand, where the heat of the discloseth them.

senses.d: To remove a cover or envelope from;; to set free from inclosure; to uncover.
q: The shells being broken, . . . the stone included in them is thereby disclosed and set at liberty.

senses.d: To lay open or expose to view; to cause to appear; to bring to light; to reveal.
q: How softly on the Spanish shore she plays, Disclosing rock, and slope, and forest brown!
Her lively looks a sprightly mind disclose.

senses.d: To make known, as that which has been kept secret or hidden; to reveal; to expose; as, events have disclosed his designs.
q: If I disclose my passion, Our friendship 's an end.

Disclose.syn: To uncover; open; unveil; discover; reveal; divulge; tell; utter.
Disclose.etym: [OE. desclosen, disclosen, fr. disclos, desclos, not shut in, open, OF. desclos, p. p. of desclore to open, F. déclore; pref. des- (L. dis-) + clore to shut, fr. L. claudere to shut. See Close, and cf. Disclusion.]

senses.d: Disclosure.
To scatter in fight; to put to rout; to defeat.
q: And his proud foes discomfit in victorious field.

senses.d: To break up and frustrate the plans of; to balk� to throw into perplexity and dejection; to disconcert.
q: Well, go with me and be not so discomfited.

Discomfit.syn: To defeat; overthrow; overpower; vanquish; conquer; baffle; frustrate; confound; discourage.
Discomfit.etym: [OF. desconfit, p. p. of desconfire, F. déconfire; fr. L. dis- + conficere to make ready, prepare, bring about. See Comfit, Fact.]

senses.d: Discomfited; overthrown.
Rout; overthrow; discomfiture.
q: Such a discomfit as shall quite despoil him.

senses.d: The act of discomfiting, or the state of being discomfited; rout; overthrow; defeat; frustration; confusion and dejection.
q: Every man's sword was against his fellow, and there was a very great discomfiture.
A hope destined to end . . . in discomfiture and disgrace.

Discomfiture.etym: [OF. desconfiture, F. déconfiture. See Discomfort, v. t., and cf. Comfiture.]

senses.d: Not content; discontented; dissatisfied.
q: Passion seemed to be much discontent, but Patience was very quiet.

senses.d: To deprive of content; to make uneasy; to dissatisfy.
Want of content; uneasiness and inquietude of mind; dissatisfaction; disquiet.
q: Now is the winter of our discontent Made glorious summer by this sun of York.
The rapacity of his father's administration had excited such universal discontent.

senses.d: A discontented person; a malcontent.
q: Thus was the Scotch nation full of discontents.

senses.d: Dissatisfied; uneasy in mind; malcontent.
q: And every one that was in distress, and every one that was in debt, and every one that was discontented, gathered themselves unto him.

senses.d: To interrupt the continuance of; to intermit, as a practice or habit; to put an end to; to cause to cease; to cease using, to stop; to leave off.
q: Set up their conventicles again, which had been discontinued.
I have discontinued school Above a twelvemonth.
Taught the Greek tongue, discontinued before in these parts the space of seven hundred years.
They modify and discriminate the voice, without appearing to discontinue it.

senses.d: To lose continuity or cohesion of parts; to be disrupted or broken off.
To be separated or severed; to part.
q: Thyself shalt discontinue from thine heritage.

senses.d: Want of concord or agreement; absence of unity or harmony in sentiment or action; variance leading to contention and strife; disagreement; — applied to persons or to things, and to thoughts, feelings, or purposes.
q: A false witness that speaketh lies, and he that soweth discord among brethren.
Peace to arise out of universal discord fomented in all parts of the empire.

senses.d: Union of musical sounds which strikes the ear harshly or disagreeably, owing to the incommensurability of the vibrations which they produce; want of musical concord or harmony; a chord demanding resolution into a concord.
q: For a discord itself is but a harshness of divers sounds m���ing.

Discord.syn: Variance; difference; opposition; contrariety; clashing; dissension; contention; strife; disagreement; dissonance.
Discord.etym: [OE. discord, descord, OF. discorde, descorde, F. discorde, from L. discordia, fr. discors, -cordis, discordant, disagreeable; dis- + cor, cordis, heart; cf. F. discord, n., and OF. descorder, discorder, F. discorder, to discord, L. discordare, from discors. See Heart, and cf. Discord, v. i.]

senses.d: To disagree; to be discordant; to jar; to clash; not to suit.
q: The one discording with the other.

Discord.etym: [OE. discorden, descorden, from the French. See Discord, n.]

senses.d: To extinguish the courage of; to dishearten; to depress the spirits of; to deprive of confidence; to deject; — the opposite of encourage; as, he was discouraged in his undertaking; he need not be discouraged from a like attempt.
q: Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged.

senses.d: To dishearten one with respect to; to discountenance; to seek to check by disfavoring; to deter one from; as, they discouraged his efforts.

Discourage.syn: To dishearten; dispirit; depress; deject; dissuade; disfavor.
Discourage.etym: [Pref. dis- + courage: cf. OF. descoragier, F. décourager: pref. des- (L. dis-) + corage, F. courage. See Courage.]

senses.d: Lack of courage; cowardliness.
To uncover.
q: Whether any man hath pulled down or discovered any church.

senses.d: To disclose; to lay open to view; to make visible; to reveal; to make known; to show (what has been secret, unseen, or unknown).
q: Go, draw aside the curtains, and discover The several caskets to this noble prince.
Prosperity doth best discover vice; but adversity doth best discover virtue.
We will discover ourselves unto them.
Discover not a secret to another.

senses.d: To obtain for the first time sight or knowledge of, as of a thing existing already, but not perceived or known; to find; to ascertain; to espy; to detect.
q: Some to discover islands far away.

senses.d: To manifest without design; to show.
q: The youth discovered a taste for sculpture.

senses.d: To explore; to examine.

Discover.syn: To disclose; bring out; exhibit; show; manifest; reveal; communicate; impart; tell; espy; find; out; detect. — To Discover, Invent. We discover what existed before, but remained unknown; we invent by forming combinations which are either entirely new, or which attain their end by means unknown before. Columbus discovered America; Newton discovered the law of gravitation; Whitney invented the cotton gin; Galileo invented the telescope.
Discover.etym: [OE. discoveren, discuren, descuren, OF. descovrir, descouvrir, F. découvrir; des- (L. dis-) + couvrir to cover. See Cover.]

senses.d: To discover or show one's self.
q: This done, they discover.
Nor was this the first time that they discovered to be followers of this world.

senses.d: Possessed of discernment, especially in avoiding error or evil, and in the adaptation of means to ends; prudent; sagacious; judicious; not rash or heedless; cautious.
q: It is the discreet man, not the witty, nor the learned, nor the brave, who guides the conversation, and gives measures to society.
Satire 's my weapon, but I 'm too discreet To run amuck, and tilt at all I meet.
The sea is silent, the sea is discreet.

senses.d: Differing; distinct.

Discreet.etym: [F. discret, L. discretus separated (whence the meaning reserved, prudent), p. p. of discernere. See Discern, and cf. Discrete.]

senses.d: Disjunction; separation.
The quality of being discreet; wise conduct and management; cautious discernment, especially as to matters of propriety and self-control; prudence; circumspection; wariness.
q: The better part of valor is discretion.
The greatest parts without discretion may be fatal to their owner.

senses.d: Discrimination.
q: Well spoken, with good accent and good discretion.

senses.d: Freedom to act according to one's own judgment; unrestrained exercise of choice or will.

Discretion.etym: [F. discrétion, L. discretio separation, difference, discernment, fr. discernere, discretum. See Discreet, Discern.]

senses.d: A feeling of contempt and aversion; the regarding anything as unworthy of or beneath one; scorn.
q: How my soul is moved with just disdain!
Disdain and scorn ride sparkling in her eyes.

senses.d: That which is worthy to be disdained or regarded with contempt and aversion.
q: Most loathsome, filthy, foul, and full of vile disdain.

senses.d: The state of being despised; shame.

Disdain.syn: Haughtiness; scorn; contempt; arrogance; pride. See Haughtiness.
Disdain.etym: [OE. desdain, disdein, OF. desdein, desdaing, F. dédain, fr. the verb. See Disdain, v. t.]

senses.d: To think unworthy; to deem unsuitable or unbecoming; as, to disdain to do a mean act.
q: Disdaining . . . that any should bear the armor of the best knight living.

senses.d: To reject as unworthy of one's self, or as not deserving one's notice; to look with scorn upon; to scorn, as base acts, character, etc.
q: When the Philistine . . . saw David, he disdained him; for he was but a youth.
'T is great, 't is manly to disdain disguise.

Disdain.syn: To contemn; despise; scorn. See Contemn.
Disdain.etym: [OE. disdainen, desdainen, OF. desdeigner, desdaigner, F. dédaigner; des- (L. dis-) + daigner to deign, fr. L. dignari to deem worthy. See Deign.]

senses.d: To be filled with scorn; to feel contemptuous anger; to be haughty.
q: And when the chief priests and scribes saw the marvels that he did . . . they disdained.

senses.d: Disdainful.
q: Revenge the jeering and disdained contempt Of this proud king.

senses.d: Lack of ease; uneasiness; trouble; vexation; disquiet.
q: So all that night they passed in great disease.
To shield thee from diseases of the world.

senses.d: An alteration in the state of the body or of some of its organs, interrupting or disturbing the performance of the vital functions, and causing or threatening pain and weakness; malady; affection; illness; sickness; disorder; — applied figuratively to the mind, to the moral character and habits, to institutions, the state, etc.
q: Diseases desperate grown, By desperate appliances are relieved.
The instability, injustice, and confusion introduced into the public counsels have, in truth, been the mortal diseases under which popular governments have every where perished.

Disease.syn: Distemper; ailing; ailment; malady; disorder; sickness; illness; complaint; indisposition; affection. — Disease, Disorder, Distemper, Malady, Affection. Disease is the leading medical term. Disorder mean� much the same, with perhaps some slight reference to an irregularity of the system. Distemper is now used by physicians only of the diseases of animals. Malady is not a medical term, and is less used than formerly in literature. Affection has special reference to the part, organ, or function disturbed; as, his disease is an affection of the lungs. A disease is usually deep-seated and permanen
Disease.etym: [OE. disese, OF. desaise; des- (L. dis-) + aise ease. See Ease.]

senses.d: To deprive of ease; to disquiet; to trouble; to distress.
q: His double burden did him sore disease.

senses.d: To derange the vital functions of; to afflict with disease or sickness; to disorder; — used almost exclusively in the participle diseased.
q: He was diseased in body and mind.

senses.d: Afflicted with disease.
q: It is my own diseased imagination that torments me.

senses.d: To mar the figure of; to render less complete, perfect, or beautiful in appearance; to deface; to deform.
q: Disfiguring not God's likeness, but their own.

Disfigure.etym: [OF. desfigurer, F. défigurer; pref. des- (L. dis-) + figurer to fashion, shape, fr. L. figurare, fr. figura figure. See Figure, and cf. Defiguration.]

senses.d: Disfigurement; deformity.
The condition of being out of favor; loss of favor, regard, or respect.
q: Macduff lives in disgrace.

senses.d: The state of being dishonored, or covered with shame; dishonor; shame; ignominy.
q: To tumble down thy husband and thyself From top of honor to disgrace's feet?

senses.d: That which brings dishonor; cause of shame or reproach; great discredit; as, vice is a disgrace to a rational being.
An act of unkindness; a disfavor.
q: The interchange continually of favors and disgraces.

Disgrace.syn: Disfavor; disesteem; opprobrium; reproach; discredit; disparagement; dishonor; shame; infamy; ignominy; humiliation.
Disgrace.etym: [F. disgrâce; pref. dis- (L. dis-) + grâce. See Grace.]

senses.d: To put out of favor; to dismiss with dishonor.
q: Flatterers of the disgraced minister.
Pitt had been disgraced and the old Duke of Newcastle dismissed.

senses.d: To do disfavor to; to bring reproach or shame upon; to dishonor; to treat or cover with ignominy; to lower in estimation.
q: Shall heap with honors him they now disgrace.
His ignorance disgraced him.

senses.d: To treat discourteously; to upbraid; to revile.
q: The goddess wroth gan foully her disgrace.

Disgrace.syn: To degrade; humble; humiliate; abase; disparage; defame; dishonor; debase.

senses.d: To change the guise or appearance of; especially, to conceal by an unusual dress, or one intended to mislead or deceive.
q: Bunyan was forced to disguise himself as a wagoner.

senses.d: To hide by a counterfeit appearance; to cloak by a false show; to mask; as, to disguise anger; to disguise one's sentiments, character, or intentions.
q: All God's angels come to us disguised.

senses.d: To affect or change by liquor; to intoxicate.
q: I have just left the right worshipful, and his myrmidons, about a sneaker of five gallons; the whole magistracy was pretty well disguised before I gave them the ship.

Disguise.syn: To conceal; hide; mask; dissemble; dissimulate; feign; pretend; secrete. See Conceal.
Disguise.etym: [OE. desguisen, disgisen, degisen, OF. desguisier, F. déguiser; pref. des- (L. dis-) + guise. See Guise.]

senses.d: A dress or exterior put on for purposes of concealment or of deception; as, persons doing unlawful acts in disguise are subject to heavy penalties.
q: There is no passion which steals into the heart more imperceptibly and covers itself under more disguises, than pride.

senses.d: Artificial language or manner assumed for deception; false appearance; counterfeit semblance or show.
q: That eye which glances through all disguises.

senses.d: Change of manner by drink; intoxication.
A masque or masquerade.
q: Disguise was the old English word for a masque.

senses.d: A vessel, as a platter, a plate, a bowl, used for serving up food at the table.
q: She brought forth butter in a lordly dish.

senses.d: The food served in a dish; hence, any particular kind of food; as, a cold dish; a warm dish; a delicious dish. “A dish fit for the gods.”
q: Home-home dishes that drive one from home.

senses.d: The state of being concave, or like a dish, or the degree of such concavity; as, the dish of a wheel.
A hollow place, as in a field.
A trough about 28 inches long, 4 deep, and 6 wide, in which ore is measured.

Dish.etym: [AS. disc, L. discus dish, disc, quoit, fr. Gr. δίσκοσ quoit, fr. δικει̑ν to throw. Cf. Dais, Desk, Disc, Discus.]

senses.d: To put in a dish, ready for the table.
To make concave, or depress in the middle, like a dish; as, to dish a wheel by inclining the spokes.
To frustrate; to beat; to ruin.
Dishonorable; shameful; indecent; unchaste; lewd.
q: Inglorious triumphs and dishonest scars.
Speak no foul or dishonest words before them .

senses.d: Dishonored; disgraced; disfigured.
q: Dishonest with lopped arms the youth appears, Spoiled of his nose and shortened of his ears.

senses.d: Wanting in honesty; void of integrity; faithless; disposed to cheat or defraud; not trustworthy; as, a dishonest man.
Characterized by fraud; indicating a want of probity; knavish; fraudulent; unjust.
q: To get dishonest gain.
The dishonest profits of men in office.

Dishonest.etym: [Pref. dis- + honest: cf. F. déshonnête, OF. deshoneste.]

senses.d: To disgrace; to dishonor; as, to dishonest a maid.
q: I will no longer dishonest my house.

senses.d: Dishonor; dishonorableness; shame.
Want of honesty, probity, or integrity in principle; want of fairness and straightforwardness; a disposition to defraud, deceive, or betray; faithlessness.
Violation of trust or of justice; fraud; any deviation from probity; a dishonest act.
Lewdness; unchastity.

To cut off from an inheritance or from hereditary succession; to prevent, as an heir, from coming into possession of any property or right, which, by law or custom, would devolve on him in the course of descent.
q: Of how fair a portion Adam disinherited his whole posterity!

senses.d: To deprive of heritage; to dispossess.
q: And disinherit Chaos, that reigns here.

senses.d: To disable with alarm or apprehensions; to depress the spirits or courage of; to deprive or firmness and energy through fear; to daunt; to appall; to terrify.
q: Be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed.
What words be these? What fears do you dismay?

senses.d: To render lifeless; to subdue; to disquiet.
q: Do not dismay yourself for this.
So flies a herd of beeves, that hear, dismayed, The lions roaring through the midnight shade.
Jove got such heroes as my sire, whose soul No fear could daunt, nor earth nor hell control.
Now the last ruin the whole host appalls; Now Greece has trembled in her wooden walls.

Dismay.syn: To terrify; fright; affright; frighten; appall; daunt; dishearthen; dispirit; discourage; deject; depress. — To Dismay, Daunt, Appall. Dismay denotes a state of deep and gloomy apprehension. To daunt supposes something more sudden and startling. To appall is the strongest term, implying a sense of terror which overwhelms the faculties.
Dismay.etym: [OE. desmaien, dismaien, OF. esmaier; pref. es- (L. ex) + OHG. magan to be strong or able; akin to E. may. In English the pref. es- was changed to dis- (L. dis-). See May, v. i.]

senses.d: To take dismay or fright; to be filled with dismay.
Loss of courage and firmness through fear; overwhelming and disabling terror; a sinking of the spirits; consternation.
q: I . . . can not think of such a battle without dismay.
Thou with a tiger spring dost leap upon thy prey, And tear his helpless breast, o'erwhelmed with wild dismay.

senses.d: Condition fitted to dismay; ruin.

Dismay.syn: Dejection; discouragement; depression; fear; fright; terror; apprehension; alarm; affright.
Dismay.etym: [Cf. OF. esmai, F. émoi. See Dismay, v. t.]

senses.d: To send away; to give leave of departure; to cause or permit to go; to put away.
q: He dismissed the assembly.
Dismiss their cares when they dismiss their flock.
Though he soon dismissed himself from state affairs.

senses.d: To discard; to remove or discharge from office, service, or employment; as, the king dismisses his ministers; the matter dismisses his servant.
To lay aside or reject as unworthy of attentions or regard, as a petition or motion in court.

Dismiss.etym: [L. dis- + missus, p. p. of mittere to send: cf. dimittere, OF. desmetre, F. démettre. See Demise, and cf. Dimit.]

senses.d: Dismission.
Neglect or refusal to obey; violation of a command or prohibition.
q: He is undutiful to him other actions, and lives in open disobedience.

senses.d: Neglecting or refusing to obey; omitting to do what is commanded, or doing what is prohibited; refractory; not observant of duty or rules prescribed by authority; — applied to persons and acts.
q: This disobedient spirit in the colonies.
Disobedient unto the word of the Lord.

senses.d: Not yielding.
q: Medicines used unnecessarily contribute to shorten life, by sooner rendering peculiar parts of the system disobedient to stimuli.

senses.d: Not to obey; to neglect or refuse to obey (a superior or his commands, the laws, etc.); to transgress the commands of (one in authority); to violate, as an order; as, refractory children disobey their parents; men disobey their Maker and the laws.
q: Not to disobey her lord's behest.

Disobey.etym: [F. désobéir; pref. dés- (L. dis-) + obéir. See Obey, and cf. Disobedient.]

senses.d: To refuse or neglect to obey; to violate commands; to be disobedient.
q: He durst not know how to disobey.

senses.d: Want of order or regular disposition; lack of arrangement; confusion; disarray; as, the troops were thrown into disorder; the papers are in disorder.
Neglect of order or system; irregularity.
q: From vulgar bounds with brave disorder part, And snatch a grace beyond the reach of art.

senses.d: Breach of public order; disturbance of the peace of society; tumult.
Disturbance of the functions of the animal economy or of the soul; sickness; derangement.

Disorder.syn: Irregularity; disarrangement; confusion; tumult; bustle; disturbance; disease; illness; indisposition; sickness; ailment; malady; distemper. See Disease.

senses.d: To disturb the order of; to derange or disarrange; to throw into confusion; to confuse.
q: Disordering the whole frame or jurisprudence.
The burden . . . disordered the aids and auxiliary rafters into a common ruin.

senses.d: To disturb or interrupt the regular and natural functions of (either body or mind); to produce sickness or indisposition in; to discompose; to derange; as, to disorder the head or stomach.
q: A man whose judgment was so much disordered by party spirit.

senses.d: To depose from holy orders.
Not in order; marked by disorder; disarranged; immethodical; as, the books and papers are in a disorderly state.
Not acting in an orderly way, as the functions of the body or mind.
Not complying with the restraints of order and law; tumultuous; unruly; lawless; turbulent; as, disorderly people; disorderly assemblies.
Offensive to good morals and public decency; notoriously offensive; as, a disorderly house.

Disorderly.syn: Irregular; immethodical; confused; tumultuous; inordinate; intemperate; unruly; lawless; vicious.

senses.d: In a disorderly manner; without law or order; irregularly; confusedly.
q: Withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly.
Savages fighting disorderly with stones.

senses.d: To dispose of speedily, as business; to execute quickly; to make a speedy end of; to finish; to perform.
q: Ere we put ourselves in arms, dispatch we The business we have talked of.
harvest men . . . almost in one fair day dispatcheth all the harvest work.

senses.d: To rid; to free.
q: I had clean dispatched myself of this great charge.

senses.d: To get rid of by sending off; to send away hastily.
q: Unless dispatched to the mansion house in the country . . . they perish among the lumber of garrets.

senses.d: To send off or away; — particularly applied to sending off messengers, messages, letters, etc., on special business, and implying haste.
q: Even with the speediest expedition I will dispatch him to the emperor's cou��.

senses.d: To send out of the world; to put to death.
q: The company shall stone them with stones, and dispatch them with their swords.

Dispatch.syn: To expedite; hasten; speed; accelerate; perform; conclude; finish; slay; kill.
Dispatch.etym: [OF. despeechier, F. dépêcher; prob. from pref. des- (L. dis-) + (assumed) LL. pedicare to place obstacles in the way, fr. L. pedica fetter, fr. pes, pedis, foot. See Foot, and cf. Impeach, Despatch.]

senses.d: To make haste; to conclude an affair; to finish a matter of business.
q: They have dispatched with Pompey.

senses.d: The act of sending a message or messenger in haste or on important business.
Any sending away; dismissal; riddance.
q: To the utter dispatch of all their most beloved comforts.

senses.d: The finishing up of a business; speedy performance, as of business; prompt execution; diligence; haste.
q: Serious business, craving quick dispatch.
To carry his scythe . . . with a sufficient dispatch through a sufficient space.

senses.d: A message dispatched or sent with speed; especially, an important official letter sent from one public officer to another; — often used in the plural; as, a messenger has arrived with dispatches for the American minister; naval or military dispatches.
A message transmitted by telegraph.

Dispatch.syn: Haste; hurry; promptness; celerity; speed. See Haste.
Dispatch.etym: [Cf. OF. despeche, F. dépêche. See Dispatch, v. t.]

senses.d: The act of dispensing or dealing out; distribution; often used of the distribution of good and evil by God to man, or more generically, of the acts and modes of his administration.
q: To respect the dispensations of Providence.

senses.d: That which is dispensed, dealt out, or appointed; that which is enjoined or bestowed
q: Neither are God's methods or intentions different in his dispensations to each private man.

senses.d: The relaxation of a law in a particular case; permission to do something forbidden, or to omit doing something enjoined; specifically, in the Roman Catholic Church, exemption from some ecclesiastical law or obligation to God which a man has incurred of his own free will (oaths, vows, etc.).
q: A dispensation was obtained to enable Dr. Barrow to marry.

senses.d: To scatter abroad; to drive to different parts; to distribute; to diffuse; to spread; as, the Jews are dispersed among all nations.
q: The lips of the wise disperse knowledge.
Two lions, in the still, dark night, A herd of beeves disperse.

senses.d: To scatter, so as to cause to vanish; to dissipate; as, to disperse vapors.
q: Dispersed are the glories.

Disperse.syn: To scatter; dissipate; dispel; spread; diffuse; distribute; deal out; disseminate.
Disperse.etym: [L. dispersus, p. p. of dispergere to strew, scatter. See Sparse.]

senses.d: To separate; to go or move into different parts; to vanish; as, the company dispersed at ten o'clock; the clouds disperse.
To distribute wealth; to share one's abundance with others.
q: He hath dispersed, he hath given to the poor.

senses.d: Scattered.

The act or process of scattering or dispersing, or the state of being scattered or separated; as, the Jews in their dispersion retained their rites and ceremonies; a great dispersion of the human family took place at the building of Babel.
q: The days of your slaughter and of your dispersions are accomplished.

senses.d: The separation of light into its different colored rays, arising from their different refrangibilities.
To unfold; to spread wide; to expand; to stretch out; to spread.
q: The northern wind his wings did broad display.

senses.d: To extend the front of (a column), bringing it into line.
To spread before the view; to show; to exhibit to the sight, or to the mind; to make manifest.
q: His statement . . . displays very clearly the actual condition of the army.

senses.d: To make an exhibition of; to set in view conspicuously or ostentatiously; to exhibit for the sake of publicity; to parade.
q: Proudly displaying the insignia of their order.

senses.d: To make conspicuous by large or prominent type.
To discover; to descry.
q: And from his seat took pleasure to display The city so adorned with towers.

Display.syn: To exhibit; show; manifest; spread out; parade; expand; flaunt.
Display.etym: [OE. displaien, desplaien, OF. despleier, desploier, F. déployer; pref. des- (L. dis-) + pleier, ploier, plier, F. ployer, plier, to fold, bend, L. plicare. See Ply, and cf. Deploy, Splay.]

senses.d: To make a display; to act as one making a show or demonstration.
An opening or unfolding; exhibition; manifestation.
q: Having witnessed displays of his power and grace.

senses.d: Ostentatious show; exhibition for effect; parade.
q: He died, as erring man should die, Without display, without parade.

senses.d: Unfolded; expanded; exhibited conspicuously or ostentatiously.
With wings expanded; — said of a bird of pray, esp. an eagle.
Set with lines of prominent type interspersed, to catch the eye.

To make not pleased; to excite a feeling of disapprobation or dislike in; to be disagreeable to; to offend; to vex; — often followed by with or at. It usually expresses less than to anger, vex, irritate, or provoke.
q: God was displeased with this thing.
Wilt thou be displeased at us forever?
This virtuous plaster will displease Your tender sides.
Adversity is so wholesome . . . why should we be displeased therewith?

senses.d: To fail to satisfy; to miss of.
q: I shall displease my ends else.

Displease.syn: To offend; disgust; vex; annoy; dissatisfy; chafe; anger; provoke; affront.
Displease.etym: [OF. desplaisir, whence F. déplaisir displeasure; pref. des- (L. dis-) + plaisir to please. See Please, and cf. Displeasure.]

senses.d: To give displeasure or offense.

The feeling of one who is displeased; irritation or uneasiness of the mind, occasioned by anything that counteracts desire or command, or which opposes justice or a sense of propriety; disapprobation; dislike; dissatisfaction; disfavor; indignation.
q: O Lord, rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure.
Undoubtedly he will relent, and turn From his displeasure.

senses.d: That which displeases; cause of irritation or annoyance; offense; injury.
q: Hast thou delight to see a wretched man Do outrage and displeasure to himself?

senses.d: State of disgrace or disfavor; disfavor.
q: He went into Poland, being in displeasure with the pope for overmuch familiarity.

Displeasure.syn: Dissatisfaction; disapprobation; disfavor; distaste; dislike; anger; hate; aversion; indignation; offense.
Displeasure.etym: [Pref. dis- + pleasure: cf. OF. desplaisir, F. déplaisir. Cf. Displease.]

senses.d: To displease.
To distribute and put in place; to arrange; to set in order; as, to dispose the ships in the form of a crescent.
q: Who hath disposed the whole world?
All ranged in order and disposed with grace.
The rest themselves in troops did else dispose.

senses.d: To regulate; to adjust; to settle; to determine.
q: The knightly forms of combat to dispose.

senses.d: To deal out; to assign to a use; to bestow for an object or purpose; to apply; to employ; to dispose of.
q: Importuned him that what he designed to bestow on her funeral, he would rather dispose among the poor.

senses.d: To give a tendency or inclination to; to adapt; to cause to turn; especially, to incline the mind of; to give a bent or propension to; to incline; to make inclined; — usually followed by to, sometimes by for before the indirect object.
q: Endure and conquer; Jove will soon dispose To future good our past and present woes.
Suspicions dispose kings to tyranny, husbands to jealousy, and wise men to irresolution and melancholy.

Dispose.syn: To set; arrange; order; distribute; adjust; regulate; adapt; fit; incline; bestow; give.
Dispose.etym: [F. disposer; pref. dis- + poser to place. See Pose.]

senses.d: To bargain; to make terms.
q: She had disposed with Cæsar.

senses.d: Disposal; ordering; management; power or right of control.
q: But such is the dispose of the sole Disposer of empires.

senses.d: Cast of mind; disposition; inclination; behavior; demeanor.
q: He hath a person, and a smooth dispose To be suspected.

senses.d: Inclined; minded.
q: When he was disposed to pass into Achaia.

senses.d: Inclined to mirth; jolly.
The act of disposing, arranging, ordering, regulating, or transferring; application; disposal; as, the disposition of a man's property by will.
q: Who have received the law by the disposition of angels.
The disposition of the work, to put all things in a beautiful order and harmony, that the whole may be of a piece.

senses.d: The state or the manner of being disposed or arranged; distribution; arrangement; order; as, the disposition of the trees in an orchard; the disposition of the several parts of an edifice.
Tendency to any action or state resulting from natural constitution; nature; quality; as, a disposition in plants to grow in a direction upward; a disposition in bodies to putrefaction.
Conscious inclination; propension or propensity.
q: How stands your disposition to be married?

senses.d: Natural or prevailing spirit, or temperament of mind, especially as shown in intercourse with one's fellow-men; temper of mind.
q: His disposition led him to do things agreeable to his quality and condition wherein God had placed him.

senses.d: Mood; humor.
q: As I perchance hereafter shall think meet To put an antic disposition on.

Disposition.syn: Disposal; adjustment; regulation; arrangement; distribution; order; method; adaptation; inclination; propensity; bestowment; alienation; character; temper; mood. — Disposition, Character, Temper. Disposition is the natural humor of a person, the predominating quality of his character, the constitutional habit of his mind. Character is this disposition influenced by motive, training, and will. Temper is a quality of the fiber of character, and is displayed chiefly when the emotions, especially the passions, are aroused.
Disposition.etym: [F. disposition, dispositio, fr. disponere to dispose; dis- + ponere to place. See Position, and cf. Dispone.]

senses.d: To put out of possession; to deprive of the actual occupancy of, particularly of land or real estate; to disseize; to eject; — usually followed by of before the thing taken away; as, to dispossess a king of his crown.
q: Usurp the land, and dispossess the swain.

senses.d: The act of disputing; a reasoning or argumentation in opposition to something, or on opposite sides; controversy in words; verbal contest respecting the truth of some fact, opinion, proposition, or argument.
A rhetorical exercise in which parties reason in opposition to each other on some question proposed.

Disputation.etym: [OE. desputeson, disputacion, OF. desputeison, F. disputation, fr. L. disputatio. See Dispute, v. i.]

senses.d: To contend in argument; to argue against something maintained, upheld, or claimed, by another; to discuss; to reason; to debate; to altercate; to wrangle.
q: Therefore disputed [reasoned, Rev. Ver.] he in synagogue with the Jews.

Dispute.etym: [OE. desputen, disputen, OF. desputer, disputer, F. disputer, from L. disputare, disputatum; dis- + putare to clean; hence, fig., to clear up, set in order, reckon, think. See Putative, Pure.]

senses.d: To make a subject of disputation; to argue pro and con; to discuss.
q: The rest I reserve it be disputed how the magistrate is to do herein.

senses.d: To oppose by argument or assertion; to attempt to overthrow; to controvert; to express dissent or opposition to; to call in question; to deny the truth or validity of; as, to dispute assertions or arguments.
q: To seize goods under the disputed authority of writs of assistance.

senses.d: To strive or contend about; to contest.
q: To dispute the possession of the ground with the Spaniards.

senses.d: To struggle against; to resist.
q: Dispute it like a man.

Dispute.syn: To controvert; contest; gainsay; doubt; question; argue; debate; discuss; impugn. See Argue.

senses.d: Verbal controversy; contest by opposing argument or expression of opposing views or claims; controversial discussion; altercation; debate.
q: Addicted more To contemplation and profound dispute.

senses.d: Contest; struggle; quarrel.

Dispute.syn: Altercation; controversy; argumentation; debate; discussion; quarrel; disagreement; difference; contention; wrangling. See Altercation.
Dispute.etym: [Cf. F. dispute. See Dispute, v. i.]

senses.d: One who disputes, or who is given to disputes; a controvertist.
q: Where is the disputer of this world?

senses.d: Deprived of quiet; impatient; restless; uneasy.
Want of quiet; want of tranquility in body or mind; uneasiness; restlessness; disturbance; anxiety.
To render unquiet; to deprive of peace, rest, or tranquility; to make uneasy or restless; to disturb.
q: Why art thou cast down, O my soul, and why art thou disquieted within me?
As quiet as these disquieted times will permit.

Disquiet.syn: To harass; disturb; vex; fret; excite; agitate.

senses.d: Disturbance of quiet in body or mind; restlessness; uneasiness.
To hide under a false semblance or seeming; to feign (something) not to be what it really is; to put an untrue appearance upon; to disguise; to mask.
q: Dissemble all your griefs and discontents.
Perhaps it was right to dissemble your love, But — why did you kick me down stairs?

senses.d: To put on the semblance of; to make pretense of; to simulate; to feign.
q: He soon dissembled a sleep.

Dissemble.syn: To conceal; disguise; cloak; cover; equivocate. See Conceal.
Dissemble.etym: [OF. dissembler to be dissimilar; pref. dis- (L. dis-) + F. sembler to seem, L. simulare to simulate; cf. L. dissimulare to dissemble. See Simulate, and cf. Dissimulate.]

senses.d: To conceal the real fact, motives, intention, or sentiments, under some pretense; to assume a false appearance; to act the hypocrite.
q: He that hateth dissembleth with his lips.
He dissembles when he assumes an air of friendship.

senses.d: One who dissembles; one who conceals his opinions or dispositions under a false appearance; a hypocrite.
q: It is the weakest sort of politicians that are the greatest dissemblers.
Priests, princes, women, no dissemblers here.

senses.d: Disagreement in opinion, usually of a violent character, producing warm debates or angry words; contention in words; partisan and contentious divisions; breach of friendship and union; strife; discord; quarrel.
q: Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them.
Debates, dissension, uproars are thy joy.
A seditious person and raiser-up of dissension among the people.

Dissension.etym: [L. dissensio: cf. F. dissension. See Dissent.]

senses.d: The act of dissembling; a hiding under a false appearance; concealment by feigning; false pretension; hypocrisy.
q: Let love be without dissimulation.
Dissimulation . . . when a man lets fall signs and arguments that he is not that he is.
Simulation is a pretense of what is not, and dissimulation a concealment of what is.

senses.d: To separate into competent parts; to disorganize; to break up; hence, to bring to an end by separating the parts, sundering a relation, etc.; to terminate; to destroy; to deprive of force; as, to dissolve a partnership; to dissolve Parliament.
q: Lest his ungoverned rage dissolve the life.

senses.d: To break the continuity of; to disconnect; to disunite; to sunder; to loosen; to undo; to separate.
q: Nothing can dissolve us.
Down fell the duke, his joints dissolved asunder.
For one people to dissolve the political bands which have connected them with another.

senses.d: To convert into a liquid by means of heat, moisture, etc.,; to melt; to liquefy; to soften.
q: As if the world were all dissolved to tears.

senses.d: To solve; to clear up; to resolve.
q: Make interpretations and dissolve doubts.

senses.d: To relax by pleasure; to make powerless.
q: Angels dissolved in hallelujahs lie.

senses.d: To annul; to rescind; to discharge or release; as, to dissolve an injunction.

Dissolve.etym: [L. dissolvere, dissolutum; dis- + solvere to loose, free. See Solve, and cf. Dissolute.]

senses.d: To waste away; to be dissipated; to be decomposed or broken up.
To become fluid; to be melted; to be liquefied.
q: A figure Trenched in ice, which with an hour's heat Dissolves to water, and doth lose his form.

senses.d: To fade away; to fall to nothing; to lose power.
q: The charm dissolves apace.

senses.d: Melting; breaking up; vanishing.
The staff for holding a bunch of flax, tow, or wool, from which the thread is drawn in spinning by hand.
q: I will the distaff hold; come thou and spin.

senses.d: Used as a symbol of the holder of a distaff; hence, a woman; women, collectively.
q: His crown usurped, a distaff on the throne.
Some say the crozier, some say the distaff was too busy.

Distaff.etym: [OE. distaf, dysestafe, AS. distaef; cf. LG. diesse the bunch of flax on a distaff, and E. dizen. See Staff.]

senses.d: Separated; having an intervening space; at a distance; away.
q: One board had two tenons, equally distant.
Diana's temple is not distant far.

senses.d: Far separated; far off; not near; remote; — in place, time, consanguinity, or connection; as, distant times; distant relatives.
q: The success of these distant enterprises.

senses.d: Reserved or repelling in manners; cold; not cordial; somewhat haughty; as, a distant manner.
q: He passed me with a distant bow.

senses.d: Indistinct; faint; obscure, as from distance.
q: Some distant knowledge.
A distant glimpse.

senses.d: Not conformable; discrepant; repugnant; as, a practice so widely distant from Christianity.

Distant.syn: Separate; far; remote; aloof; apart; asunder; slight; faint; indirect; indistinct.
Distant.etym: [F., fr. L. distans, -antis, p. pr. of distare to stand apart, be separate or distant; dis- + stare to stand. See Stand.]

senses.d: Distinguished; having the difference marked; separated by a visible sign; marked out; specified.
q: Wherever thus created — for no place Is yet distinct by name.

senses.d: Marked; variegated.
q: The which was dight With divers flowers distinct with rare delight.

senses.d: Separate in place; not conjunct; not united by growth or otherwise; — with from.
q: The intention was that the two armies which marched out together should afterward be distinct.

senses.d: Not identical; different; individual.
q: To offend, and judge, are distinct offices.

senses.d: So separated as not to be confounded with any other thing; not liable to be misunderstood; not confused; well-defined; clear; as, we have a distinct or indistinct view of a prospect.
q: Relation more particular and distinct.

Distinct.syn: Separate; unconnected; disjoined; different; clear; plain; conspicuous; obvious.
Distinct.etym: [L. distinctus, p. p. of distinguere: cf. F. distinct. See Distinguish.]

senses.d: To distinguish.
A marking off by visible signs; separation into parts; division.
q: The distinction of tragedy into acts was not known.

senses.d: The act of distinguishing or denoting the differences between objects, or the qualities by which one is known from others; exercise of discernment; discrimination.
q: To take away therefore that error, which confusion breedeth, distinction is requisite.

senses.d: That which distinguishes one thing from another; distinguishing quality; sharply defined difference; as, the distinction between real and apparent good.
q: The distinction betwixt the animal kingdom and the inferior parts of matter.

senses.d: Estimation of difference; regard to differences or distinguishing circumstance.
q: Maids, women, wives, without distinction, fall.

senses.d: Conspicuous station; eminence; superiority; honorable estimation; as, a man of distinction.
q: Your country's own means of distinction and defense.

Distinction.syn: Difference; variation, variety; contrast; diversity; contrariety; disagreement; discrimination; preference; superiority; rank; note; eminence.

senses.d: With distinctness; not confusedly; without the blending of one part or thing another; clearly; plainly; as, to see distinctly.
With meaning; significantly.
q: Thou dost snore distinctly; There's meaning in thy snores.

senses.d: Separated; drawn asunder.
Insane; mad.

Distract.etym: [L. distractus, p. p. of distrahere to draw asunder; dis- + trahere to draw. See Trace, and cf. Distraught.]

senses.d: To draw apart or away; to divide; to disjoin.
q: A city . . . distracted from itself.

senses.d: To draw (the sight, mind, or attention) in different directions; to perplex; to confuse; as, to distract the eye; to distract the attention.
q: Mixed metaphors . . . distract the imagination.

senses.d: To agitate by conflicting passions, or by a variety of motives or of cares; to confound; to harass.
q: Horror and doubt distract His troubled thoughts.

senses.d: To unsettle the reason of; to render insane; to craze; to madden; — most frequently used in the participle, distracted.
q: A poor mad soul; . . . poverty hath distracted her.

senses.d: Mentally disordered; unsettled; mad.
q: My distracted mind.

senses.d: The act of distracting; a drawing apart; separation.
q: To create distractions among us.

senses.d: That which diverts attention; a diversion.
A diversity of direction; detachment.
q: His power went out in such distractions as Beguiled all species.

senses.d: State in which the attention is called in different ways; confusion; perplexity.
q: That ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction.

senses.d: Confusion of affairs; tumult; disorder; as, political distractions.
q: Never was known a night of such distraction.

senses.d: Agitation from violent emotions; perturbation of mind; despair.
q: The distraction of the children, who saw both their parents together, would have melted the hardest heart.

senses.d: Derangement of the mind; madness.

Distraction.syn: Perplexity; confusion; disturbance; disorder; dissension; tumult; derangement; madness; raving; franticness; furiousness.

senses.d: Extreme pain or suffering; anguish of body or mind; as, to suffer distress from the gout, or from the loss of friends.
q: Not fearing death nor shrinking for distress.

senses.d: That which occasions suffering; painful situation; misfortune; affliction; misery.
q: Affliction's sons are brothers in distress.

senses.d: A state of danger or necessity; as, a ship in distress, from leaking, loss of spars, want of provisions or water, etc.

The act of distraining; the taking of a personal chattel out of the possession of a wrongdoer, by way of pledge for redress of an injury, or for the performance of a duty, as for nonpayment of rent or taxes, or for injury done by cattle, etc.
q: If he were not paid, he would straight go and take a distress of goods and cattle.
The distress thus taken must be proportioned to the thing distrained for.

Distress.syn: Affliction; suffering; pain; agony; misery; torment; anguish; grief; sorrow; calamity; misfortune; trouble; adversity. See Affliction.
Distress.etym: [OE. destresse, distresse, OF. destresse, destrece, F. détresse, OF. destrecier to distress, (assumed) LL. districtiare, fr. L. districtus, p. p. of distringere. See Distrain, and cf. Stress.]

senses.d: To cause pain or anguish to; to pain; to oppress with calamity; to afflict; to harass; to make miserable.
q: We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed.

senses.d: To compel by pain or suffering.
q: Men who can neither be distressed nor won into a sacrifice of duty.

senses.d: To seize for debt; to distrain.

Distress.syn: To pain; grieve; harass; trouble; perplex; afflict; worry; annoy.

senses.d: To divide among several or many; to deal out; to apportion; to allot.
q: She did distribute her goods to all them that were nearest of kindred.

senses.d: To dispense; to administer; as, to distribute justice.
To divide or separate, as into classes, orders, kinds, or species; to classify; to assort, as specimens, letters, etc.
To separate (type which has been used) and return it to the proper boxes in the cases.
To employ (a term) in its whole extent; to take as universal in one premise.
q: A term is said to be distributed when it is taken universal, so as to stand for everything it is capable of being applied to.

Distribute.syn: To dispense; deal out; apportion; allot; share; assign; divide.
Distribute.etym: [L. distributus, p. p. of distribuere to divide, distribute; dis- + tribuere to assign, give, allot. See Tribute.]

senses.d: To make distribution.
q: Distributing to the necessity of saints.

senses.d: That distributes; dealing out.
The act of distributing or dispensing; the act of dividing or apportioning among several or many; apportionment; as, the distribution of an estate among heirs or children.
q: The phenomena of geological distribution are exactly analogous to those of geography.

senses.d: Separation into parts or classes; arrangement of anything into parts; disposition; classification.
That which is distributed.
A resolving a whole into its parts.
The sorting of types and placing them in their proper boxes in the cases.

The steps or operations by which steam is supplied to and withdrawn from the cylinder at each stroke of the piston; viz., admission, suppression or cutting off, release or exhaust, and compression of exhaust steam prior to the next admission.

Distribution.syn: Apportionments; allotment; dispensation; disposal; dispersion; classification; arrangement.

senses.d: A trench made in the earth by digging, particularly a trench for draining wet land, for guarding or fencing inclosures, or for preventing an approach to a town or fortress. In the latter sense, it is called also a moat or a fosse.
Any long, narrow receptacle for water on the surface of the earth.

Ditch.etym: [OE. dich, orig. the same word as dik. See Dike.]

senses.d: To dig a ditch or ditches in; to drain by a ditch or ditches; as, to ditch moist land.
To surround with a ditch.
To throw into a ditch; as, the engine was ditched and turned on its side.
To dig a ditch or ditches.
One who, or that which, dives.
q: Divers and fishers for pearls.

senses.d: Fig.: One who goes deeply into a subject, study, or business.
Any bird of certain genera, as Urinator (formerly Colymbus), or the allied genus Colymbus, or Podiceps, remarkable for their agility in diving.
Different in kind or species; diverse.
q: Every sect of them hath a divers posture.
Thou shalt not sow thy vineyard with divers seeds.

senses.d: Several; sundry; various; more than one, but not a great number; as, divers philosophers. Also used substantively or pronominally.
q: Divers of Antonio's creditors.

Divers.etym: [F. divers, L. diversus turned in different directions, different, p. p. of divertere. See Divert, and cf. Diverse.]

senses.d: Different; unlike; dissimilar; distinct; separate.
q: The word . . . is used in a sense very diverse from its original import.
Our roads are diverse: farewell, love! said she.

senses.d: Capable of various forms; multiform.
q: Eloquence is a great and diverse thing.

Diverse.etym: [The same word as divers. See Divers.]

senses.d: In different directions; diversely.
To turn aside.
q: The redcross knight diverst, but forth rode Britomart.

senses.d: A state of difference; dissimilitude; unlikeness.
q: They will prove opposite; and not resting in a bare diversity, rise into a contrariety.

senses.d: Multiplicity of difference; multiformity; variety.
Variegation.

Diversity.etym: [F. diversité, L. diversitas, fr. diversus. See Diverse.]

senses.d: To part asunder (a whole); to sever into two or more parts or pieces; to sunder; to separate into parts.
q: Divide the living child in two.

senses.d: To cause to be separate; to keep apart by a partition, or by an imaginary line or limit; as, a wall divides two houses; a stream divides the towns.
q: Let it divide the waters from the waters.

senses.d: To make partition of among a number; to apportion, as profits of stock among proprietors; to give in shares; to distribute; to mete out; to share.
q: True justice unto people to divide.
Ye shall divide the land by lot.

senses.d: To disunite in opinion or interest; to make discordant or hostile; to set at variance.
q: If a kingdom be divided against itself, that kingdom can not stand.
Every family became now divided within itself.

senses.d: To separate into two parts, in order to ascertain the votes for and against a measure; as, to divide a legislative house upon a question.
To subject to arithmetical division.
To separate into species; — said of a genus or generic term.
To mark divisions on; to graduate; as, to divide a sextant.
To play or sing in a florid style, or with variations.

Divide.syn: To sever; dissever; sunder; cleave; disjoin; disunite; detach; disconnect; part; distribute; share.
Divide.etym: [L. dividere, divisum; di- = dis- + root signifying to part; cf. Skr. vyadh to pierce; perh. akin to L. vidua widow, and E. widow. Cf. Device, Devise.]

senses.d: To be separated; to part; to open; to go asunder.
q: The Indo-Germanic family divides into three groups.

senses.d: To cause separation; to disunite.
q: A gulf, a strait, the sea intervening between islands, divide less than the matted forest.

senses.d: To break friendship; to fall out.
To have a share; to partake.
To vote, as in the British Parliament, by the members separating themselves into two parties (as on opposite sides of the hall or in opposite lobbies), that is, the ayes dividing from the noes.
q: The emperors sat, voted, and divided with their equals.

senses.d: A dividing ridge of land between the tributaries of two streams; a watershed.
Parted; disunited; distributed.
Cut into distinct parts, by incisions which reach the midrib; — said of a leaf.
One who, or that which, divides; that which separates anything into parts.
One who deals out to each his share.
q: Who made me a judge or a divider over you?

senses.d: One who, or that which, causes division.
q: Hate is of all things the mightiest divider.
Money, the great divider of the world.

senses.d: An instrument for dividing lines, describing circles, etc., compasses. See Compasses.
That divides; separating; marking divisions; graduating.
The act of divining; a foreseeing or foretelling of future events; the pretended art discovering secret or future by preternatural means.
q: There shall not be found among you any one that . . . useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter.

senses.d: An indication of what is future or secret; augury omen; conjectural presage; prediction.
q: Birds which do give a happy divination of things to come.

Divination.etym: [L. divinatio, fr. divinare, divinatum, to foresee, foretell, fr. divinus: cf. F. divination. See Divine.]

senses.d: Of or belonging to God; as, divine perfections; the divine will.
Proceeding from God; as, divine judgments.
Appropriated to God, or celebrating his praise; religious; pious; holy; as, divine service; divine songs; divine worship.
Pertaining to, or proceeding from, a deity; partaking of the nature of a god or the gods.
Godlike; heavenly; excellent in the highest degree; supremely admirable; apparently above what is human. In this application, the word admits of comparison; as, the divinest mind. Sir J. Davies.
q: A divine sentence is in the lips of the king.
But not to one in this benighted age Is that diviner inspiration given.

senses.d: Presageful; foreboding; prescient.
q: Yet oft his heart, divine of something ill, Misgave him.

senses.d: Relating to divinity or theology.
q: Church history and other divine learning.

Divine.syn: Supernatural; superhuman; godlike; heavenly; celestial; pious; holy; sacred; preëminent.

senses.d: One skilled in divinity; a theologian.
A minister of the gospel; a priest; a clergyman.
q: The first divines of New England were surpassed by none in extensive erudition.

Divine.etym: [L. divinus a soothsayer, LL., a theologian. See Divine, a.]

senses.d: To foresee or foreknow; to detect; to anticipate; to conjecture.
q: A sagacity which divined the evil designs.

senses.d: To foretell; to predict; to presage.
q: Darest thou . . . divine his downfall?

senses.d: To render divine; to deify.
q: Living on earth like angel new divined.

Divine.syn: To foretell; predict; presage; prophesy; prognosticate; forebode; guess; conjecture; surmise.
Divine.etym: [L. divinare: cf. F. deviner. See Divination.]

senses.d: To use or practice divination; to foretell by divination; to utter prognostications.
q: The prophets thereof divine for money.

senses.d: To have or feel a presage or foreboding.
q: Suggest but truth to my divining thoughts.

senses.d: To conjecture or guess; as, to divine rightly.
One who professes divination; one who pretends to predict events, or to reveal occult things, by supernatural means.
q: The diviners have seen a lie, and have told false dreams; they comfort in vain.

senses.d: A conjecture; a guesser; one who makes out occult things.
That divines; for divining.
The act or process of diving anything into parts, or the state of being so divided; separation.
q: I was overlooked in the division of the spoil.

senses.d: That which divides or keeps apart; a partition.
The portion separated by the divining of a mass or body; a distinct segment or section.
q: Communities and divisions of men.

senses.d: Disunion; difference in opinion or feeling; discord; variance; alienation.
q: There was a division among the people.

senses.d: Difference of condition; state of distinction; distinction; contrast.
q: I will put a division between my people and thy people.

senses.d: Separation of the members of a deliberative body, esp. of the Houses of Parliament, to ascertain the vote.
q: The motion passed without a division.

senses.d: The process of finding how many times one number or quantity is contained in another; the reverse of multiplication; also, the rule by which the operation is performed.
The separation of a genus into its constituent species.
Two or more brigades under the command of a general officer.
One of the groups into which a fleet is divided.
A course of notes so running into each other as to form one series or chain, to be sung in one breath to one syllable.
The distribution of a discourse into parts; a part so distinguished.

Division.syn: compartment; section; share; allotment; distribution; separation; partition; disjunction; disconnection; difference; variance; discord; disunion.
Division.etym: [F. division, L. divisio, from dividere. See Divide.]

senses.d: A legal dissolution of the marriage contract by a court or other body having competent authority. This is properly a divorce, and called, technically, divorce a vinculo matrimonii.
The decree or writing by which marriage is dissolved.
Separation; disunion of things closely united.
q: To make divorce of their incorporate league.

senses.d: That which separates.

Divorce.etym: [F. divorce, L. divortium, fr. divortere, divertere, to turn different ways, to separate. See Divert.]

senses.d: To dissolve the marriage contract of, either wholly or partially; to separate by divorce.
To separate or disunite; to sunder.
q: It was divorced from its old sense.

senses.d: To make away; to put away.
q: Nothing but death Shall e'er divorce my dignities.

senses.d: Dissolution of the marriage tie; divorce; separation.
q: Let him write her a divorcement.
The divorcement of our written from our spoken language.

senses.d: A syllable attached to the first tone of the major diatonic scale for the purpose of solmization, or solfeggio. It is the first of the seven syllables used by the Italians as manes of musical tones, and replaced, for the sake of euphony, the syllable Ut, applied to the note C. In England and America the same syllables are used by many as a scale pattern, while the tones in respect to absolute pitch are named from the first seven letters of the alphabet.
To place; to put.
To cause; to make; — with an infinitive.
q: My lord Abbot of Westminster did do shewe to me late certain evidences.
I shall . . . your cloister do make.
A fatal plague which many did to die.
We do you to wit [i.e., We make you to know] of the grace of God bestowed on the churches of Macedonia.

senses.d: To bring about; to produce, as an effect or result; to effect; to achieve.
q: The neglecting it may do much danger.
He waved indifferently 'twixt doing them neither good not harm.

senses.d: To perform, as an action; to execute; to transact to carry out in action; as, to do a good or a bad act; do our duty; to do what I can.
q: Six days shalt thou labor and do all thy work.
We did not do these things.
You can not do wrong without suffering wrong.

senses.d: To bring to an end by action; to perform completely; to finish; to accomplish; — a sense conveyed by the construction, which is that of the past participle done.
To make ready for an object, purpose, or use, as food by cooking; to cook completely or sufficiently; as, the meat is done on one side only.

To put or bring into a form, state, or condition, especially in the phrases, to do death, to put to death; to slay; to do away (often do away with), to put away; to remove; to do on, to put on; to don; to do off, to take off, as dress; to doff; to do into, to put into the form of; to translate or transform into, as a text.
q: Done to death by slanderous tongues.
The ground of the difficulty is done away.
Suspicions regarding his loyalty were entirely done away.
To do on our own harness, that we may not; but we must do on the armor of God.
Then Jason rose and did on him a fair Blue woolen tunic.
Though the former legal pollution be now done off, yet there is a spiritual contagion in idolatry as much to be shunned.
It has been done into verse: it has been done into modern English.

senses.d: To cheat; to gull; to overreach.
q: He was not be done, at his time of life, by frivolous offers of a compromise that might have secured him seventy-five per cent.

senses.d: To see or inspect; to explore; as, to do all the points of interest.
To cash or to advance money for, as a bill or note.

Do.etym: [AS. dōn; akin to D. doen, OS. duan, OHG. tuon, G. thun, Lith. deti, OSlav. dēti, OIr. dénim I do, Gr. τιθέναι to put, Skr. dhā, and to E. suffix -dom, and prob. to L. facere to do, E. fact, and perh. to L. -dere in some compounds, as addere to add, credere to trust. √65. Cf. Deed, Deem, Doom, Fact,

senses.d: To act or behave in any manner; to conduct one's self.
q: They fear not the Lord, neither do they after . . . the law and commandment.

senses.d: To fare; to be, as regards health; as, they asked him how he did; how do you do to-day?
To succeed; to avail; to answer the purpose; to serve; as, if no better plan can be found, he will make this do.
q: You would do well to prefer a bill against all kings and parliaments since the Conquest; and if that won't do; challenge the crown.

senses.d: Deed; act; fear.
Ado; bustle; stir; to do.
q: A great deal of do, and a great deal of trouble.

senses.d: A cheat; a swindle.
To perform work upon, about, for, or at, by way of caring for, looking after, preparing, cleaning, keeping in order, or the like.
q: The sergeants seem to do themselves pretty well.

senses.d: To deal with for good and all; to finish up; to undo; to ruin; to do for.
q: Sometimes they lie in wait in these dark streets, and fracture his skull, . . . or break his arm, or cut the sinew of his wrist; and that they call doing him.

senses.d: A teacher; one skilled in a profession, or branch of knowledge; a learned man.
q: One of the doctors of Italy, Nicholas Macciavel.

senses.d: An academical title, originally meaning a man so well versed in his department as to be qualified to teach it. Hence: One who has taken the highest degree conferred by a university or college, or has received a diploma of the highest degree; as, a doctor of divinity, of law, of medicine, of music, or of philosophy. Such diplomas may confer an honorary title only.
One duly licensed to practice medicine; a member of the medical profession; a physician.
q: By medicine life may be prolonged, yet death Will seize the doctor too.

senses.d: Any mechanical contrivance intended to remedy a difficulty or serve some purpose in an exigency; as, the doctor of a calico-printing machine, which is a knife to remove superfluous coloring matter; the doctor, or auxiliary engine, called also donkey engine.
The friar skate.

Doctor.etym: [OF. doctur, L. doctor, teacher, fr. docere to teach. See Docile.]

senses.d: To treat as a physician does; to apply remedies to; to repair; as, to doctor a sick man or a broken cart.
To confer a doctorate upon; to make a doctor.
To tamper with and arrange for one's own purposes; to falsify; to adulterate; as, to doctor election returns; to doctor whisky.
To practice physic.
Teaching; instruction.
q: He taught them many things by parables, and said unto them in his doctrine, Hearken.

senses.d: That which is taught; what is held, put forth as true, and supported by a teacher, a school, or a sect; a principle or position, or the body of principles, in any branch of knowledge; any tenet or dogma; a principle of faith; as, the doctrine of atoms; the doctrine of chances.
q: Articles of faith and doctrine.
Unpracticed he to fawn or seek for power By doctrines fashioned to the varying hour.

Doctrine.etym: [F. doctrine, L. doctrina, fr. doctor. See Doctor.]

senses.d: A large, extinct bird (Didus ineptus), formerly inhabiting the Island of Mauritius. It had short, half-fledged wings, like those of the ostrich, and a short neck and legs; — called also dronte. It was related to the pigeons.

Dodo.etym: [Said to be fr. Pg. doudo silly, foolish (cf. Booby); this is fr. Prov. E. dold, the same word as E. dolt.]

senses.d: A female deer or antelope; specifically, the female of the fallow deer, of which the male is called a buck. Also applied to the female of other animals, as the rabbit. See the Note under Buck.

Doe.etym: [AS. dā; cf. Dan. daa, daa-dyr, deer, and perh. L. dama. √66.]

senses.d: A feat. See Do, n.
One who does; one who performs or executes; one who is wont and ready to act; an actor; an agent.
q: The doers of the law shall be justified.

senses.d: An agent or attorney; a factor.
A quadruped of the genus Canis, esp. the domestic dog (C. familiaris).
A mean, worthless fellow; a wretch.
q: What is thy servant, which is but a dog, that he should do this great thing?

senses.d: A fellow; — used humorously or contemptuously; as, a sly dog; a lazy dog.
One of the two constellations, Canis Major and Canis Minor, or the Greater Dog and the Lesser Dog. Canis Major contains the Dog Star (Sirius).
An iron for holding wood in a fireplace; a firedog; an andiron.
A grappling iron, with a claw or claws, for fastening into wood or other heavy articles, for the purpose of raising or moving them.

Dog.etym: [AS. docga; akin to D. dog mastiff, Dan. dogge, Sw. dogg.]

senses.d: To hunt or track like a hound; to follow insidiously or indefatigably; to chase with a dog or dogs; to worry, as if by dogs; to hound with importunity.
q: I have been pursued, dogged, and waylaid.
Your sins will dog you, pursue you.
Eager ill-bred petitioners, who do not so properly supplicate as hunt the person whom they address to, dogging him from place to place, till they even extort an answer to their rude requests.

senses.d: Anything done; a deed; an action good or bad; hence, in the plural, conduct; behavior. See Do.
q: To render an account of his doings.

senses.d: Full of dole or grief; expressing or exciting sorrow; sorrowful; sad; dismal.
q: With screwed face and doleful whine.
Regions of sorrow, doleful shades.

Doleful.syn: Piteous; rueful; sorrowful; woeful; melancholy; sad gloomy; dismal; dolorous; woe-begone.

senses.d: Sovereign or supreme authority; the power of governing and controlling; independent right of possession, use, and control; sovereignty; supremacy.
q: I praised and honored him that liveth forever, whose dominion is an everlasting dominion.
To choose between dominion or slavery.

senses.d: Superior prominence; predominance; ascendency.
q: Objects placed foremost ought . . . have dominion over things confused and transient.

senses.d: That which is governed; territory over which authority is exercised; the tract, district, or county, considered as subject; as, the dominions of a king. Also used figuratively; as, the dominion of the passions.
A supposed high order of angels; dominations. See Domination, 3.
q: By him were all things created . . . whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers.

Dominion.syn: Sovereignty; control; rule; authority; jurisdiction; government; territory; district; region.
Dominion.etym: [LL. dominio, equiv. to L. dominium. See Domain, Dungeon.]

senses.d: Performed; executed; finished.
It is done or agreed; let it be a match or bargain; — used elliptically.
Given; executed; issued; made public; — used chiefly in the clause giving the date of a proclamation or public act.

Done.etym: [Prob. corrupted from OF. doné, F. donné, p. p. of OF. doner, F. donner, to give, issue, fr. L. donare to give. See Donate, and cf. Donee.]

senses.d: An opening in the wall of a house or of an apartment, by which to go in and out; an entrance way.
q: To the same end, men several paths may tread, As many doors into one temple lead.

senses.d: The frame or barrier of boards, or other material, usually turning on hinges, by which an entrance way into a house or apartment is closed and opened.
q: At last he came unto an iron door That fast was locked.

senses.d: Passage; means of approach or access.
q: I am the door; by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved.

senses.d: An entrance way, but taken in the sense of the house or apartment to which it leads.
q: Martin's office is now the second door in the street.

Door.etym: [OE. dore, dure, AS. duru; akin to OS. dura, dor, D. deur, OHG. turi, door, tor gate, G. thür, thor, Icel. dyrr, Dan. dör, Sw. dörr, Goth. daur, Lith. durys, Russ. dvere, Olr. dorus, L. fores, Gr. �; cf. Skr. dur, dvāra. √246. Cf. Foreign.]

senses.d: One who guards the entrance of a house or apartment; a porter; a janitor.

A large European scaraboid beetle (Geotrupes stercorarius), which makes a droning noise while flying. The name is also applied to allied American species, as the June bug. Called also dorr, dorbeetle, or dorrbeetle, dorbug, dorrfly, and buzzard clock.

Dor.etym: [Cf. AS. dora drone, locust, D. tor beetle, L. taurus a kind of beetle. Cf. Dormouse.]

senses.d: A trick, joke, or deception.

Dor.etym: [Cf. Dor a beetle, and Hum, Humbug.]

senses.d: To make a fool of; to deceive.
of Do.
A marriage portion; dowry.

Dot.etym: [F., fr. L. dos, dotis, dowry. See Dower, and cf. Dote dowry.]

senses.d: A small point or spot, made with a pen or other pointed instrument; a speck, or small mark.
Anything small and like a speck comparatively; a small portion or specimen; as, a dot of a child.

Dot.etym: [Cf. AS. dott small spot, speck; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: To mark with dots or small spots; as, to dot a line.
To mark or diversify with small detached objects; as, a landscape dotted with cottages.
To make dots or specks.
A marriage portion. See 1st Dot, n.
Natural endowments.
To act foolishly.
q: He wol make him doten anon right.

senses.d: To be weak-minded, silly, or idiotic; to have the intellect impaired, especially by age, so that the mind wanders or wavers; to drivel.
q: Time has made you dote, and vainly tell Of arms imagined in your lonely cell.
He survived the use of his reason, grew infatuated, and doted long before he died.

senses.d: To be excessively or foolishly fond; to love to excess; to be weakly affectionate; — with on or upon; as, the mother dotes on her child.
q: Sing, siren, for thyself, and I will dote.
What dust we dote on, when 't is man we love.

Dote.etym: [OE. doten; akin to OD. doten, D. dutten, to doze, Icel. dotta to nod from sleep, MHG. t�zen to keep still: cf. F. doter, OF. radoter (to dote, rave, talk idly or senselessly), which are from the same source.]

senses.d: An imbecile; a dotard.
Stupid; foolish.
q: Senseless speech and doted ignorance.

senses.d: Half-rotten; as, doted wood.
of Do.
That dotes; silly; excessively fond.
Twofold; multiplied by two; increased by its equivalent; made twice as large or as much, etc.
q: Let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me.
Darkness and tempest make a double night.

senses.d: Being in pairs; presenting two of a kind, or two in a set together; coupled.
q: The swan, on still St. Mary's lake, Float double, swan and shadow.

senses.d: Divided into two; acting two parts, one openly and the other secretly; equivocal; deceitful; insincere.
q: With a double heart do they speak.

senses.d: Having the petals in a flower considerably increased beyond the natural number, usually as the result of cultivation and the expense of the stamens, or stamens and pistils. The white water lily and some other plants have their blossoms naturally double.

Double.etym: [OE. doble, duble, double, OF. doble, duble, double, F. double, fr. L. duplus, fr. the root of duo two, and perh. that of plenus full; akin to Gr. διπλόοσ double. See Two, and Full, and cf. Diploma, Duple.]

senses.d: Twice; doubly.
q: I was double their age.

senses.d: To increase by adding an equal number, quantity, length, value, or the like; multiply by two; as, to double a sum of money; to double a number, or length.
q: Double six thousand, and then treble that.

senses.d: To make of two thicknesses or folds by turning or bending together in the middle; to fold one part upon another part of; as, to double the leaf of a book, and the like; to clinch, as the fist; — often followed by up; as, to double up a sheet of paper or cloth.
q: Then the old man Was wroth, and doubled up his hands.

senses.d: To be the double of; to exceed by twofold; to contain or be worth twice as much as.
q: Thus reënforced, against the adverse fleet, Still doubling ours, brave Rupert leads the way.

senses.d: To pass around or by; to march or sail round, so as to reverse the direction of motion.
q: Sailing along the coast, the doubled the promontory of Carthage.

senses.d: To unite, as ranks or files, so as to form one from each two.

Double.etym: [OE. doblen, dublen, doublen, F. doubler, fr. L. duplare, fr. duplus. See Double, a.]

senses.d: To be increased to twice the sum, number, quantity, length, or value; to increase or grow to twice as much.
q: 'T is observed in particular nations, that within the space of three hundred years, notwithstanding all casualties, the number of men doubles.

senses.d: To return upon one's track; to turn and go back over the same ground, or in an opposite direction.
q: Doubling and turning like a hunted hare.
Doubling and doubling with laborious walk.

senses.d: To play tricks; to use sleights; to play false.
q: What penalty and danger you accrue, If you be found to double.

senses.d: To set up a word or words a second time by mistake; to make a doublet.
Twice as much; twice the number, sum, quantity, length, value, and the like.
q: If the thief be found, let him pay double.

senses.d: Among compositors, a doublet (see Doublet, 2.); among pressmen, a sheet that is twice pulled, and blurred.
That which is doubled over or together; a doubling; a plait; a fold.
q: Rolled up in sevenfold double Of plagues.

senses.d: A turn or circuit in running to escape pursues; hence, a trick; a shift; an artifice.
q: These men are too well acquainted with the chase to be flung off by any false steps or doubles.

senses.d: Something precisely equal or counterpart to another; a counterpart. Hence, a wraith.
q: My charming friend . . . has, I am almost sure, a double, who preaches his afternoon sermons for him.
