senses.d: A player or singer who prepares to take the part of another player in his absence; a substitute.
Double beer; strong beer.
A feast in which the antiphon is doubled, hat is, said twice, before and after the Psalms, instead of only half being said, as in simple feasts.
A game between two pairs of players; as, a first prize for doubles.
An old term for a variation, as in Bach's Suites.
A person or thing that is the counterpart of another; a duplicate; copy; (Obs.) transcript; — now chiefly used of persons. Hence, a wraith.
q: My charming friend . . . has, I am almost sure, a double, who preaches his afternoon sermons for him.

senses.d: To waver in opinion or judgment; to be in uncertainty as to belief respecting anything; to hesitate in belief; to be undecided as to the truth of the negative or the affirmative proposition; to b e undetermined.
q: Even in matters divine, concerning some things, we may lawfully doubt, and suspend our judgment.
To try your love and make you doubt of mine.

senses.d: To suspect; to fear; to be apprehensive.

Doubt.syn: To waver; vacillate; fluctuate; hesitate; demur; scruple; question.
Doubt.etym: [OE. duten, douten, OF. duter, doter, douter, F. douter, fr. L. dubitare; akin to dubius doubtful. See Dubious.]

senses.d: To question or hold questionable; to withhold assent to; to hesitate to believe, or to be inclined not to believe; to withhold confidence from; to distrust; as, I have heard the story, but I doubt the truth of it.
q: To admire superior sense, and doubt their own!
I doubt not that however changed, you keep So much of what is graceful.

senses.d: To suspect; to fear; to be apprehensive of.
q: Edmond good man and doubted God.
I doubt some foul play.
That I of doubted danger had no fear.

senses.d: To fill with fear; to affright.
q: The virtues of the valiant Caratach More doubt me than all Britain.

senses.d: A fluctuation of mind arising from defect of knowledge or evidence; uncertainty of judgment or mind; unsettled state of opinion concerning the reality of an event, or the truth of an assertion, etc.; hesitation.
q: Doubt is the beginning and the end of our efforts to know.

Doubt, in order to be operative in requiring an acquittal, is not the want of perfect certainty (which can never exist in any question of fact) but a defect of proof preventing a reasonable assurance of quilt.

senses.d: Uncertainty of condition.
q: Thy life shall hang in doubt before thee.

senses.d: Suspicion; fear; apprehension; dread.
q: I stand in doubt of you.
Nor slack her threatful hand for danger's doubt.

senses.d: Difficulty expressed or urged for solution; point unsettled; objection.
q: To every doubt your answer is the same.

Doubt.syn: Uncertainty; hesitation; suspense; indecision; irresolution; distrust; suspicion; scruple; perplexity; ambiguity; skepticism.
Doubt.etym: [OE. dute, doute, F. doute, fr. douter to doubt. See Doubt, v. i.]

senses.d: Not settled in opinion; undetermined; wavering; hesitating in belief; also used, metaphorically, of the body when its action is affected by such a state of mind; as, we are doubtful of a fact, or of the propriety of a measure.
q: Methinks I should know you, and know this man; Yet I am doubtful.
With doubtful feet and wavering resolution.

senses.d: Admitting of doubt; not obvious, clear, or certain; questionable; not decided; not easy to be defined, classed, or named; as, a doubtful case, hue, claim, title, species, and the like.
q: Beauty is but a vain and doubtful good.
Is it a great cruelty to expel from our abode the enemy of our peace, or even the doubtful friend ?

senses.d: Characterized by ambiguity; dubious; as, a doubtful expression; a doubtful phrase.
Of uncertain issue or event.
q: We . . . have sustained one day in doubtful fight.
The strife between the two principles had been long, fierce, and doubtful.

senses.d: Fearful; apprehensive; suspicious.
q: I am doubtful that you have been conjunct And bosomed with her.

Doubtful.syn: Wavering; vacillating; hesitating; undetermined; distrustful; dubious; uncertain; equivocal; ambiguous; problematical; questionable.

senses.d: That is uncertain; that distrusts or hesitates; having doubts.
Free from fear or suspicion.
q: Pretty child, sleep doubtless and secure.

senses.d: Undoubtedly; without doubt.
Paste of bread; a soft mass of moistened flour or meal, kneaded or unkneaded, but not yet baked; as, to knead dough.
Anything of the consistency of such paste.

Dough.etym: [OE. dagh, dogh, dow, AS. dāh; akin to D. deeg, G. teig, Icel. deig, Sw. deg, Dan. deig, Goth. daigs; also, to Goth. deigan to knead, L. fingere to form, shape, Skr. dih to smear; cf. Gr. � wall, � to touch, handle. �. Cf. Feign, Figure, Dairy, Duff.]

senses.d: A pigeon of the genus Columba and various related genera. The species are numerous.
A word of endearment for one regarded as pure and gentle.
q: O my dove, . . . let me hear thy voice.

Dove.etym: [OE. dove, duve, douve, AS. d�fe; akin to OS. d�ba, D. duif, OHG. t�ba, G. taube, Icel. d�fa, Sw. dufva, Dan. due, Goth. d�b�; perh. from the root of E. dive.]

senses.d: Fine, soft, hairy outgrowth from the skin or surface of animals or plants, not matted and fleecy like wool
q: And the first down begins to shade his face.

senses.d: That which is made of down, as a bed or pillow; that which affords ease and repose, like a bed of down
q: When in the down I sink my head, Sleep, Death's twin brother, times my breath.
Thou bosom softness, down of all my cares!

Down.etym: [Akin to LG. dune, dun, Icel. dūnn, Sw. dun, Dan. duun, G. daune, cf. D. dons; perh. akin to E. dust.]

senses.d: To cover, ornament, line, or stuff with down.
A bank or rounded hillock of sand thrown up by the wind along or near the shore; a flattish-topped hill; — usually in the plural.
q: Hills afford prospects, as they must needs acknowledge who have been on the downs of Sussex.
She went by dale, and she went by down.

senses.d: A tract of poor, sandy, undulating or hilly land near the sea, covered with fine turf which serves chiefly for the grazing of sheep; — usually in the plural.
q: Seven thousand broad-tailed sheep grazed on his downs.

senses.d: A road for shipping in the English Channel or Straits of Dover, near Deal, employed as a naval rendezvous in time of war.
q: On the 11th we run up the channel . . . at noon we were abreast of Dover, and about three came to an anchor in the Downs, and went ashore at Deal.

senses.d: A state of depression; low state; abasement.
q: It the downs of life too much outnumber the ups.

Down.etym: [OE. dun, doun, AS. dūn; of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. dūn hill, fortified hill, Gael. dun heap, hillock, hill, W. din a fortified hill or mount; akin to E. town. See Town, and cf. Down, adv. & prep., Dune.]

senses.d: In the direction of gravity or toward the center of the earth; toward or in a lower place or position; below; — the opposite of up.

From a higher to a lower position, literally or figuratively; in a descending direction; from the top of an ascent; from an upright position; to the ground or floor; to or into a lower or an inferior condition; as, into a state of humility, disgrace, misery, and the like; into a state of rest; — used with verbs indicating motion.
q: It will be rain to-night. Let it come down.
I sit me down beside the hazel grove.
And that drags down his life.
There is not a more melancholy object in the learned world than a man who has written himself down.
The French . . . shone down [i.e., outshone] the English.

senses.d: In a low or the lowest position, literally or figuratively; at the bottom of a descent; below the horizon; on the ground; in a condition of humility, dejection, misery, and the like; in a state of quiet.
q: I was down and out of breath.
The moon is down; I have not heard the clock.
He that is down needs fear no fall.

senses.d: From a remoter or higher antiquity.
q: Venerable men! you have come down to us from a former generation.

senses.d: From a greater to a less bulk, or from a thinner to a thicker consistence; as, to boil down in cookery, or in making decoctions.

Down.etym: [For older adown, AS. ad�n, ad�ne, prop., from or off the hill. See 3d Down, and cf. Adown, and cf. Adown.]

senses.d: In a descending direction along; from a higher to a lower place upon or within; at a lower place in or on; as, down a hill; down a well.
Hence: Towards the mouth of a river; towards the sea; as, to sail or swim down a stream; to sail down the sound.
To cause to go down; to make descend; to put down; to overthrow, as in wrestling; hence, to subdue; to bring down.
q: I remember how you downed Beauclerk and Hamilton, the wits, once at our house.

senses.d: To go down; to descend.
Downcast; as, a down look.
Downright; absolute; positive; as, a down denial.
Downward; going down; sloping; as, a down stroke; a down grade; a down train on a railway.
The act of sitting down; repose; a resting.
q: Thou knowest my downsitting and my uprising.

senses.d: From a higher place to a lower; in a descending course; as, to tend, move, roll, look, or take root, downward or downwards.
q: Their heads they downward bent.

senses.d: From a higher to a lower condition; toward misery, humility, disgrace, or ruin.
q: And downward fell into a groveling swine.

senses.d: From a remote time; from an ancestor or predecessor; from one to another in a descending line.
q: A ring the county wears, That downward hath descended in his house, From son to son, some four or five descents.

senses.d: Moving or extending from a higher to a lower place; tending toward the earth or its center, or toward a lower level; declivous.
q: With downward force That drove the sand along he took his way.

senses.d: Descending from a head, origin, or source; as, a downward line of descent.
Tending to a lower condition or state; depressed; dejected; as, downward thoughts.
A gift; endowment.
The money, goods, or estate, which a woman brings to her husband in marriage; a bride's portion on her marriage. See Note under Dower.
A gift or presents for the bride, on espousal. See Dower.
q: Ask me never so much dowry and gift, and I will give . . .; but give me the damsel to wife.

Dowry.etym: [Contr. from dowery; cf. LL. dotarium. See Dower.]

senses.d: A confection; a comfit; a drug.

To draw slowly or heavily onward; to pull along the ground by main force; to haul; to trail; — applied to drawing heavy or resisting bodies or those inapt for drawing, with labor, along the ground or other surface; as, to drag stone or timber; to drag a net in fishing.
q: Dragged by the cords which through his feet were thrust.
The grossness of his nature will have weight to drag thee down.
A needless Alexandrine ends the song That, like a wounded snake, drags its slow length along.

senses.d: To break, as land, by drawing a drag or harrow over it; to harrow; to draw a drag along the bottom of, as a stream or other water; hence, to search, as by means of a drag.
q: Then while I dragged my brains for such a song.

senses.d: To draw along, as something burdensome; hence, to pass in pain or with difficulty.
q: Have dragged a lingering life.

Drag.etym: [OE. draggen; akin to Sw. dragga to search with a grapnel, fr. dragg grapnel, fr. draga to draw, the same word as E. draw. � See Draw.]

senses.d: To be drawn along, as a rope or dress, on the ground; to trail; to be moved onward along the ground, or along the bottom of the sea, as an anchor that does not hold.
To move onward heavily, laboriously, or slowly; to advance with weary effort; to go on lingeringly.
q: The day drags through, though storms keep out the sun.
Long, open panegyric drags at best.

senses.d: To serve as a clog or hindrance; to hold back.
q: A propeller is said to drag when the sails urge the vessel faster than the revolutions of the screw can propel her.

senses.d: To fish with a dragnet.
The act of dragging; anything which is dragged.
A net, or an apparatus, to be drawn along the bottom under water, as in fishing, searching for drowned persons, etc.
A kind of sledge for conveying heavy bodies; also, a kind of low car or handcart; as, a stone drag.
A heavy coach with seats on top; also, a heavy carriage.
A heavy harrow, for breaking up ground.
Anything towed in the water to retard a ship's progress, or to keep her head up to the wind; esp., a canvas bag with a hooped mouth, so used. See Drag sail (below).
q: My lectures were only a pleasure to me, and no drag.

senses.d: Motion affected with slowness and difficulty, as if clogged.
The bottom part of a flask or mold, the upper part being the cope.
A steel instrument for completing the dressing of soft stone.

The difference between the speed of a screw steamer under sail and that of the screw when the ship outruns the screw; or between the propulsive effects of the different floats of a paddle wheel. See Citation under Drag, v. i., 3.

Drag.etym: [See Drag, v. t., and cf. Dray a cart, and 1st Dredge.]

senses.d: A fabulous animal, generally represented as a monstrous winged serpent or lizard, with a crested head and enormous claws, and regarded as very powerful and ferocious.
q: The dragons which appear in early paintings and sculptures are invariably representations of a winged crocodile.
Thou breakest the heads of the dragons in the waters.
Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder; the young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet.
He laid hold on the dragon, that old serpent, which is the Devil and Satan, and bound him a thousand years.

senses.d: A fierce, violent person, esp. a woman.
A constellation of the northern hemisphere figured as a dragon; Draco.
A luminous exhalation from marshy grounds, seeming to move through the air as a winged serpent.
A short musket hooked to a swivel attached to a soldier's belt; — so called from a representation of a dragon's head at the muzzle.

A small arboreal lizard of the genus Draco, of several species, found in the East Indies and Southern Asia. Five or six of the hind ribs, on each side, are prolonged and covered with weblike skin, forming a sort of wing. These prolongations aid them in making long leaps from tree to tree. Called also flying lizard.
A variety of carrier pigeon.
A fabulous winged creature, sometimes borne as a charge in a coat of arms.

Dragon.etym: [F. dragon, L. draco, fr. Gr. δράκων, prob. fr. δέρκεσθαι, δράκειν, to look (akin to Skr. darç to see), and so called from its terrible eyes. Cf. Drake a dragon, Dragoon.]

senses.d: A weight; in Apothecaries' weight, one eighth part of an ounce, or sixty grains; in Avoirdupois weight, one sixteenth part of an ounce, or 27.34375 grains.
A minute quantity; a mite.
q: Were I the chooser, a dram of well-doing should be preferred before many times as mush the forcible hindrance of evildoing.

senses.d: As much spirituous liquor as is usually drunk at once; as, a dram of brandy; hence, a potation or potion; as, a dram of poison.
A Persian daric.

Dram.etym: [OF. drame, F. drachme, L. drachma, drachm, drachma, fr. Gr. δραχμή, prop., a handful, fr. δράσσεσθαι to grasp. Cf. Drachm, Drachma.]

senses.d: To drink drams; to ply with drams.
of Drink.
Wild oats, or darnel grass. See Drake a plant.
The act of drawing or pulling
q: A general custom of using oxen for all sort of draught would be, perhaps, the greatest improvement.

senses.d: The drawing of a bowstring.
q: She sent an arrow forth with mighty draught.

senses.d: Act of drawing a net; a sweeping the water for fish.
q: Upon the draught of a pond, not one fish was left.

senses.d: The act of drawing liquor into the mouth and throat; the act of drinking.
q: In his hands he took the goblet, but a while the draught forbore.

senses.d: A sudden attack or drawing upon an enemy.
q: By drawing sudden draughts upon the enemy when he looketh not for you.

senses.d: The act of selecting or detaching soldiers; a draft (see Draft, n., 2)
The act of drawing up, marking out, or delineating; representation.
That which is drawn
q: Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught.
He laid down his pipe, and cast his net, which brought him a very great draught.

senses.d: The force drawn; a detachment; — in this sense usually written draft.
The quantity drawn in at once in drinking; a potion or potation.
q: Disguise thyself as thou wilt, still, Slavery, . . . still thou art a bitter draught.
Low lies that house where nut-brown draughts inspired.

senses.d: A sketch, outline, or representation, whether written, designed, or drawn; a delineation.
q: A draught of a Toleration Act was offered to the Parliament by a private member.
No picture or draught of these things from the report of the eye.

senses.d: An order for the payment of money; — in this sense almost always written draft.

Draught.etym: [The same as draft, the spelling with gh indicating an older pronunciation. See Draft, n., Draw.]

senses.d: Used for drawing vehicles, loads, etc.; as, a draught beast; draught hooks.
Relating to, or characterized by, a draft, or current of air.
Used in making drawings; as, draught compasses.
Drawn directly from the barrel, or other receptacle, in distinction from bottled; on draught; — said of ale, cider, and the like.
To draw out; to call forth. See Draft.
To diminish or exhaust by drawing.
q: The Parliament so often draughted and drained.

senses.d: To draw in outline; to make a draught, sketch, or plan of, as in architectural and mechanical drawing.
old imp. of Drive.
To cause to move continuously by force applied in advance of the thing moved; to pull along; to haul; to drag; to cause to follow.
q: He cast him down to ground, and all along Drew him through dirt and mire without remorse.
He hastened to draw the stranger into a private room.
Do not rich men oppress you, and draw you before the judgment seats?
The arrow is now drawn to the head.

senses.d: To influence to move or tend toward one's self; to exercise an attracting force upon; to call towards itself; to attract; hence, to entice; to allure; to induce.
q: The poet Did feign that Orpheus drew trees, stones, and floods.
All eyes you draw, and with the eyes the heart.

senses.d: To cause to come out for one's use or benefit; to extract; to educe; to bring forth; as: (a) To bring or take out, or to let out, from some receptacle, as a stick or post from a hole, water from a cask or well, etc.
q: The drew out the staves of the ark.
Draw thee waters for the siege.
I opened the tumor by the point of a lancet without drawing one drop of blood.

senses.d: To pull from a sheath, as a sword.
q: I will draw my sword, my hand shall destroy them.

senses.d: To extract; to force out; to elicit; to derive.
q: Spirits, by distillations, may be drawn out of vegetable juices, which shall flame and fume of themselves.
Until you had drawn oaths from him.

senses.d: To obtain from some cause or origin; to infer from evidence or reasons; to deduce from premises; to derive.
q: We do not draw the moral lessons we might from history.

senses.d: To take or procure from a place of deposit; to call for and receive from a fund, or the like; as, to draw money from a bank.

To take from a box or wheel, as a lottery ticket; to receive from a lottery by the drawing out of the numbers for prizes or blanks; hence, to obtain by good fortune; to win; to gain; as, he drew a prize.
To select by the drawing of lots.
q: Provided magistracies were filled by men freely chosen or drawn.

senses.d: To remove the contents of
q: Sucking and drawing the breast dischargeth the milk as fast as it can generated.

senses.d: To extract the bowels of; to eviscerate; as, to draw a fowl; to hang, draw, and quarter a criminal.
q: In private draw your poultry, clean your tripe.

senses.d: To take into the lungs; to inhale; to inspire; hence, also, to utter or produce by an inhalation; to heave.
q: Drew, or seemed to draw, a dying groan.

Draw.etym: [OE. dra”en, drahen, draien, drawen, AS. dragan; akin to Icel. & Sw. draga, Dan. drage to draw, carry, and prob. to OS. dragan to bear, carry, D. dragen, G. tragen, Goth. dragan; cf. Skr. dhraj to move along, glide; and perh. akin to Skr. dhar to hold, bear. √73. Cf. 2d Drag, Dray a cart, 1st Dredge

senses.d: To pull; to exert strength in drawing anything; to have force to move anything by pulling; as, a horse draws well; the sails of a ship draw well.
To draw a liquid from some receptacle, as water from a well.
q: The woman saith unto him, Sir, thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep.

senses.d: To exert an attractive force; to act as an inducement or enticement.
q: Keep a watch upon the particular bias of their minds, that it may not draw too much.

senses.d: To have efficiency as an epispastic; to act as a sinapism; — said of a blister, poultice, etc.
To have draught, as a chimney, flue, or the like; to furnish transmission to smoke, gases, etc.
To unsheathe a weapon, especially a sword.
q: So soon as ever thou seest him, draw; and as thou drawest, swear horrible.

senses.d: To perform the act, or practice the art, of delineation; to sketch; to form figures or pictures.
To become contracted; to shrink.

To move; to come or go; literally, to draw one's self; — with prepositions and adverbs; as, to draw away, to move off, esp. in racing, to get in front; to obtain the lead or increase it; to draw back, to retreat; to draw level, to move up even (with another); to come up to or overtake another; to draw off, to retire or retreat; to draw on, to advance; to draw up, to form in array; to draw near, nigh, or towards, to approach; to draw together, to come together, to collect.
To make a draft or written demand for payment of money deposited or due; — usually with on or upon.
q: You may draw on me for the expenses of your journey.

senses.d: To admit the action of pulling or dragging; to undergo draught; as, a carriage draws easily.
To sink in water; to require a depth for floating.
The act of drawing; draught.
A lot or chance to be drawn.
A drawn game or battle, etc.
That part of a bridge which may be raised, swung round, or drawn aside; the movable part of a drawbridge. See the Note under Drawbridge.
To play (a short-length ball directed at the leg stump) with an inclined bat so as to deflect the ball between the legs and the wicket.
To leave (a contest) undecided; as, the battle or game was drawn.
The result of drawing, or state of being drawn;
That which is drawn or is subject to drawing.
One who, or that which, draws
That which is drawn
The act of pulling, or attracting.

The act or the art of representing any object by means of lines and shades; especially, such a representation when in one color, or in tints used not to represent the colors of natural objects, but for effect only, and produced with hard material such as pencil, chalk, etc.; delineation; also, the figure or representation drawn.
The process of stretching or spreading metals as by hammering, or, as in forming wire from rods or tubes and cups from sheet metal, by pulling them through dies.
The process of pulling out and elongating the sliver from the carding machine, by revolving rollers, to prepare it for spinning.
The distribution of prizes and blanks in a lottery.
A joiner's tool having a blade with a handle at each end, used to shave off surfaces, by drawing it toward one; a shave; — called also drawshave, and drawing shave.
A tool used for the purpose of making an incision along the path a saw is to follow, to prevent it from tearing the surface of the wood.
To fear in a great degree; to regard, or look forward to, with terrific apprehension.
q: When at length the moment dreaded through so many years came close, the dark cloud passed away from Johnson's mind.

Dread.etym: [AS. dr�dan, in comp.; akin to OS. drādan, OHG. trātan, both only in comp.]

senses.d: To be in dread, or great fear.
q: Dread not, neither be afraid of them.

senses.d: Great fear in view of impending evil; fearful apprehension of danger; anticipatory terror.
q: The secret dread of divine displeasure.
The dread of something after death.

senses.d: Reverential or respectful fear; awe.
q: The fear of you, and the dread of you, shall be upon every beast of the earth.
His scepter shows the force of temporal power, The attribute to awe and majesty, Wherein doth sit the dread and fear of kings.

senses.d: An object of terrified apprehension.
A person highly revered.
Fury; dreadfulness.
Doubt; as, out of dread.

Dread.syn: Awe; fear; affright; terror; horror; dismay; apprehension. See Reverence.

senses.d: Exciting great fear or apprehension; causing terror; frightful; dreadful.
q: A dread eternity! how surely mine.

senses.d: Inspiring with reverential fear; awful' venerable; as, dread sovereign; dread majesty; dread tribunal.
Full of dread or terror; fearful.
Inspiring dread; impressing great fear; fearful; terrible; as, a dreadful storm.
q: For all things are less dreadful than they seem.

senses.d: Inspiring awe or reverence; awful.

Dreadful.syn: Fearful; frightful; terrific; terrible; horrible; horrid; formidable; tremendous; awful; venerable. See Frightful.

senses.d: The thoughts, or series of thoughts, or imaginary transactions, which occupy the mind during sleep; a sleeping vision.
q: Dreams are but interludes which fancy makes.
I had a dream which was not all a dream.

senses.d: A visionary scheme; a wild conceit; an idle fancy; a vagary; a revery; — in this sense, applied to an imaginary or anticipated state of happiness; as, a dream of bliss; the dream of his youth.
q: There sober thought pursued the amusing theme, Till Fancy colored it and formed a dream.
It is not them a mere dream, but a very real aim which they propose.

Dream.etym: [Akin to OS. drōm, D. droom, G. traum, Icel. draumr, Dan. & Sw. dröm; cf. G. trügen to deceive, Skr. druh to harm, hurt, try to hurt. AS. dreám joy, gladness, and OS. drōm joy are, perh., different words; cf. Gr. θρυ̑λοσ noise.]

senses.d: To have ideas or images in the mind while in the state of sleep; to experience sleeping visions; — often with of; as, to dream of a battle, or of an absent friend.
To let the mind run on in idle revery or vagary; to anticipate vaguely as a coming and happy reality; to have a visionary notion or idea; to imagine.
q: Here may we sit and dream Over the heavenly theme
They dream on in a constant course of reading, but not digesting

Dream.etym: [Cf. AS. drēman, drȳman, to rejoice. See Dream, n.]

senses.d: To have a dream of; to see, or have a vision of, in sleep, or in idle fancy; — often followed by an objective clause.
q: Your old men shall dream dreams
At length in sleep their bodies they compose, And dreamt the future fight
And still they dream that they shall still succeed

senses.d: One who dreams.
A visionary; one lost in wild imaginations or vain schemes of some anticipated good; as, a political dreamer.
Corrupt or defiling matter contained in a liquid, or precipitated from it; refuse; feculence; lees; grounds; sediment; hence, the vilest and most worthless part of anything; as, the dregs of society.
q: We, the dregs and rubbish of mankind.

Dreg.etym: [Prob. from Icel. dregg; akin to Sw. drägg, cf. Icel. & Sw. draga to draw. Cf. Draw.]

senses.d: To direct; to put right or straight; to regulate; to order.
q: At all times thou shalt bless God and pray Him to dress thy ways.
To Grisild again will I me dresse.

senses.d: To arrange in exact continuity of line, as soldiers; commonly to adjust to a straight line and at proper distance; to align; as, to dress the ranks.
To treat methodically with remedies, bandages, or curative appliances, as a sore, an ulcer, a wound, or a wounded or diseased part.

To adjust; to put in good order; to arrange; specifically: (a) To prepare for use; to fit for any use; to render suitable for an intended purpose; to get ready; as, to dress a slain animal; to dress meat; to dress leather or cloth; to dress or trim a lamp; to dress a garden; to dress a horse, by currying and rubbing; to dress grain, by cleansing it; in mining and metallurgy, to dress ores, by sorting and separating them.
q: And the Lord God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it.
When he dresseth the lamps he shall burn incense.
Three hundred horses . . . smoothly dressed.
Dressing their hair with the white sea flower.
If he felt obliged to expostulate, he might have dressed his censures in a kinder form.

senses.d: To cut to proper dimensions, or give proper shape to, as to a tool by hammering; also, to smooth or finish.
To put in proper condition by appareling, as the body; to put clothes upon; to apparel; to invest with garments or rich decorations; to clothe; to deck.
q: Dressed myself in such humility.
Prove that ever Idress myself handsome till thy return.

senses.d: To break and train for use, as a horse or other animal.

Dress.syn: To attire; apparel; clothe; accouter; array; robe; rig; trim; deck; adorn; embellish.
Dress.etym: [OF. drecier to make straight, raise, set up, prepare, arrange, F. dresser, (assumed) LL. directiare, fr. L. dirigere, directum, to direct; dis- + regere to rule. See Right, and cf. Address, Adroit, Direct, Dirge.]

senses.d: To arrange one's self in due position in a line of soldiers; — the word of command to form alignment in ranks; as, Right, dress!
To clothe or apparel one's self; to put on one's garments; to pay particular regard to dress; as, to dress quickly.
q: To flaunt, to dress, to dance, to thrum.

senses.d: That which is used as the covering or ornament of the body; clothes; garments; habit; apparel.
A lady's gown; as, silk or a velvet dress.
Attention to apparel, or skill in adjusting it.
q: Men of pleasure, dress, and gallantry.

senses.d: The system of furrows on the face of a millstone.
One who dresses; one who put in order or makes ready for use; one who on clothes or ornaments.
A kind of pick for shaping large coal.
An assistant in a hospital, whose office it is to dress wounds, sores, etc.
A table or bench on which meat and other things are dressed, or prepared for use.
q: The pewter plates on the dresser Caught and reflected the flame, as shields of armies the sunshine.

senses.d: A piece of chamber furniture consisting of a chest of drawers, or bureau, with a mirror.
of Draw.
To endure.
q: So causeless such drede for to drie.

senses.d: To swallow anything liquid, for quenching thirst or other purpose; to imbibe; to receive or partake of, as if in satisfaction of thirst; as, to drink from a spring.
q: Gird thyself, and serve me, till have eaten and drunken; and afterward thou shalt eat and drink.
He shall drink of the wrath the Almighty.
Drink of the cup that can not cloy.

senses.d: To quaff exhilarating or intoxicating liquors, in merriment or feasting; to carouse; to revel; hence, to lake alcoholic liquors to excess; to be intemperate in the �se of intoxicating or spirituous liquors; to tipple.
q: And they drank, and were merry with him.
Bolingbroke always spoke freely when he had drunk freely.
I drink to the general joy of the whole table, And to our dear friend Banquo.

Drink.etym: [AS. drincan; akin to OS. drinkan, D. drinken, G. trinken, Icel. drekka, Sw. dricka, Dan. drikke, Goth. drigkan. Cf. Drench, Drunken, Drown.]

senses.d: To swallow (a liquid); to receive, as a fluid, into the stomach; to imbibe; as, to drink milk or water.
q: There lies she with the blessed gods in bliss, There drinks the nectar with ambrosia mixed.
The bowl of punch which was brewed and drunk in Mrs. Betty's room.

senses.d: To take in (a liquid), in any manner; to suck up; to absorb; to imbibe.
q: And let the purple violets drink the stream.

senses.d: To take in; to receive within one, through the senses; to inhale; to hear; to see.
q: To drink the cooler air,
My ears have not yet drunk a hundred words Of that tongue's utterance.
Let me . . . drink delicious poison from thy eye.

senses.d: To smoke, as tobacco.
q: And some men now live ninety years and past, Who never drank to tobacco first nor last.

senses.d: Liquid to be swallowed; any fluid to be taken into the stomach for quenching thirst or for other purposes, as water, coffee, or decoctions.
q: Give me some drink, Titinius.

senses.d: Specifically, intoxicating liquor; as, when drink is on, wit is out.
One who drinks; as, the effects of tea on the drinker; also, one who drinks spirituous liquors to excess; a drunkard.
The act of one who drinks; the act of imbibing.
The practice of partaking to excess of intoxicating liquors.
An entertainment with liquors; a carousal.

To impel or urge onward by force in a direction away from one, or along before one; to push forward; to compel to move on; to communicate motion to; as, to drive cattle; to drive a nail; smoke drives persons from a room.
q: A storm came on and drove them into Pylos.
Shield pressed on shield, and man drove man along.
Go drive the deer and drag the finny prey.

senses.d: To urge on and direct the motions of, as the beasts which draw a vehicle, or the vehicle borne by them; hence, also, to take in a carriage; to convey in a vehicle drawn by beasts; as, to drive a pair of horses or a stage; to drive a person to his own door.
q: How . . . proud he was to drive such a brother!

senses.d: To urge, impel, or hurry forward; to force; to constrain; to urge, press, or bring to a point or state; as, to drive a person by necessity, by persuasion, by force of circumstances, by argument, and the like.
q: He, driven to dismount, threatened, if I did not do the like, to do as much for my horse as fortune had done for his.

senses.d: To carry or; to keep in motion; to conduct; to prosecute.
q: The trade of life can not be driven without partners.

senses.d: To clear, by forcing away what is contained.
q: To drive the country, force the swains away.

senses.d: To dig Horizontally; to cut a horizontal gallery or tunnel.
To pass away; — said of time.

Drive.etym: [AS. drīfan; akin to OS. drīban, D. drijven, OHG. trīban, G. treiben, Icel. drīfa, Goth. dreiban. Cf. Drift, Drove.]

senses.d: To rush and press with violence; to move furiously.
q: Fierce Boreas drove against his flying sails.
Under cover of the night and a driving tempest.
Time driveth onward fast, And in a little while our lips are dumb.

senses.d: To be forced along; to be impelled; to be moved by any physical force or agent; to be driven.
q: The hull drives on, though mast and sail be torn.
The chaise drives to Mr. Draper's chambers.

senses.d: To go by carriage; to pass in a carriage; to proceed by directing or urging on a vehicle or the animals that draw it; as, the coachman drove to my door.
To press forward; to aim, or tend, to a point; to make an effort; to strive; — usually with at.
q: Let them therefore declare what carnal or secular interest he drove at.

senses.d: To distrain for rent.
Driven.
The act of driving; a trip or an excursion in a carriage, as for exercise or pleasure; — distinguished from a ride taken on horseback.
A place suitable or agreeable for driving; a road prepared for driving.
Violent or rapid motion; a rushing onward or away; esp., a forced or hurried dispatch of business.
q: The Murdstonian drive in business.

senses.d: In type founding and forging, an impression or matrix, formed by a punch drift.
A collection of objects that are driven; a mass of logs to be floated down a river.
To make a drive, or stroke from the tee.
Specif., in various games, as tennis, baseball, etc., to propel (the ball) swiftly by a direct stroke or forcible throw.
In various games, as tennis, cricket, etc., the act of player who drives the ball; the stroke or blow; the flight of the ball, etc., so driven.
A stroke from the tee, generally a full shot made with a driver; also, the distance covered by such a stroke.
An implement used for driving;
of Drive. Also adj.
One who, or that which, drives; the person or thing that urges or compels anything else to move onward.
The person who drives beasts or a carriage; a coachman; a charioteer, etc.; hence, also, one who controls the movements of a locomotive.
An overseer of a gang of slaves or gang of convicts at their work.

A part that transmits motion to another part by contact with it, or through an intermediate relatively movable part, as a gear which drives another, or a lever which moves another through a link, etc. Specifically:
The driving wheel of a locomotive.
An attachment to a lathe, spindle, or face plate to turn a carrier.
A crossbar on a grinding mill spindle to drive the upper stone.
The after sail in a ship or bark, being a fore-and-aft sail attached to a gaff; a spanker.
Having great force of impulse; as, a driving wind or storm.
Communicating force; impelling; as, a driving shaft.
The act of forcing or urging something along; the act of pressing or moving on furiously.
Tendency; drift.
The Arabian camel (Camelus dromedarius), having one hump or protuberance on the back, in distinction from the Bactrian camel, which has two humps.

Dromedary.etym: [F. dromadaire, LL. dromedarius, fr. L. dromas (sc. camelus), fr. Gr. δρομάσ running, from δραμείν, used as aor. of τρέχειν to run; cf. Skr. dram to run.]

senses.d: The quantity of fluid which falls in one small spherical mass; a liquid globule; a minim; hence, also, the smallest easily measured portion of a fluid; a small quantity; as, a drop of water.
q: With minute drops from off the eaves.
As dear to me as are the ruddy drops That visit my sad heart.
That drop of peace divine.

senses.d: That which resembles, or that which hangs like, a liquid drop; as a hanging diamond ornament, an earring, a glass pendant on a chandelier, a sugarplum (sometimes medicated), or a kind of shot or slug.
Same as Gutta.
Whatever is arranged to drop, hang, or fall from an elevated position; also, a contrivance for lowering something
Any medicine the dose of which is measured by drops; as, lavender drops.
The depth of a square sail; — generally applied to the courses only.
Act of dropping; sudden fall or descent.

Drop.etym: [OE. drope, AS. dropa; akin to OS. dropo, D. drop, OHG. tropo, G. tropfen, Icel. dropi, Sw. droppe; and Fr. AS. dreópan to drip, drop; akin to OS. driopan, D. druipen, OHG. triofan, G. triefen, Icel. drj�pa. Cf. Drip, Droop.]

senses.d: To pour or let fall in drops; to pour in small globules; to distill.
q: The recording angel, as he wrote it down, dropped a tear upon the word and blotted it out forever.

senses.d: To cause to fall in one portion, or by one motion, like a drop; to let fall; as, to drop a line in fishing; to drop a courtesy.
To let go; to dismiss; to set aside; to have done with; to discontinue; to forsake; to give up; to omit.
q: They suddenly drop't the pursuit.
That astonishing ease with which fine ladies drop you and pick you up again.
The connection had been dropped many years.
Dropping the too rough H in Hell and Heaven.

senses.d: To bestow or communicate by a suggestion; to let fall in an indirect, cautious, or gentle manner; as, to drop hint, a word of counsel, etc.
To lower, as a curtain, or the muzzle of a gun, etc.
To send, as a letter; as, please drop me a line, a letter, word.
To give birth to; as, to drop a lamb.
To cover with drops; to variegate; to bedrop.
q: Show to the sun their waved coats dropped with gold.

Drop.etym: [OE. droppen, AS. dropan, v. i. See Drop, n.]

senses.d: To fall in drops.
q: The kindly dew drops from the higher tree, And wets the little plants that lowly dwell.

senses.d: To fall, in general, literally or figuratively; as, ripe fruit drops from a tree; wise words drop from the lips.
q: Mutilations of which the meaning has dropped out of memory.
When the sound of dropping nuts is heard.

senses.d: To let drops fall; to discharge itself in drops.
q: The heavens . . . dropped at the presence of God.

senses.d: To fall dead, or to fall in death.
q: Nothing, says Seneca, so soon reconciles us to the thoughts of our own death, as the prospect of one friend after another dropping round us.

senses.d: To come to an end; to cease; to pass out of mind; as, the affair dropped.
To come unexpectedly; — with in or into; as, my old friend dropped in a moment.
q: Takes care to drop in when he thinks you are just seated.

senses.d: To fall or be depressed; to lower; as, the point of the spear dropped a little.
To fall short of a mark.
q: Often it drops or overshoots by the disproportion of distance.

senses.d: To be deep in extent; to descend perpendicularly; as, her main topsail drops seventeen yards.
The action of causing to drop or of letting drop; falling.
That which falls in drops; the excrement or dung of animals.
An unnatural collection of serous fluid in any serous cavity of the body, or in the subcutaneous cellular tissue.

Dropsy.etym: [OE. dropsie, dropesie, OF. idropisie, F. hydropisie, L. hydropisis, fr. Gr. � dropsy, fr. � water. See Water, and cf. Hydropsy.]

senses.d: The scum or refuse matter which is thrown off, or falls from, metals in smelting the ore, or in the process of melting; recrement.
Rust of metals.
Waste matter; any worthless matter separated from the better part; leavings; dregs; refuse.
q: All world's glory is but dross unclean.
At the devil's booth are all things sold, Each ounce of dross coats its ounce of gold.

Dross.etym: [AS. dros, fr. dreósan to fall. See Dreary.]

senses.d: Dryness; want of rain or of water; especially, such dryness of the weather as affects the earth, and prevents the growth of plants; aridity.
q: The drought of March hath pierced to the root.
In a drought the thirsty creatures cry.

senses.d: Thirst; want of drink.
Scarcity; lack.
q: A drought of Christian writers caused a dearth of all history.

Drought.etym: [OE. droght, drougth, dru”ð, AS. drugað, from drugian to dry. See Dry, and cf. Drouth, which shows the original final sound.]

senses.d: of Drive.
A collection of cattle driven, or cattle collected for driving; a number of animals, as oxen, sheep, or swine, driven in a body.
Any collection of irrational animals, moving or driving forward; as, a finny drove.
A crowd of people in motion.
q: Where droves, as at a city gate, may pass.

senses.d: A road for driving cattle; a driftway.
A narrow drain or channel used in the irrigation of land.
A broad chisel used to bring stone to a nearly smooth surface; — called also drove chisel.

Drove.etym: [AS. drāf, fr. drīfan to drive. See Drive.]

senses.d: To drive, as cattle or sheep, esp. on long journeys; to follow the occupation of a drover.
q: He's droving now with Conroy's sheep along the Castlereagh.

senses.d: To finish, as stone, with a drove or drove chisel.
To be suffocated in water or other fluid; to perish in water.
q: Methought, what pain it was to drown.

Drown.etym: [OE. drunen, drounen, earlier drunknen, druncnien, AS. druncnian to be drowned, sink, become drunk, fr. druncen drunken. See Drunken, Drink.]

senses.d: To overwhelm in water; to submerge; to inundate.
To deprive of life by immersion in water or other liquid.
To overpower; to overcome; to extinguish; — said especially of sound.
q: Most men being in sensual pleasures drowned.
My private voice is drowned amid the senate.

senses.d: State of being drowsy.
Inclined to drowse; heavy with sleepiness; lethargic; dozy.
q: Dapples the drowsy east with spots of gray.
To our age's drowsy blood Still shouts the inspiring sea.

senses.d: Disposing to sleep; lulling; soporific.
q: The drowsy hours, dispensers of all good.

senses.d: Dull; stupid.

Drowsy.syn: Sleepy; lethargic; dozy; somnolent; comatose; dull heavy; stupid.

senses.d: Intoxicated with, or as with, strong drink; inebriated; drunken; — never used attributively, but always predicatively; as, the man is drunk (not, a drunk man).
q: Be not drunk with wine, where in is excess.
Drunk with recent prosperity.

senses.d: Drenched or saturated with moisture or liquid.
q: I will make mine arrows drunk with blood.

Drunk.etym: [OE. dronke, drunke, dronken, drunken, AS. druncen. Orig. the same as drunken, p. p. of drink. See Drink.]

senses.d: A drunken condition; a spree.
One who habitually drinks strong liquors immoderately; one whose habit it is to get drunk; a toper; a sot.
q: The drunkard and glutton shall come to poverty.

senses.d: Overcome by strong drink; intoxicated by, or as by, spirituous liquor; inebriated.
q: Drunken men imagine everything turneth round.

senses.d: Saturated with liquid or moisture; drenched.
q: Let the earth be drunken with our blood.

senses.d: Pertaining to, or proceeding from, intoxication.
q: The drunken quarrels of a rake.

Drunken.etym: [AS. druncen, prop., that has drunk, p. p. of drincan, taken as active. See Drink, v. i., and cf. Drunk.]

senses.d: The state of being drunken with, or as with, alcoholic liquor; intoxication; inebriety; — used of the casual state or the habit.
q: The Lacedemonians trained up their children to hate drunkenness by bringing a drunken man into their company.

senses.d: Disorder of the faculties, resembling intoxication by liquors; inflammation; frenzy; rage.
q: Passion is the drunkenness of the mind.

Drunkenness.syn: Intoxication; inebriation; inebriety. — Drunkenness, Intoxication, Inebriation. Drunkenness refers more to the habit; intoxication and inebriation, to specific acts. The first two words are extensively used in a figurative sense; a person is intoxicated with success, and is drunk with joy. “This plan of empire was not taken up in the first intoxication of unexpected success.”

senses.d: Free from moisture; having little humidity or none; arid; not wet or moist; deficient in the natural or normal supply of moisture, as rain or fluid of any kind; — said especially: (a) Of the weather: Free from rain or mist.
q: The weather, we agreed, was too dry for the season.

senses.d: Of vegetable matter: Free from juices or sap; not succulent; not green; as, dry wood or hay.
Of animals: Not giving milk; as, the cow is dry.
Of persons: Thirsty; needing drink.
q: Give the dry fool drink.

senses.d: Of the eyes: Not shedding tears.
q: Not a dry eye was to be seen in the assembly.

senses.d: Of certain morbid conditions, in which there is entire or comparative absence of moisture; as, dry gangrene; dry catarrh.
Destitute of that which interests or amuses; barren; unembellished; jejune; plain.
q: These epistles will become less dry, more susceptible of ornament.

senses.d: Characterized by a quality somewhat severe, grave, or hard; hence, sharp; keen; shrewd; quaint; as, a dry tone or manner; dry wit.
q: He was rather a dry, shrewd kind of body.

senses.d: Exhibiting a sharp, frigid preciseness of execution, or the want of a delicate contour in form, and of easy transition in coloring.

Dry.etym: [OE. dru�e, druye, drie, AS. dryge; akin to LG. dröge, D. droog, OHG. trucchan, G. trocken, Icel. draugr a dry log. Cf. Drought, Drouth, 3d Drug.]

senses.d: To make dry; to free from water, or from moisture of any kind, and by any means; to exsiccate; as, to dry the eyes; to dry one's tears; the wind dries the earth; to dry a wet cloth; to dry hay.

Dry.etym: [AS. drygan; cf. drugian to grow dry. See Dry, a.]

senses.d: To grow dry; to become free from wetness, moisture, or juice; as, the road dries rapidly.
To evaporate wholly; to be exhaled; — said of moisture, or a liquid; — sometimes with up; as, the stream dries, or dries up.
To shrivel or wither; to lose vitality.
q: And his hand, which he put forth against him, dried up, so that he could not pull it in again to him.

senses.d: Owed, as a debt; that ought to be paid or done to or for another; payable; owing and demandable.
Justly claimed as a right or property; proper; suitable; becoming; appropriate; fit.
q: Her obedience, which is due to me.
With dirges due, in sad array, Slow through the churchway path we saw him borne.

senses.d: Such as (a thing) ought to be; fulfilling obligation; proper; lawful; regular; appointed; sufficient; exact; as, due process of law; due service; in due time.
Appointed or required to arrive at a given time; as, the steamer was due yesterday.
Owing; ascribable, as to a cause.
q: This effect is due to the attraction of the sun.

Due.etym: [OF. deu, F. dû, p. p. of devoir to owe, fr. L. debere. See Debt, Habit, and cf. Duty.]

senses.d: Directly; exactly; as, a due east course.

That which is owed; debt; that which one contracts to pay, or do, to or for another; that which belongs or may be claimed as a right; whatever custom, law, or morality requires to be done; a fee; a toll.
q: He will give the devil his due.
Yearly little dues of wheat, and wine, and oil.

senses.d: Right; just title or claim.
q: The key of this infernal pit by due . . . I keep.

senses.d: To endue.
A leader; a chief; a prince.
q: Hannibal, duke of Carthage.
All were dukes once, who were “duces” — captains or leaders of their people.

senses.d: In England, one of the highest order of nobility after princes and princesses of the royal blood and the four archbishops of England and Ireland.
In some European countries, a sovereign prince, without the title of king.

Duke.etym: [F. duc, fr. L. dux, ducis, leader, commander, fr. ducere to lead; akin to AS. teón to draw; cf. AS. heretoga (here army) an army leader, general, G. herzog duke. See Tue, and cf. Doge, Duchess, Ducat, Duct, Adduce, Deduct.]

senses.d: To play the duke.
q: Lord Angelo dukes it well in his absence.

senses.d: An instrument, having stretched metallic wires which are beaten with two light hammers held in the hands of the performer.
An ancient musical instrument in use among the Jews. Dan. iii. 5. It is supposed to be the same with the psaltery.

Dulcimer.etym: [It. dolcemele,r Sp. dulcemele, fr. L. dulcis sweet + melos song, melody, Gr. �; cf. OF. doulcemele. See Dulcet, and Melody.]

senses.d: Slow of understanding; wanting readiness of apprehension; stupid; doltish; blockish.
q: She is not bred so dull but she can learn.

senses.d: Slow in action; sluggish; unready; awkward.
q: This people's heart is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing.
O, help my weak wit and sharpen my dull tongue.

senses.d: Insensible; unfeeling.
q: Think me not So dull a devil to forget the loss Of such a matchless wife.

senses.d: Not keen in edge or point; lacking sharpness; blunt.
Not bright or clear to the eye; wanting in liveliness of color or luster; not vivid; obscure; dim; as, a dull fire or lamp; a dull red or yellow; a dull mirror.
Heavy; gross; cloggy; insensible; spiritless; lifeless; inert.
q: As turning the logs will make a dull fire burn, so changes of study a dull brain.

senses.d: Furnishing little delight, spirit, or variety; uninteresting; tedious; cheerless; gloomy; melancholy; depressing; as, a dull story or sermon; a dull occupation or period; hence, cloudy; overcast; as, a dull day.
q: Along life's dullest, dreariest walk.

Dull.syn: Lifeless; inanimate; dead; stupid; doltish; heavy; sluggish; sleepy; drowsy; gross; cheerless; tedious; irksome; dismal; dreary; clouded; tarnished; obtuse. See Lifeless.
Dull.etym: [AS. dol foolish; akin to gedwelan to err, D. dol mad, dwalen to wander, err, G. toll mad, Goth. dwals foolish, stupid, cf. Gr. � turbid, troubled, Skr. dhvr to cause to fall. Cf. Dolt, Dwale, Dwell, Fraud.]

senses.d: To deprive of sharpness of edge or point.
q: Borrowing dulls the edge of husbandry.

senses.d: To make dull, stupid, or sluggish; to stupefy, as the senses, the feelings, the perceptions, and the like.
q: Those she has Will stupefy and dull the sense a while.
Use and custom have so dulled our eyes.

senses.d: To render dim or obscure; to sully; to tarnish.
To deprive of liveliness or activity; to render heavy; to make inert; to depress; to weary; to sadden.
q: Attention of mind . . . wasted or dulled through continuance.

senses.d: To become dull or stupid.
Destitute of the power of speech; unable; to utter articulate sounds; as, the dumb brutes.
q: To unloose the very tongues even of dumb creatures.

senses.d: Not willing to speak; mute; silent; not speaking; not accompanied by words; as, dumb show.
q: This spirit, dumb to us, will speak to him.
To pierce into the dumb past.

senses.d: Lacking brightness or clearness, as a color.
q: Her stern was painted of a dumb white or dun color.

Dumb.etym: [AS. dumb; akin to D. dom stupid, dumb, Sw. dumb, Goth. dumbs; cf. Gr. � blind. See Deaf, and cf. Dummy.]

senses.d: To put to silence.
The excrement of an animal.

Dung.etym: [AS. dung; akin to G. dung, dünger, OHG. tunga, Sw. dynga; cf. Icel. dyngja heap, Dan. dynge, MHG. tunc underground dwelling place, orig., covered with dung. Cf. Dingy.]

senses.d: To manure with dung.
To immerse or steep, as calico, in a bath of hot water containing cow dung; — done to remove the superfluous mordant.
To void excrement.
A close, dark prison, common�, under ground, as if the lower apartments of the donjon or keep of a castle, these being used as prisons.
q: Down with him even into the deep dungeon.
Year after year he lay patiently in a dungeon.

Dungeon.etym: [OE. donjoun highest tower of a castle, tower, prison, F. donjon tower or platform in the midst of a castle, turret, or closet on the top of a house, a keep of a castle, LL. domnio, the same word as LL. dominus lord. See Dame, Don, and cf. Dominion, Domain, Demesne, Danger, Donjon.]

senses.d: To shut up in a dungeon.
A heap of dung.
Any mean situation or condition; a vile abode.
q: He . . . lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill.

senses.d: Major; in the major mode; as, C dur, that is, C major.

Dur.etym: [G., fr. L. durus hard, firm, vigorous.]

senses.d: Short form for Dura mater.
Able to endure or continue in a particular condition; lasting; not perishable or changeable; not wearing out or decaying soon; enduring; as, durable cloth; durable happiness.
q: Riches and honor are with me; yea, durable riches and righteousness.
An interest which from its object and grounds must be so durable.

Durable.syn: Lasting; permanent; enduring; firm; stable; continuing; constant; persistent. See Lasting.
Durable.etym: [L. durabilis, fr. durare to last: cf. F. durable. See Dure.]

senses.d: Hard; harsh; severe; rough; toilsome.
q: The winter is severe, and life is dure and rude.

Dure.etym: [L. durus; akin to Ir. & Gael. dur �, stubborn, W. dir certain, sure, cf. Gr. � force.]

senses.d: To last; to continue; to endure.
q: Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while.

Dure.etym: [F. durer, L. durare to harden, be hardened, to endure, last, fr. durus hard. See Dure, a.]

senses.d: of Dare. See Dare, v. i.
Fine, dry particles of earth or other matter, so comminuted that they may be raised and wafted by the wind; that which is crumbled to minute portions; fine powder; as, clouds of dust; bone dust.
q: Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.
Stop! — for thy tread is on an empire's dust.

senses.d: A single particle of earth or other matter.
The earth, as the resting place of the dead.
q: For now shall sleep in the dust.

senses.d: The earthy remains of bodies once alive; the remains of the human body.
q: And you may carve a shrine about my dust.

senses.d: Figuratively, a worthless thing.
q: And by the merit of vile gold, dross, dust.

senses.d: Figuratively, a low or mean condition.
q: raiseth up the poor out of the dust.

senses.d: Gold dust

Dust.etym: [AS. dust; cf. LG. dust, D. duist meal dust, OD. doest, donst, and G. dunst vapor, OHG. tunist, dunist, a blowing, wind, Icel. dust dust, Dan. dyst mill dust; perh. akin to L. fumus smoke, E. fume. √71.]

senses.d: To free from dust; to brush, wipe, or sweep away dust from; as, to dust a table or a floor.
To sprinkle with dust.
To reduce to a fine powder; to levigate.
That which is due; payment.
q: When thou receivest money for thy labor or ware, thou receivest thy duty.

senses.d: That which a person is bound by moral obligation to do, or refrain from doing; that which one ought to do; service morally obligatory.
q: Forgetting his duty toward God, his sovereign lord, and his country.

senses.d: Hence, any assigned service or business; as, the duties of a policeman, or a soldier; to be on duty.
q: With records sweet of duties done.
To employ him on the hardest and most imperative duty.
Duty is a graver term than obligation. A duty hardly exists to do trivial things; but there may be an obligation to do them.

senses.d: Specifically, obedience or submission due to parents and superiors.
Respect; reverence; regard; act of respect; homage.

The efficiency of an engine, especially a steam pumping engine, as measured by work done by a certain quantity of fuel; usually, the number of pounds of water lifted one foot by one bushel of coal (94 lbs. old standard), or by 1 cwt. (112 lbs., England, or 100 lbs., United States).
Tax, toll, impost, or customs; excise; any sum of money required by government to be paid on the importation, exportation, or consumption of goods.
An animal or plant which is much below the ordinary size of its species or kind; especially, a diminutive human being.

Dwarf.etym: [OE. dwergh, dwerf, dwarf, AS. dweorg, dweorh; akin to D. dwerg, MHG. twerc, G. zwerg, Icel. dvergr, Sw. & Dan. dverg; of unknown origin.]

senses.d: To hinder from growing to the natural size; to make or keep small; to stunt.
q: Even the most common moral ideas and affections . . . would be stunted and dwarfed, if cut off from a spiritual background.

senses.d: To become small; to diminish in size.
q: Strange power of the world that, the moment we enter it, our great conceptions dwarf.

senses.d: To delay; to linger.
To abide; to remain; to continue.
q: I 'll rather dwell in my necessity.
Thy soul was like a star and dwelt apart.

senses.d: To abide as a permanent resident, or for a time; to live in a place; to reside.
q: The parish in which I was born, dwell, and have possessions.
The poor man dwells in a humble cottage near the hall where the lord of the domain resides.

Dwell.syn: To inhabit; live; abide; sojourn; reside; continue; stay; rest.
Dwell.etym: [OE. dwellen, dwelien, to err, linger, AS. dwellan to deceive, hinder, delay, dwelian to err; akin to Icel. dvelja to delay, tarry, Sw. dväljas to dwell, Dan. dvæle to linger, and to E. dull. See Dull, and cf. Dwale.]

senses.d: To inhabit.
An inhabitant; a resident; as, a cave dweller.
Habitation; place or house in which a person lives; abode; domicile.
q: Hazor shall be a dwelling for dragons.
God will deign To visit oft the dwellings of just men.
Philip's dwelling fronted on the street.

senses.d: of Dwell.
To stain; to color; to give a new and permanent color to, as by the application of dyestuffs.
q: Cloth to be dyed of divers colors.
The soul is dyed by its thoughts.
He might truly be termed a legitimate son of the revenue system dyed in the wool.

senses.d: Color produced by dyeing.
Material used for dyeing; a dyestuff.
Same as Die, a lot.
In the act of dying; destined to death; mortal; perishable; as, dying bodies.
Of or pertaining to dying or death; as, dying bed; dying day; dying words; also, simulating a dying state.
The act of expiring; passage from life to death; loss of life.
